contributing.title: 🤝 Contributing
contributing.text: 🤝 Contributing This page is for someone who wants to change Go Renderer. At the end you will know where each part lives, how to build and test it, and how a change is proposed. The layout of the code Each folder is one idea, and dependencies point one way: the scene knows nothing of OpenGL. Folder What lives there Needs graphics , immediate , window Vectors and matrices, the immediate-mode Renderer contract, a program's window and loop plain Go scene , scene/sample , loaders The retained scene, glTF files, the sample island plain Go internal/shading What every backend's shaders agree on; the sources live in each backend plain Go internal/sceneplan What a frame draws, decided once for every backend; internal, as only the module's backends use it plain Go input , camera , draw2d , frameloop Input (what programs read, and the Feed backends write), the camera and its controllers, 2D draw lists, the clock plain Go opengl , opengl/overlay , windowloop The desktop backend: GLFW, OpenGL 4.1, the overlay cgo metal The Metal backend on macOS (Objective-C) cgo, macOS gles , browser , android OpenGL ES renderers, the web page, the Android activity WebAssembly or the NDK nintendo3ds The Nintendo 3DS, through citro3d TinyGo software , vulkan , webgpu Backends of the immediate-mode contract, to be built later: every function returns <backend>.not-implemented — failure Error codes shared by every package — viewer , cmd/… The viewer and the programs cgo docs/ These pages; docs/5-reference is generated — The bigger picture is in the architecture . Building and testing You need Go (the version in go.mod ) and the headers of troubleshooting . gofmt -l . # prints nothing when everything is formatted go vet ./... go test ./... Tests that need OpenGL open a hidden window, and skip themselves without a display. To run them on a computer with no screen, use Xvfb ( xvfb-run go test ./opengl ); the CI has no display, so it skips them. The examples in *_test.go ( ExampleFlatRenderer , ExampleState_Pressed …) are the guides' code: if a guide's code changes, change its example. After changing a public name or its comment, regenerate the reference: python3 docs/5-reference/generate.py What the CI checks .github/workflows/test.yaml runs on every push and pull request: Job Checks test gofmt , go vet ./... and go test ./... on Ubuntu, with the OpenGL, X11 and Wayland headers browser go vet with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm of every package a web page uses It does not build Metal (macOS), Android or the 3DS yet, and it does not draw frames. A change to those parts is tried by hand: say what you tried. .github/workflows/publish-docs.yaml publishes docs/ as a website on every push to main . Hand-written and AI-written code Part of this project is written by hand by its author, and part by an AI assistant under his direction. The README's AI disclosure lists which. Hand-written by the author: the immediate-mode Renderer contract (now immediate , with window ), the graphics maths, the first OpenGL work, and the software , vulkan , metal (its stubs) and webgpu backends. On 2026-10-22 the author asked the AI to refactor them to the guidelines (whole-word names, coded errors, no panics or prints); that refactoring is pending his review. Do not change them further without asking him. AI-written work goes on a feature/… branch, never on main . Its commits end with a Co-Authored-By: line, and the author merges it after review. Until then it is pending review. Proposing a change A small fix goes straight to a pull request. A change that spans several files or sessions starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/ , numbered in order: Part What it says Status Proposed, approved or built, with the author's approval of the proposal and of the plan Why The problem, with facts What A table of requirements, each with an id (R1, R2…) and how it is checked Out of scope What it will not do Open questions for the author The decisions only he can take Result What was built, filled in at the end The author approves the proposal before a plan is written, and the plan before code. The first one is towards version 1.0 . Writing docs Pages are for people: one task per guide, the shortest working code first, short sentences, and a picture where something is spatial. Every code block runs as shown. Update the docs in the same commit as the behaviour they describe.

get-started.title: Get started

sections.text: 2. Get Go Renderer and open the sample

get-started.text: Get started This page takes you from nothing to a window showing a 3D scene you built in Go, in about fifteen minutes. You need to know a little Go (packages, functions, structs); you need no graphics experience. What you will do Install Go and a C compiler, which the window needs. Get Go Renderer and open its sample island. Write a program of your own that shows a box on a square of grass. ⚠️ Go Renderer is an educational project, not a finished product: its API still changes from one week to the next. Pin the commit you build against. 1. Install the tools You need Why How Go 1.25 or later The language go.dev/dl , then go version A C compiler The window (GLFW) and OpenGL are reached through cgo Linux: gcc ; macOS: xcode-select --install ; Windows: MinGW-w64 on the PATH OpenGL 4.1 and its headers What draws on Linux and Windows (macOS draws through Metal) Linux (Debian, Ubuntu): sudo apt install libgl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev ; Fedora: sudo dnf install mesa-libGL-devel libXcursor-devel libXrandr-devel libXinerama-devel libXi-devel libXxf86vm-devel wayland-devel libxkbcommon-devel Check cgo is on: go env CGO_ENABLED should print 1 . 2. Get Go Renderer and open the sample Go Renderer is not published as versioned modules yet. Clone it into a folder that will hold your own programs too; later on, Go UI and Go UI for Android go beside it. mkdir workspace && cd workspace git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer cd go-renderer go run ./cmd/visor -sample island A window opens on a small made-up island. Drag with the left button to turn around it, scroll to come closer, press Tab to walk on it and N to jump to the night. Every control is in the viewer's page . 💡 No display? On a server or in a container, -capture island.png draws one frame into a picture instead, and xvfb-run go run ./cmd/visor -sample island -capture island.png gives it a screen to draw on. 3. Your first scene Make a module beside Go Renderer, and point it at your copy: cd .. && mkdir first-scene && cd first-scene go mod init example.com/first-scene go mod edit -require github.com/akrck02/go-renderer@v0.0.0 -replace github.com/akrck02/go-renderer=../go-renderer Write main.go : package main import ( "log" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/graphics" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/viewer" ) func main() { world := scene.New() // an empty scene with a sun and a sky ground := &scene.Mesh{ Positions: []float32{-20, 0, -20, 20, 0, -20, 20, 0, 20, -20, 0, 20}, // x, y, z of four corners Indices: []uint32{0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2}, // two triangles Material: &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: graphics.Vector{0.3, 0.6, 0.25, 1}}, Ground: true, // the walker can stand on it } ground.ComputeNormals() world.Nodes = append(world.Nodes, &scene.Node{Name: "ground", Transform: graphics.Identity(), Mesh: ground}) if err := viewer.Run(world, viewer.DefaultOptions(), "First scene", nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } go mod tidy go run . A green square in the sunlight: that is a scene. Three ideas carry everything else in Go Renderer: A scene.Scene holds what there is to draw: nodes placed in the world, each with a mesh (triangles) and a material (how its surface is shaded), and an environment (sun, sky, fog, water). You describe the scene once; the renderer uploads it to the graphics card and draws it every frame. This is a retained scene: to change it, you change the structs. viewer.Run opens the window, gives you cameras and draws until the window closes. The first lesson's island: a white tower on a green hill Where next If you want to… Read Learn step by step, building an island with a lighthouse, a forest, the sea and labels The tutorial Understand how it fits together Architecture Look up a type or a function The reference Put buttons and panels over your scene Go UI Open a scene made in Blender or Go Scene Builder Lesson 6: scenes from files ← Documentation · Tutorial →

guides/3ds.title: 🎮 On the Nintendo 3DS

sections.text: What is different about the PICA200

guides/3ds.text: 🎮 On the Nintendo 3DS Status: a first step (October 2026). Package nintendo3ds draws through the 3DS's graphics chip, the PICA200, with citro3d: cmd/triangle3ds turns a triangle of three colours on the top screen at 60 frames a second, and cmd/island3ds flies round the sample island with nintendo3ds.SceneRenderer . It runs as homebrew, from the Homebrew Launcher, built with a TinyGo that has a nintendo3ds target (a separate fork of TinyGo, not part of this repository). The triangle is checked in the Azahar emulator; the loading and planning figures below come from a New 3DS XL. How it fits together Layer What it does Your program Builds a scene and moves things with graphics ; the renderers plan each frame nintendo3ds The top screen, vertex shaders, vertex buffers and matrices, over citro3d (this package) citro3d, libctru devkitPro's libraries for the GPU and the system, reached through cgo TinyGo nintendo3ds Builds the program as a .3dsx for the Homebrew Launcher The rest of go-renderer is plain Go and already runs there: on the console, encoding/json , image/png , loaders.ReadScene and the sample island load, and planning a frame of the island takes under a millisecond. The tests of graphics , scene , internal/sceneplan , camera , draw2d , input and frameloop pass in the emulator. What is different about the PICA200 No fragment shaders. Vertex shaders are written in the PICA200's assembly ( .v.pica ) and assembled with devkitPro's picasso ; colours come out of a few fixed stages. nintendo3ds sets the first one to pass the vertex colour through. Matrices row by row, components backwards. citro3d stores a matrix as four rows, and each row as w, z, y, x. graphics.Matrix is column by column; nintendo3ds.GPUMatrix lays it out (tested on any computer). A screen on its side. The 3DS's screens are portrait panels turned a quarter turn, and depth runs from -1 to 0. nintendo3ds.OrthographicTilt is citro3d's Mtx_OrthoTilt for a right-handed view, as everywhere in go-renderer: what is visible lies between z = 0 and z = -far. cmd/triangle3ds checks it against citro3d's own on the console. Vertex buffers outside the Go heap. nintendo3ds.NewVertexBuffer copies vertices to the linear memory the GPU reads, so the garbage collector never scans them. The scene renderer nintendo3ds.SceneRenderer draws a scene.Scene the way gles does: lit meshes and instances, the light of the time of day, fog and translucent water, planned by internal/sceneplan . What changes on the PICA200: Light worked out on the processor. Lighting every vertex on the GPU held the sample island to 30 frames a second on a New 3DS XL: the GPU took 34 ms a frame, the processor 0.4 ms. Sun and sky change slowly, so nintendo3ds/bake.go lights each vertex once, when a mesh is uploaded (sun, sky and ground light, glow, flat by brightness, then the screen's gamma), and keeps its colour in four bytes: a vertex is 16 bytes instead of 40. A mesh is baked again only when the light, the mesh or its node's turn changes. nintendo3ds/shaders/baked.v.pica then only places each vertex and fogs it by its distance to the camera, linearly: 27 instructions instead of 95. A mesh keeps at most four bakes, one per way it is turned; past that the least recently drawn one is baked again, so a node that keeps turning doesn't fill linear memory. Moving nodes on the GPU. Baking is right for a landscape, wrong for a ship that turns every frame: each turn means a new bake. A node marked Moving ( scene.Node ) is drawn through the full shader instead, from a copy of the mesh uploaded once: in a test with sixty ships flying around the camera, a frame went from 40 ms of processor time to 16. No seabed without water. The planner measures the meshes under the water for the sea floor's light whenever one of them changes; a scene without water skips it, or a few dozen moving meshes were measured vertex by vertex every frame. Water on the GPU, on a coarser grid. Water's reflection of the sky depends on where the camera looks from, so water goes through the full shader, nintendo3ds/shaders/scene.v.pica (gles's scene shader done per vertex, with its smoothstep fog and the chip's lg2 and ex2 for gamma). The planner's water grid of 256 × 256 cells, made for the desktop's waves, was 131 072 of the island's 160 756 triangles; nintendo3ds asks for 32 × 32 ( Planner.WaterGridDivisions ), still fine near the camera for the fog. Not the chip's own fog. The PICA200 can fog in fixed function, from a table of 128 steps of the depth buffer; but depth is far from linear (with the near plane at 0.1 and the far one at 20 000, the whole island's fog would fall in the first step), so nintendo3ds fogs per vertex. OpenGL's matrices, turned. internal/sceneplan plans frames with OpenGL's clip space; one fixed matrix ( nintendo3ds.GPUViewProjection ) gives the PICA200's quarter turn and depth range. Turning graphics.OrthographicOpenGL with it gives nintendo3ds.OrthographicTilt (tested on any computer). 16-bit indices. Meshes with more than 65 535 vertices are drawn in pieces ( nintendo3ds/split.go ). Instances merged on the processor, as in gles : the merging moved to internal/sceneplan ( MergedBatch ), which both renderers share. Meshes in linear memory, uploaded once and again only when Dirty . The bottom screen nintendo3ds.FlatRenderer paints a draw2d.List (an interface: go-ui's, or a program's own) on the bottom screen, as gles.FlatRenderer does in browsers and on phones: opengl/overlay lays the list out as rectangles of one atlas of glyphs, icons and rounded corners, and they are drawn in one call. On the PICA200 the atlas is a texture of one byte per pixel (A8), which has to be laid out in the chip's own way: tiles of 8 × 8 pixels, from the bottom of the picture, Morton order inside each tile ( nintendo3ds/texture.go , tested on any computer); a colour stage then multiplies each rectangle's alpha by the atlas's coverage. Pictures ( draw2d images) are the overlay's second atlas, of straight RGBA pixels, tiled the same way as an RGBA8 texture (whose bytes the chip reads as alpha, blue, green, red); their rectangles multiply the picture by their colour and then by the coverage, which rounds their corners. Rectangles are drawn in runs, with or without a picture, in the list's order, so what is painted over what stays the same. Both atlases have to stay within the chip's 1024 × 1024 pixels, and a picture that changes uploads the whole pictures atlas again. The chip has no fragment shader to read one picture sharp and another blended, so a sharp picture ( draw2d.Image 's Sharp , for pixel art) makes its whole list read the pictures atlas at the nearest pixel: a game's top screen is sharp, the interface below stays smooth. Both screens are drawn in one frame: nintendo3ds.BeginFrame , then SceneRenderer.PaintStereo for the top screen and FlatRenderer.Paint for the bottom one, then nintendo3ds.EndFrame . ( Draw and DrawStereo begin and end a frame themselves, for a program with the top screen only.) go-3ds puts go-ui on the bottom screen this way. Point lights in 3D A scene's point lights ( scene.Scene.Lights ) are baked too: their light is added to the sun's when a mesh's colours are worked out, with the same fade as the other backends' shaders. Each draw takes the few lamps the planner chooses for it, and its colours depend on them and on where the mesh stands, so a lamp that stands still costs nothing a frame, and a lamp that moves bakes again the meshes it reaches (three in cmd/lamps3ds , which kept 60 frames a second in Azahar; the console is still to be measured). Light is worked out at the vertices, as everything here is: a lamp's pool shows on a floor only where it has vertices, so a floor of two triangles stays dark between its corners, and one cut into a grid (a terrain is one) shows it. Every node a mesh is drawn by under lamps keeps a bake of its own (up to 64 a mesh), since each stands in a different light. A node that moves under lamps without being marked Moving is baked again every frame it moves, its old bakes given back once the 64 are used: mark it Moving. A node marked Moving is lit on the GPU instead, by the sun, the sky and the four lamps the planner chose for it, at its vertices as a bake is (the turning cube in cmd/lamps3ds ). Instances (a forest) take the lamps that reach any of them, listed in a fixed order so that the camera moving does not bake them again. 2D lights A draw list's lights (see the overlay's guide ) are drawn as on the other backends: added into a picture of light, which then multiplies the screen. The chip has no fragment shader to fade a point light, so it reads the fade from a texture of sixteen discs , one for each inner share of the radius, made once at start: a light takes the nearest. The picture of light is a 256 × 128 texture the GPU draws into, half the top screen's resolution, and the chip's own blends add the lights and multiply by them. The ambient is painted into it as a rectangle of a constant colour, not cleared in: citro3d's clears run apart from the draws, before all of a frame's, so two lists lit in one frame (both screens) would share the last one's ambient. A list keeps its lights' corners between frames, as it keeps its rectangles'. Eight lights on the top screen keep 60 frames a second in Azahar, at about 3 ms a frame ( cmd/lights3ds ); the console itself is still to be measured. Both screens, and the controls The API names the screens for what they are to any program, not for where the 3DS has them: the top one is the main Screen ( nintendo3ds.OpenScreen ), the bottom one the SecondScreen ( OpenSecondScreen , SecondScreenWidth ), the 3D slider the DepthSlider , the circle pad and the C-stick a reading's Stick and RightStick . The 3DS's own words stay in the comments, for whoever knows the console. nintendo3ds.Surface is either screen: SceneRenderer.PaintOn and FlatRenderer.PaintOn draw a scene or an interface on the top one or the bottom one (which has a depth buffer, so a scene can be shown where it can be touched). go-ui's window for the 3DS uses it to swap the screens with SELECT. nintendo3ds.ReadControls reads the buttons, the circle pad and the touch screen, and nintendo3ds.Controls turns them into input.State : the cross is the arrow keys, L and R minus and plus, A Enter, B Escape and the system's back, the circle pad the stick ( input.State.Stick ) and the touch screen the pointer (tested on any computer). The cameras read the stick as a game's player moves: the orbit and the plan move their target over the ground, the walk walks. The C-stick (a New 3DS's) and the gyroscope are services of their own, started only when a game asks: nintendo3ds.StartMotionControls starts both and says which did, and from then on each reading has RightStick() (the C-stick, from -1 to 1, as Stick() for the circle pad) and Gyroscope (how fast the console turns, in degrees a second). StopMotionControls stops them, as the gyroscope uses power. nintendo3ds.OpenScreen asks a New 3DS for its fast mode (804 MHz and the second-level cache): libctru leaves the processor at 268 MHz otherwise, a third of what it can do. FlatRenderer keeps the corners of every list it paints, one buffer per list painted in a frame. A list that draws the same as the frame before (its fingerprint says so) is drawn again from them, without being laid out: an interface that does not change costs the processor almost nothing. Each rectangle is four corners and two triangles of a fixed index buffer, written straight into linear memory. nintendo3ds.ReadMemory tells how much of the console's memory is free: the linear memory the GPU reads, the video memory and the application's region, which holds the Go heap. It is cheap enough to read every second, for a program that shows its own resources. Memory TinyGo's collector does not move what it keeps, so garbage made over and over fragments the heap until a large block no longer fits. nintendo3ds keeps its bake and upload buffers and reuses them, and lets go of a mesh, on the GPU and in its caches, once it has not been drawn for a second: a program that makes its scene again (a plan whose machines change colour) leaves nothing behind. Keeping a frame short Measure before changing anything: go-ui's window.LastFrameTimes splits a frame into waiting for the GPU, painting the scene, what is drawn over it, the interface, and handing the frame over. The processor's time to prepare an interface is not where it costs; laying it out as rectangles is. The overlay costs by the rectangle. FlatRenderer lays a list out only when it draws something else than the frame before; an interface that stands still costs almost nothing. A part that changes every frame (a clock, an animation, figures read every second) makes its whole list be laid out again: keep it small, or update it seldom. Pixel-art shapes are many rectangles. A window with an outline, a frame, rounded corners in steps and a shadow is fifteen or more; a key with a lip, twenty. They are cheap while they stand still and dear on the frames they change. A graph is two rectangles a column (the filled part and the track), not one a block. The scene's own drawing goes in both eyes. With 3D on, World.Overlay.Drawing is painted twice: keep it to a sight and a label. Waiting for the GPU is the time the PICA200 took for the frame before: triangles, filled pixels and blending. Fewer triangles far away, and fewer layers of transparent rectangles, lower it. The New 3DS's fast mode is on: nintendo3ds.OpenScreen asks for it. Garbage TinyGo's collector stops the program while it runs, so a frame should make as little garbage as it can. nintendo3ds , the overlay and the scene planner make none in a steady frame: their lists and buffers are kept and filled again. What a program builds every frame is the rest; tinygo-3ds's NINTENDO3DS.md lists what makes garbage in TinyGo that would not in Go, and how to find it. In 3D The top screen shows a picture for each eye when the 3D slider is up. SceneRenderer.DrawStereo plans the frame once, for the camera between the eyes, and draws it twice: each eye's camera is moved sideways by half the separation, looking the same way, and its picture is shifted so that what lies at the focal distance falls on the plane of the screen ( nintendo3ds.EyeViewProjection , tested on any computer); nearer comes out of the screen, farther goes in. nintendo3ds.DepthSlider reads the slider; a program usually makes the separation grow with it. Drawing twice doubles the GPU's work: the sample island goes from about 5 to 10 ms a frame. A problem a frame works around (a texture that outgrew the GPU's largest) is written as a warning: line on the console. Elsewhere it goes to the program's log/slog logger; on the 3DS that package alone would add about 42 KB to every .3dsx , so the overlay leaves it out there. Building tinygo build -target=nintendo3ds -o triangle3ds.3dsx ./cmd/triangle3ds Copy the .3dsx to /3ds/ on the SD card and open it from the Homebrew Launcher. Not yet How fast the renderer is on the console with the coarser water (baking the light alone went from 30 to 36 frames a second: the chip was held back by the number of triangles more than by the shader). Positions in shorts and fewer triangles far away are the next steps if it is not enough. A sun that moves all the time bakes the meshes again whenever a colour would change by a step. Reading scenes from the SD card: TinyGo's os has no file system there yet, so scenes are embedded in the program. Collection pauses: about 170 ms in the emulator for an 80 MB heap with 30 MB alive. Making little garbage every frame keeps them rare.

guides/android.title: 📱 On Android
guides/android.text: 📱 On Android Status: a first step (October 2026). Package android runs a Go Renderer program as an Android application: Go UI's interfaces, and the 3D scene under them, draw on an Android 16 emulator and on a Pixel 6 Pro. There is no golang.org/x/mobile, and no Java but one small class for screen readers: the program is a shared library that Android's own NativeActivity loads. Go UI's docs/android.md has the screenshots, the build and what was tested. How it fits together Layer What it does Your program The same code as on the desktop and in a browser Go UI window window.Run : an interface, and a scene under it android The activity, its window and touches, a thread that draws (this package) gles FlatRenderer and SceneRenderer , over gles.Functions (shared with browsers) Android NativeActivity loads the program, a shared library built with the NDK Piece Where The library's entry point and the activity's callbacks, EGL, the screen's density android/activity.c The callbacks handed to the drawing thread; starting main android/activity.go , android/callmain The drawing thread: waiting, the frame cap, steps and frames android/loop.go Touches and a hardware keyboard android/input.go ; fingers as the pointer in input.TouchPointer OpenGL ES, called directly android/gl.go The system's bars and theme, and the wallpaper's palettes, through JNI android/system.c , android/palettes.go What a screen reader (TalkBack) reads, and what it asks android/screenreader.go , screenreader.c , android/java/ScreenReader.java The text the on-screen keyboard edits: words, suggestions, the word being composed android/keyboard.go , android/textinput.go , textinput.c , android/java/TextInput.java Starting. Android loads the library and calls ANativeActivity_onCreate . Go does not run main.main in a shared library by itself, so the first time the library finds it by name and calls it ( callmain , a few lines of assembly: a package with cgo cannot hold Go assembly). It also hands Go the application's own folder, which becomes os.TempDir : the Go runtime read the environment when the library loaded, before C could set it. One drawing thread. Android calls the activity's callbacks on its own interface thread; they are handed to a thread of the program's own, which holds the OpenGL ES context and an Android looper. The looper wakes it for touches (the input queue is attached to it, so the looper is prepared to accept a queue with no callback), for the activity's news, for a frame a control asked for ( RequestFrame ) and for Wake ; in between it sleeps. When Android takes a window or an input queue away, its callback waits until the drawing thread has let it go, as Android requires. Frames. Like the desktop and the browser, it draws only when something happens, and a frame that would look like the one shown is not drawn, except on a new surface (back from the background), which is empty until painted: a screen with no scene stayed black there. After a rotation, EGL's surface keeps the old size until a frame has been shown, so the window paints at once and once more at the new size; before, a rotated screen kept the old frame, laid out for the other way round. The bars and the cutout. CurrentInsets gives what the status bar, the gesture or navigation bar and a camera's cutout cover, on every side: a phone on its side has its cutout at the left or the right. A package whose theme sets windowLayoutInDisplayCutoutMode to shortEdges paints beside the cutout too, and keeps its controls clear of it with those insets. It draws at most Options.MaxFramesPerSecond a second, 60 by default: a phone refreshes at 90 or 120 Hz, and a finger dragging a 3D view sends touch events far more often. When the context is new (the first frame, or back from the background), the drawing function is told, and makes its renderers again. When it closes. The Go runtime writes a crash's report (with the failing goroutine's stack) to the application's folder; LastCrash gives it to the next run, and Graphics names the phone's OpenGL ES and GPU. A phone shows a person nothing when an application closes. What the program writes to its standard output and error (a log.Fatal , a panic) goes to Android's log a line at a time, under the tag Go ( adb logcat -s Go ), with a line when the runtime starts and one when it starts main . The wallpaper's colours. On Android 12 and later the phone makes five palettes from its wallpaper ( system_accent1_0 … system_neutral2_1000 , the colours its own applications use). SystemPalettes returns them as last read: with the theme, when the activity comes back or its configuration changes, which is when they change. An older phone has none, and says so. The window's news can come first. Android may hand the activity its window before the drawing thread has its looper: telling it then wakes nothing. The thread wakes its own looper once as it makes it, so the first wait reads what is already there. Without that, a OnePlus 7 Pro (Android 10) stayed on a blank window, its drawing thread asleep with the window's news unread. Why its own activity The first step used golang.org/x/mobile (gomobile), which gives a Go program an activity, an EGL surface and its events with no Java. It worked, with two costs: Its OpenGL bindings are compiled against the OpenGL ES 2 headers, and it asks for a version 2 context. Go Renderer's gles keeps to OpenGL ES 2 for that reason (see in a web browser ), which WebGL2 also accepts. Each OpenGL call goes to another thread through a channel, three at a time. A CPU profile taken on the phone found it was about two thirds of what a frame cost: runtime.futex 34 %, libc 17 %, cgocall 13 %, the scheduler 11 %. With direct calls, on a Pixel 6 Pro: With x/mobile Its own activity Dragging the sample island for 10 s (Go UI's example) 82 % of a core 41 % A 3D scene of a few hundred moving models, playing 84 % 31 % Idle 0 0 The package asks for an OpenGL ES 3 context when the phone has one (both phones tried give 3.x), so instanced drawing can come later behind the same gles.Functions . Building CC=$ANDROID_NDK_HOME/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/darwin-x86_64/bin/aarch64-linux-android26-clang \ CGO_ENABLED=1 GOOS=android GOARCH=arm64 \ go build -buildmode=c-shared -ldflags=-extldflags=-Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -o libprogram.so . A package then holds lib/arm64-v8a/libprogram.so and a manifest whose activity is android.app.NativeActivity , with android.app.lib_name set to program . For a screen reader it also holds classes.dex , compiled from android/java/ScreenReader.java ( javac , then the build tools' d8 ), and says android:hasCode="true" ; without it, the program runs with no screen reader. Go UI for Android's go-ui-apk does it all with the Android SDK's tools. The 16 KB alignment is what phones with 16 KB memory pages (Android 15 and later) need. Typing and notifications The on-screen keyboard. ShowKeyboard(typing) brings the keyboard up while a text field is typed in and puts it away after (Go UI's window calls it with Context.Typing ). NativeActivity's own call for it does nothing on recent Androids, so the window's InputMethodManager is asked through JNI, with the NDK's call as a fallback. A finger coming down while typing asks again, for a person who put the keyboard away and touched the field to have it back. Every key, from either keyboard, is given the character Android's own KeyEvent.getUnicodeChar says it types: any layout's letters, accented ones, digits and symbols. A package whose activity has windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize" shrinks while the keyboard is up, so what is typed in stays in sight. The window itself keeps its size; what changes is how much of its bottom the keyboard covers, which Android tells through onContentRectChanged : the insets are read again then, as the keyboard comes and goes. What the keyboard edits. A phone's keyboard does not type key by key: it edits the focused view's text through an InputConnection . It suggests words from the text around the caret, keeps the word it is still making underlined ( composing : a prediction, a Chinese or Japanese reading) until it commits it or a suggestion replaces it, and deletes around the caret. NativeActivity's view offers no connection, so the package carries a small view of its own, TextInput.java : a pixel in the corner, drawing nothing, focused while a field is typed in. It keeps a copy of the field's text for the keyboard and tells Go the whole state after each edit. the program's field TextInput.java (a copy of the text) the keyboard EditText(field, text, secret) ──────► set: the text, the caret, the composing ──► suggests from it TakeTextEdit(field) ◄────── edited: the whole text after each edit ◄── commits, composes, deletes Both sides edit at once (a hardware key goes to Go; a word goes to Java), so each of the keyboard's edits is numbered: Go's text says which edit it comes after, and a text from before the latest one is dropped, as the keyboard has typed since. An edit of a field no longer typed in is dropped too. Positions cross as UTF-16 units, as Java counts them, and become characters in Go: an emoji is one character and two units. A secret field asks for a password's keyboard, with no suggestions; Enter is the keyboard's Done , which reaches Go as the Enter key. A package without the class (made by an older tool) types key by key, as before. Tried on the Android 14 emulator with Android's own keyboard: "harb" composes underlined, its suggestion "harbour" replaces it, a hardware key and the keyboard's backspace edit the same text, and a password gets no suggestions. A finger lifted leaves nothing under it. After the frame where a finger is lifted ( input.TouchPointer ), the pointer goes off the window ( State.PointerLeaves ): with a mouse, the control under the pointer is lit, and on a touch screen the last control touched stayed so. Notifications. Notify(id, title, text) puts a notification in the phone's shade, as other applications' are, on a channel of the program's ( Channel , which the application's settings list): touching it opens the program. Android 13 and later show them only once the person allows it: NotificationsAllowed tells, and AskForNotifications shows Android's question (the package names android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS ). Tried on a OnePlus 7 Pro (Android 10). Buzzes. Feel(feeling) gives one of the buzzes Android's own views give ( View.performHapticFeedback on the window's view): FeelingTick for something chosen, FeelingConfirm when something went through, FeelingReject when something went wrong or needs a look, FeelingLongPress when a touch becomes a long press ( FeelLongPress() too). It follows the person's setting for touch feedback and needs no permission. Confirm and reject came with Android 11: before it, a confirm is a tick and a reject the long press's buzz, the strongest the older phones have. No black before the first frame. Android takes its starting screen away as soon as the window is there, while the program's first frame may still be on its way (the Go runtime starting, fonts read). The window is cleared to the theme's plain white or black the moment its surface opens, so the starting screen gives way to a plain background, never to black. The phone's services. TextScale() is the person's text size (Settings › Display › Font size), read with the theme. The input state's clipboard is Android's own ClipboardManager , so text fields copy and paste with other applications. OpenLink(link) opens a link in the application that shows it (an ACTION_VIEW intent: a web page, mailto: , tel: , geo: ), and Share(title, text) offers a text through the system's sheet ( ACTION_SEND in a chooser). Options.Hidden is called on the drawing thread when the activity pauses: Android may end the program after that without a word, so it is the moment to keep what must survive. Options.Shown is called when it resumes (at the start too): the moment to play again a sound Hidden stopped. Films. OpenVideo(path) decodes a film's pictures with the phone's own decoders (the NDK's MediaCodec : MP4 and WebM, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, AV1), a step at a time from the goroutine that draws: Advance(until, pixels) decodes up to a moment and copies the picture due by then. The pictures come out in the decoder's own buffers, laid out as its output format says: the three planes one after another (I420, from software decoders such as the emulator's) or the luma then the chroma interleaved (NV12, from most hardware decoders), with rows padded to the decoder's liking. YUVPlanes.ToRGBA turns them into colours, in video's limited range, with the high-definition standard's weights from 720 lines up. Drawing into an AImageReader looked simpler but, on a OnePlus 7 Pro, the decoder then wrote its pictures compressed in its maker's own layout, which no processor reads: green noise. The sound is not played yet. The back gesture. Android's back (the gesture from a side, or the button) is the program's: the window records it ( State.PressBack ), and the part of the program the person is in answers it ( State.TakeBack , Go UI's Context.Back ): a dialog closes, a screen goes back to the one before. A back nobody answers sends the program to the background ( moveTaskToBack ), as a phone's own applications do at their first screen; it comes back as it was. When the on-screen keyboard is up, the back puts it away first, as everywhere on Android. Screen readers A screen reader (TalkBack, or any accessibility service) reads what a view holds through the view's AccessibilityNodeProvider , an abstract Java class: JNI can call Java, but cannot make a subclass, and a proxy only stands in for interfaces. So the package carries one class, ScreenReader.java , embedded in package android/java for the tool that compiles it. Everything else stays in Go and C. the program's interface the nodes of a frame: what each is, where, its state (go-ui makes them) android (Go) ShowAccessibleNodes: sent only when they change, in screen pixels, text as UTF-16 screenreader.c the Java arrays, and the class's native methods ScreenReader.java a virtual view per node, answering TalkBack; its focus and actions back to Go Installing. Each time Android makes the activity (a rotation too), ANativeActivity_onCreate loads the class through the activity's class loader and puts a provider on the view NativeActivity shows. It listens for accessibility turning on and off: ScreenReaderOn tells, and while it is off the program makes no nodes at all. A finger exploring the screen. While TalkBack is on, Android turns a finger into hover events, which reach the input queue like touches. They go to Java, which finds the smallest node under the finger and tells TalkBack it came onto it; TalkBack reads it and puts its focus there. What TalkBack asks. A double tap is a click on the node it is on, a double tap held a long click, a swipe with two fingers or the volume keys on a slider a scroll, and text the screen reader types, pastes or dictates into a field replaces its text ( ReaderSetText , with the action's Text ). Java passes them on ( TakeReaderActions ) and wakes the drawing thread; the interface does them in the next frame. Where TalkBack's focus is ( ScreenReaderFocus ) comes the same way, for the program to ring it: the window is a native surface, where Android draws no ring of its own. Text as UTF-16. JNI's own UTF-8 is not quite UTF-8: an emoji in a label sent that way stops a program. Labels cross as Java keeps them, and so does a field's new text on its way back. Not yet Keyboards for Chinese and Japanese, which compose the same way, are not tried yet. Long presses. Instanced drawing with OpenGL ES 3, and the full scene renderer (shadows, sky, waves) on phones. ← All the documentation

guides/architecture.title: 🧭 Architecture
guides/architecture.text: 🧭 Architecture Go Renderer is a small renderer written in Go to learn how 3D graphics work from the inside. It offers two ways to draw: Immediate mode : your program says "draw this triangle, this image, this model" every frame. Simple, and good for learning the pipeline. A retained scene : a whole world (terrain, towns, forests, sea, sky) is loaded once from a glTF file and the renderer draws it every frame, as fast as it can. This is what the viewer and the simulators use. The renderer only draws. It does not know what a town or a season is: other programs change the scene, and it shows the result. Packages Package Role graphics Vectors, matrices, coordinate spaces and transformations window A program in a window: what the window is ( Options ), what runs every frame ( Callbacks : a fixed-step Update , Draw ) and what both share ( Application ) immediate The hand-written immediate-mode contract: Renderer , Mesh , Model opengl , metal Backends behind the contract ( opengl.Window and opengl.Renderer ); OpenGL is the complete one. metal also has FlatWindow and FlatRenderer , which draw a flat interface through Metal on macOS ( design ) software , vulkan , webgpu Backends behind the contract that will be built later. Until then every function returns its package's NotImplemented code ( software.not-implemented , vulkan.not-implemented , webgpu.not-implemented ), checked with errors.Is failure Error codes: failure.Define declares one, failure.Wrap adds details; check them with errors.Is internal/shading What the backends' shaders agree on (a sharp picture's offset, ambient light, the backdrop blur's weights); each backend keeps its own shader sources (the OpenGL ones in opengl/*_shaders.go ) internal/sceneplan Decides what a frame of a scene draws, for any backend: the draw commands in order, culling and levels of detail, instance batches, where the shadow and seabed maps look scene/sample A made-up island that uses every feature the renderers draw, for tests and comparisons gles Renderers written once for OpenGL ES (WebGL2 in browsers, Android): a flat FlatRenderer and a simple SceneRenderer , over a small interface each platform implements ( in a browser ) browser Built only for WebAssembly: a canvas as the window, its events as input, WebGL2, and the loop over requestAnimationFrame android Built only for Android: the program as a NativeActivity's shared library, its window, touches and drawing thread, direct OpenGL ES calls ( on Android ) frameloop The fixed-step clock and update step that the desktop and browser loops share windowloop The window loop both OpenGL and Metal use: GLFW events and input, drawing on demand, the fixed-step clock, redrawing while resizing, the pointer's shape and lock scene The retained, backend-independent scene, with its overlay (labels, header, notices) loaders glTF 2.0 loading, including the renderer's extras opengl/overlay Lays out the overlay as rectangles of one atlas of glyphs, icons and rounded corners (no graphics context needed) draw2d A list of flat shapes (rounded rectangles, shadows, text, icons, pictures, clips, layers) to paint over the view, filled by a program or an interface library input A backend-independent snapshot of keyboard and mouse state: held keys and buttons, presses and releases, double clicks, typed characters, clipboard, pointer shape, and what an interface claimed camera The Camera and its controllers: orbit, walk and map; the ray through a point of the window ( RayThrough ) and where it meets a plane or the ground viewer The interactive explorer behind cmd/visor cmd/visor The viewer as a program The immediate-mode contract An application implements an update and a draw, and calls the renderer every frame: type Renderer interface { RenderPolygon(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, coordinates []graphics.Vector, shader *string, fill bool) error RenderTriangle(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, coordinates []graphics.Vector, shader *string, fill bool) error RenderRectangle(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, centre graphics.Vector, width, height float32, shader *string, fill bool) error RenderImage(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, bytes []byte, centre graphics.Vector, width, height float32, shader *string) error RenderObject(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, vertices []graphics.Vector, shader *string) error RenderModel(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, model *Model, shader *string) error SetMatrices(projection, view, model graphics.Matrix) } Coordinates can be given in local, world or viewport space; the backend does the transformations. window.Application.Update runs at a fixed time step before every frame, so motion does not depend on the frame rate. An application that is mostly still (a window of controls) sets DrawOnDemand : the loop then sleeps in glfw.WaitEvents and draws only when input arrives, when the program asked for a frame with input.State.RequestFrame (a caret's next blink), or when another goroutine calls opengl.Wake (or windowloop.Wake ). Each such frame runs one update step, and a frame with input is followed by one more so hover looks catch up with a layout that just changed. Idle, it uses no processor. Application.Unchanged lets an application say a frame would repeat the last one shown (Go UI compares draw2d.List.Fingerprint ), and the loop then neither draws nor presents it. In the default, continuous mode a frame is drawn only after an update step, so a display faster than the updates does not draw the same picture twice. While a window is being resized, it is redrawn from GLFW's refresh callback, since macOS holds the loop until the mouse is let go. This loop lives in windowloop and knows nothing about the graphics interface: windowloop.Run takes the window, the application and a function that draws and shows one frame. The OpenGL backend and the Metal flat window both use it, so they behave the same way. The retained scene scene.Scene is a description of a 3D scene that does not depend on any backend: Nodes with transforms, children, names and tags (the glTF extras), drawing meshes. Meshes with positions, per-vertex normals and colours, indices and a material : lit , unlit , water or waterfall , with an optional procedural pattern (cobbles, masonry, plaster, shingles, planks, grass), a glow, a sway (how much the wind bends it) and a depth bias. Instances : one mesh drawn many times (GPU instancing), each copy with its transform and tint. Levels of detail : simpler versions of a mesh for when it looks small on screen. The environment : sun, sky, fog, water plane, wind, snow and foliage tint, and the vertical exaggeration. scene.Sky describes the sky over a whole day, and Environment.Daylight() derives, from the sun's height, the sky colours and the light of the moment (sun by day, moon by night). Meshes and instances can be marked Dirty so a simulation changes them and the backend uploads them again; Instances.MarkChanged(indices...) uploads only the instances that changed. GroundHeight(x, z) answers the height of the walkable meshes through a grid index. Loading loaders.LoadScene reads glTF 2.0 ( .glb or .gltf ): the node hierarchy, COLOR_0 , quantized attributes ( KHR_mesh_quantization : integer positions, normals, colours and indices), EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing (with a _COLOR per instance), and the renderer's extras : environment, sky, water, material kinds, levels of detail and walkable ground. loaders.ReadScene reads the same from a .glb 's content (any io.Reader ), for programs with no file system (a web page) or that carry their scene inside them. The scene renderers There are two, which draw the same frame: opengl.SceneRenderer and, on macOS, metal.SceneRenderer (the viewer chooses with -backend ; Metal by default on macOS). What a frame draws is decided once, in internal/sceneplan , which makes no graphics calls; each backend only uploads and draws that plan, with shaders that are faithful translations of each other. Their captures of the sample island match except for rounding and where two surfaces lie in the same plane ( cmd/visor 's TestMetalDrawsTheSceneLikeOpenGL ; measurements ). Each uploads each mesh once and draws instanced geometry in a single call, so a forest of a hundred thousand trees costs a few draw calls. Every frame goes through the same passes: Culling. Instances are kept in grid cells; cells outside the view frustum are skipped, and each cell picks a level of detail by its size on screen. Shadows. A shadow map fitted around the camera target, rendered from the sun, filtered with PCF ( ShadowSettings ). Sky. A procedural day gradient, twilight glow, stars that turn around the celestial pole, a moon with phases that lights the night, clouds that drift with the wind, constellations, or skybox images (equirectangular panoramas or six cube faces, one for the day and one for the night). Scene. Sun or moon light with sky ambient, fog, procedural surface patterns, glowing materials, snow on surfaces facing up, the season's tint on foliage, wind sway on plants. Water. Coloured by its depth, read from a top-down depth map of the ground that is rendered once per scene (and again when a ground mesh is Dirty ); waves, foam on the shore, tides that rise and fall differently from place to place, and waterfalls. Overlay. Labels over things in the world, a header and fading notices, and on top of them a free 2D drawing ( Overlay.Drawing , a draw2d.List ), in screen space with one texture atlas and one draw call (see the overlay ). Input, cameras and the viewer The window backend feeds input with a snapshot of the keyboard and the mouse: what is held, and what happened since the last update step (keys and buttons that went down or up, keys repeated by the system, characters typed, which click of a double click a press was). An interface drawn over the view can claim the mouse or the keyboard for a step ( ClaimMouse , ClaimKeyboard ); the viewer gives its cameras and shortcuts State.Unclaimed() , a copy without what was claimed, so a slider being dragged does not turn the camera. camera.Orbit (drag, pan, zoom), camera.Walk (first person on the ground) and camera.Map (a flat map, from above or isometric) turn it into a camera placement. A game pad is read by position, whatever its maker: PadA is always the bottom face button. What is printed on that button is not: A on an Xbox pad, ✕ on a PlayStation pad, B on a Nintendo pad. State.PadLayout() says which ( XboxLayout , PlayStationLayout , NintendoLayout ), so a game can write a hint with the name the player sees. The window loop sets it when a pad connects, from the USB vendor in the pad's GUID ( PadLayoutFromGUID ); the browser from the vendor in the Gamepad API's id ( PadLayoutFromName ). A vendor it does not know, Android and the 3DS read as an Xbox pad: the layout most pads copy (and the 3DS's own buttons already carry Nintendo's names). On a touch screen the first finger is the pointer ( input.TouchPointer ): it moves the cursor and holds the left button, so a tap is a click and a drag turns the orbit. A second finger lets the button go, and every finger on the screen is in State.Touches . input.TwoFingers turns two fingers, from one step to the next, into a Gesture : how much they spread apart, how much they turned and how far their middle moved. Orbit.Gesture follows it as a map does: the ground between the fingers stays between them while they pinch, twist and move; Walk.Steer walks as an on-screen stick says and Walk.Turn looks around by a finger's movement. The interface's copy ( Unclaimed ) keeps the touches, so a program can tell which finger is on its own control. A camera with an OrthographicHeight is drawn without perspective: it shows that many scene units from the bottom to the top of the window, and shadows and levels of detail follow that size instead of the distance to the camera. The viewer package puts it all together: cameras, sun, fog, shadows, vertical exaggeration, headless captures and benchmarks. viewer.Run takes an optional update function called at every fixed step, so another program can change the scene while it is shown. Without one, the viewer draws on demand: only while input arrives, a key is held or the view is still moving. viewer.Edit is for programs that edit the scene: they run at every step with a viewer.View that turns the pointer into a point on the ground, and the viewer still draws on demand. Simulations The renderer draws the scene as it is and knows nothing about simulations. Moving things, wind gusts, drifting clouds, the day cycle or growing cities live in the sibling project Go Simulator , which changes the scene through viewer.Run . The renderer only reads the state they leave: node transforms, Environment.Wind , Sky.Clouds.Offset , the sun direction, the snow line and the foliage tint. ← All the documentation

guides/drawing-in-2d.text: ✏️ Drawing in 2D This guide is for a Go programmer who wants flat shapes on screen: a card, a label, a line drawing. At the end you will know every command of a draw2d.List and how to show one. The shortest program A draw2d.List is plain data: a list of shapes for one frame. A renderer paints it. Here a window draws nothing else, so it uses opengl.FlatRenderer : package main import ( "log" "runtime" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/draw2d" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/opengl" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/opengl/overlay" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/window" ) func init() { runtime.LockOSThread() } // windows live on the main thread func main() { var renderer *opengl.FlatRenderer var drawing draw2d.List var tower draw2d.Path tower.MoveTo(0, 10) tower.LineTo(1, 0) tower.LineTo(3, 0) tower.LineTo(4, 10) tower.Close() app := &window.Application{ Options: window.Options{Title: "Drawing in 2D", Width: 480, Height: 240, FlatOnly: true}, Input: input.NewState(), } app.Draw = func(app *window.Application) error { if renderer == nil { // the OpenGL context exists from the first frame var err error if renderer, err = opengl.NewFlatRenderer(overlay.Fonts{}); err != nil { return err } } drawing.Reset() card := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 24, Width: 260, Height: 64} drawing.Shadow(card, 12, 12, 4, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f33")) drawing.Rectangle(card, 12, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff"), draw2d.MustHex("#dde3ea"), 1) drawing.Icon("lightbulb", 44, 48, 16, draw2d.MustHex("#e0a020")) drawing.Text("The lighthouse is lit", 70, 61, 14, draw2d.Medium, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) drawing.Stroke(&tower, 360, 40, 14, 3, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) state := app.Input scale := float32(state.FramebufferWidth) / float32(state.WindowWidth) // 2 on a high-density screen renderer.Draw(&drawing, draw2d.MustHex("#eef2f6"), state.FramebufferWidth, state.FramebufferHeight, scale) return nil } if err := (&opengl.Window{}).Run(app); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } go run . opens the window above. Its body is ExampleFlatRenderer in opengl/example_test.go , so go test ./opengl checks that it still compiles. A few things to notice: Coordinates are layout pixels from the top-left corner, like the cursor in input.State . The renderer multiplies them by scale , so a 14-pixel text has the same size on every screen. The list is filled again every frame. Reset empties it but keeps its memory, so a frame allocates nothing. FlatOnly asks for a window without a depth buffer: a flat interface does not need one. Over a 3D scene, the same list goes in world.Overlay.Drawing instead (see the overlay ). In a browser, gles.FlatRenderer paints it, and on the 3DS nintendo3ds.FlatRenderer . Rectangles, shadows, text and icons These four make most interfaces. The examples of this page are in draw2d/example_test.go , and go test ./draw2d runs them and checks what they print. var drawing draw2d.List card := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 24, Width: 240, Height: 64} drawing.Shadow(card, 12, 12, 4, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f33")) drawing.Rectangle(card, 12, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff"), draw2d.MustHex("#dde3ea"), 1) drawing.Icon("lightbulb", 44, 48, 16, draw2d.MustHex("#e0a020")) drawing.Text("The lighthouse is lit", 70, 61, 14, draw2d.Medium, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) fmt.Println(len(drawing.Commands), "commands") // 4 commands Command What it draws Shadow(area, radius, blur, drop, colour) A soft shadow for a rounded rectangle, falling drop pixels Rectangle(area, radius, fill, border, width) A rounded rectangle; its border is drawn inside the area Icon(name, x, y, size, colour) A Lucide icon in a square Text(text, x, baseline, size, weight, colour) One line of text; y is its baseline, not its top Put the shadow first: later commands cover earlier ones. Colours come from draw2d.MustHex , with an optional opacity as the last two digits. Clips and layers A clip cuts what follows to a rectangle. A layer lifts what follows above lower layers, whatever order it was added in: menus and tooltips use it. var drawing draw2d.List box := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 120, Width: 120, Height: 32} drawing.Rectangle(box, 6, draw2d.MustHex("#f4f6f8"), draw2d.Transparent, 0) drawing.PushClip(box.Inset(8)) drawing.Text("A line too long for its box", 32, 141, 13, draw2d.Regular, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) drawing.PopClip() drawing.SetLayer(1) // drawn over layer 0, whatever comes after tip := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 100, Y: 100, Width: 90, Height: 26} drawing.Rectangle(tip, 4, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f"), draw2d.Transparent, 0) drawing.Text("Lighthouse", 108, 117, 12, draw2d.Regular, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff")) fmt.Println(drawing.Commands[1].HasClip, drawing.Commands[3].Layer) // true 1 Clips nest: a clip inside another keeps only what both share. A command wholly outside the clip is left out as it is added, so a long scrolled list costs only its visible rows. Images A draw2d.Image is a picture the program keeps between frames, so the renderer uploads it once. DecodeImage reads a PNG, JPEG or GIF; NewBlankImage makes one to fill pixel by pixel: const side = 8 tiles := draw2d.NewBlankImage(side, side) tiles.Sharp = true // pixel art: no blending between pixels for y := range side { for x := range side { if (x+y)%2 == 0 { tiles.Pixels.Set(x, y, color.NRGBA{R: 40, G: 120, B: 200, A: 255}) } } } var drawing draw2d.List white := draw2d.Color{1, 1, 1, 1} // a white tint shows the picture as it is drawing.Image(tiles, draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 24, Width: 64, Height: 64}, 8, white) After changing its pixels, call tiles.Changed() so the renderer uploads them again (a video's next frame). Lights over images and frosted glass are in the overlay . Paths and strokes A draw2d.Path is a line of straight pieces and curves, in the program's own units. Build it with MoveTo , LineTo , CurveTo and Close , or add a whole Circle or RoundedRectangle . List.Stroke then draws its line: var tower draw2d.Path tower.MoveTo(0, 10) // the path's own units: here, one per metre tower.LineTo(1, 0) tower.LineTo(3, 0) tower.LineTo(4, 10) tower.Close() var sun draw2d.Path sun.Circle(0, 0, 1) var drawing draw2d.List drawing.Stroke(&tower, 40, 30, 12, 3, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) // 12 layout pixels a metre drawing.Stroke(&sun, 120, 40, 10, 2, draw2d.MustHex("#e0a020")) fmt.Println(tower.Bounds()) // {0 0 4 10} Stroke(path, x, y, scale, width, colour) puts the path's point (0, 0) at (x, y) of the screen, and makes each of its units scale layout pixels. width is the line's thickness in layout pixels, whatever the scale. CurveTo is SVG's C : a cubic Bézier curve with two control points. Why a stroke is a cached picture A list only knows rectangles, text and pictures: that keeps every renderer small, from OpenGL to the 3DS. So a stroke is drawn on the processor into a picture of its own, a mask . The mask is white, and the line's coverage is its opacity, with smoothed edges. The list shows it tinted with the colour, like any image. Drawing the mask costs time, so the path keeps it. It is drawn again only when the scale or the width changes. Moving the stroke or changing its colour costs nothing more. So: Keep paths between frames , as the program above does with tower . A path made anew every frame draws its mask every frame. Change the colour freely ; change the size only when needed (a zoom, not every frame). A stroke is a picture , so it covers and is covered like one, and follows clips and layers. Not yet Paths are strokes only: there is no fill of a shape's inside yet, and no dashed lines.

guides/gltf-extras.title: 🧾 glTF extras read by the renderer
guides/gltf-extras.text: 🧾 glTF extras read by the renderer glTF describes geometry and materials, but not things like the sky at night, the tide or which surfaces you can walk on. The renderer reads those from the file's extras : free JSON that glTF allows on scenes, nodes, meshes and materials. Any program that writes glTF (Go Scene Builder does) can use them. scene extras.environment : sunDirection , sunColor , skyZenith , skyHorizon , groundAmbient , ambient , fog {color, near, far} , water {level, deep, shallow, size, waveLength, floorDepth, colorDepth, shoreFade, variation} (the sea fades into the shore over shoreFade of depth, with a line of foam; water meshes such as rivers keep their own colour and do not follow the variation), verticalScale , wind {direction, strength} , sky : nightZenith , nightHorizon , nightAmbient , twilightColor , celestialPole : vectors stars {density, brightness, twinkle, daytimeVisibility} moon {direction, size (degrees), color, phase (0 new, 0.5 full), light} or false clouds {coverage, color, speed, scale} constellations [{name, stars: [[x, y, z], ...] as seen at midnight, lines: [[first, second], ...], color}] dayImage , nightImage : "panorama.png" or {faces: [+X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z]} , paths relative to the glTF file (PNG or JPEG); the night image turns with the stars water.variation : a surface that rises and falls with one harmonic that differs from place to place (tides): {minimum: [x, z], maximum: [x, z], columns, rows, inPhase: accessor, inQuadrature: accessor, angle} ; the offset at a point is inPhase·cos(angle) + inQuadrature·sin(angle) . A simulation moves the angle ( Water.Variation.Angle ); walking uses Water.LevelAt(x, z) material extras.kind : lit | unlit | water | waterfall ; extras.depthBias : share of its distance the surface is pulled towards the camera, so rivers and roads lying on the terrain stay visible over its simpler far versions; extras.sway : how much the wind bends it (plants modelled with height 1 and the base at the origin) mesh extras.detail : [{"mesh": index, "screenSize": fraction of the screen height}, ...] , simpler versions from finer to coarser; the renderer culls instanced nodes by cells and picks a level per cell mesh, primitive or node extras.ground: true : walkable surface node extras.label , icon , badge , label_color , pinned : the overlay . A node with a label (text), an icon (a Lucide name) or a badge (a short text) gets a label above it, as high as its mesh; label_color ( "#rrggbb" ) tints the icon and the badge. With pinned (a number) it becomes that line of the header instead: {"label": "12:00", "icon": "clock", "pinned": 1} ← All the documentation

guides/metal.text: 🍎 Metal: a backend for flat drawing Status: built (October 2026): the flat path, which Go UI's window draws through on macOS by default, and the 3D scene renderer, which the viewer draws through on macOS by default (see The 3D scene renderer below). This page started as the design; What was built and Measured say how it turned out. Pending a look on screen: live resizing by dragging an edge, and a second screen with another scale. Why OpenGL has been deprecated on macOS since 2018 and is frozen at version 4.1. On Apple silicon it runs as a translation layer over Metal (the driver reports "4.1 Metal"). It still ships in macOS 26. Apple has announced no removal, but there are warning signs: a report from a macOS 27 beta of an OpenGL application that would not start, and Chrome, which dropped its OpenGL backend on macOS and draws only through Metal. It is not needed for performance or battery today. An interface that draws on demand sleeps while idle, and each frame it does draw is one draw call; the translation layer costs about 0.1–0.2 ms of such a frame. Metal is insurance, plus a few things OpenGL cannot do on macOS: smooth live resizing ( presentsWithTransaction ), choosing the low-power GPU, and pacing frames with the display. What was built Piece Where The window and its CAMetalLayer , the pipeline, the atlas texture, instanced quads, the frame, captures metal/flat_darwin.m (Objective-C), metal/flat_darwin.go (cgo) Packing the painter's quads into 36-byte instances metal/instances.go , with tests The window's loop through Metal, and one-frame captures metal/flat_window_darwin.go ( FlatWindow ) The loop both backends share windowloop (moved out of opengl , which now calls it) The metal.unavailable code ( metal.Unavailable ), and a FlatWindow that returns it outside macOS metal/errors.go , metal/flat_other.go Choosing the backend: Options.Backend , `-backend automatic metal Where it differs from the design below: An instance is 36 bytes, not 32: the screen and atlas rectangles stay as floats (the atlas places glyphs at half pixels), and the colour is four bytes. The layer keeps two drawables ( maximumDrawableCount = 2 ) instead of three: a window that draws on demand never queues more than one frame, and each drawable is a whole window of pixels. A new atlas texture each time the atlas changes , instead of replaceRegion on the changed rectangle: a frame still being drawn keeps reading the old texture, and the atlas changes only when glyphs or corners are added. Uploading only the changed rectangle is left for later, as on the OpenGL path. The OpenGL path keeps its six vertices per quad for now; moving it to the same instances is step 5 of Go UI's performance audit. Measured On a laptop with an Apple M4 and a 60 Hz screen, macOS 26, a 1280 × 800 window on a high-density screen. Captures: the register application captured through both backends differs in fewer than 1 % of its pixels, by at most 1/255 in a channel (the colour rounded to a byte), light and dark. Go UI's cmd/app test TestMetalDrawsLikeOpenGL checks it. The register application, idle (drawing on demand): OpenGL Metal Memory (system footprint) 93–102 MB 66–70 MB Processor 0 % 0 % A window whose content changes every frame for 20 seconds (60 frames a second), then stays still (a probe with 30 lines of text, -continuous ): OpenGL Metal Processor while changing 13.6 % of a core 9 % GPU while changing 19–20 % 12–16 % Memory while changing 163 MB 107 MB Memory once still 109 MB 60 MB Most of the memory saved is the window's buffers and the driver's caches: OpenGL on macOS runs on a translation layer over Metal, which keeps more buffers and caches of its own. The 3D scene renderer Built after the flat path, in the same way: One plan, two backends. What a frame draws (commands in order, culling, levels of detail, instance batches, the shadow and seabed regions) moved out of opengl into internal/sceneplan , which makes no graphics calls. OpenGL's captures came out identical, pixel for pixel, before and after the move. metal.SceneRenderer draws the same plan. Shaders translated one to one ( metal/scene_shaders.go ), compiled at start with precise maths: the noise behind the patterns, stars and clouds takes sines of large numbers, and fast maths would round them differently. The uniform blocks are mirrored in Go byte for byte, checked by tests on both sides. A thin Objective-C layer ( scene_darwin.m ): buffers, textures, pipelines, passes and draw calls; the logic stays in Go. A frame waits for the previous one, so buffers can be rewritten in place (a simulation moving instances). Memoryless depth buffer where the GPU allows it (Apple silicon): nothing reads it after the frame, so it takes no memory. The viewer chooses with -backend (Metal on macOS, falling back to OpenGL), and the visor opens a built-in sample island ( -sample island ) and draws at a fixed time ( -time ) for captures that can be compared. Measured with the sample island and an indoor scene of many models, 1280 × 800 on a high-density screen, drawing every frame: OpenGL Metal Captures differ only by rounding (1/255) and where two surfaces share a plane Draw calls and triangles 15 and 160 756 the same Processor per frame (benchmark) 0.76 ms 0.32 ms Processor, the viewer open 17.5 % of a core 11.4 % GPU busy 52–73 % 60–92 % (precise maths) Memory 305–322 MB 214–230 MB Not tested yet: sky images (panoramas and cube faces), a second screen, simulations that move instances every frame. Scope First: the flat path, FlatRenderer — everything an interface-only window needs (Go UI's window package). It is small: about 25 OpenGL calls, two short shaders, one atlas texture and one draw call a frame. Later (now done, see above): the 3D scene renderer (shadows, sky, water, levels of detail, instancing; about 3400 lines and 660 lines of GLSL). That is three to six weeks and a decision of its own (see Options ). Options Option Fit Native Metal through cgo and Objective-C cgo is already required by GLFW, so nothing new. Smallest and most direct; how Gio draws on Apple systems. Chosen for the flat path. Metal through purego (no cgo) How Ebitengine does it. No gain while GLFW needs cgo anyway, and the bindings are ours to write. WebGPU through wgpu-native One renderer for Metal, Vulkan, OpenGL ES and Direct3D, with WGSL shaders: attractive for the 3D renderer and Android. A large native library and young Go bindings. Reconsider when porting the 3D renderer. Android keeps its own small OpenGL ES flat renderer, as planned in Go UI's docs/android.md . How it fits together Layer What it does Go UI window Chooses the backend: Metal on macOS, OpenGL elsewhere ( -backend to force one) draw2d.List Unchanged: what an interface draws overlay painter Unchanged: turns the list into quads of one atlas (plain Go, no OpenGL) metal.FlatRenderer New: uploads the atlas and the quads, one draw call, presents the drawable window loop Shared by both backends: GLFW events, drawing on demand, the resize follower GLFW Creates the window; with Metal it creates no OpenGL context ( NoAPI ) The painter lives in opengl/overlay but imports nothing from OpenGL, so the Metal renderer uses it as it is. Moving it to a neutral package (for example draw2d/paint ) is a tidy-up for later. The pieces 1. The window and the layer (metal/, Objective-C through cgo) GLFW creates the window with glfw.ClientAPI set to glfw.NoAPI : no OpenGL context. window.GetCocoaWindow() gives the NSWindow ; its content view gets a CAMetalLayer ( wantsLayer = YES , layer = metalLayer ). The layer: device : the system's default device, or the low-power one when there is a choice. pixelFormat : BGRA8Unorm . framebufferOnly = YES , opaque = YES , contentsScale = the screen's backing scale. displaySyncEnabled = YES , unless vsync is off. drawableSize follows the framebuffer size callback. The scale follows the window when it moves to another screen. Live resize: while the window is being resized, presentsWithTransaction = YES and the frame is drawn from the refresh callback (as the OpenGL loop already does). This presents the new size in the same transaction as the window's frame, so nothing stretches. 2. The flat renderer (metal.FlatRenderer) It has the same method as the OpenGL one: func NewFlatRenderer(window *glfw.Window, vsync bool) (*FlatRenderer, error) func (renderer *FlatRenderer) Draw(list *draw2d.List, background draw2d.Color, width, height int, scale float32) One pipeline: the vertex and fragment functions, with blending set in the pipeline the same way as the OpenGL path's BlendFuncSeparate . Instanced quads: about 32 bytes each (screen rectangle, atlas rectangle, colour), drawn as a four-vertex triangle strip per instance. Today's OpenGL path uses 192 bytes per quad, so the OpenGL path should take the same layout at the same time and both stay alike. Vertex buffers: three, used in turn and guarded by a semaphore, so the CPU never writes one the GPU is still reading. A buffer grows by doubling and is kept between frames. The atlas: an R8Unorm texture. replaceRegion uploads only the rectangle that changed; a larger texture is made only when the atlas grows. The shaders: about 30 lines of Metal Shading Language: position to clip space, atlas coverage times colour. They are compiled from source when the renderer starts ( newLibraryWithSource ), so building needs no Xcode, only the command-line tools. The frame: take the next drawable; a render pass that clears to the background; one draw call; present; commit. No depth buffer. 3. A loop shared by both backends Today the window loop lives in opengl.Run . Its parts are not about OpenGL: GLFW events, drawing on demand, frame requests and Wake , the resize follower, cursor shape and lock, the fixed-step clock. They move to a package both backends use. Each backend gives the loop a small interface to make its window and to draw and show a frame. The OpenGL backend keeps its behaviour, and its tests must pass unchanged. The existing hand-written metal.Metal and metal.MetalRenderer stubs (the immediate-mode Renderer contract) are left as they are. Filling them in is a separate decision for the author. 4. Captures without a screen -capture draws into an off-screen texture with shared storage and reads it back into a PNG, as the OpenGL path does with ReadPixels . The same frame captured through both backends must match within a small tolerance. That comparison is the main test of the port. 5. Choosing the backend (Go UI) window.Options.Backend : Automatic (Metal on macOS when a device exists, else OpenGL), Metal or OpenGL . The flag -backend forces one. If Metal fails to start, the window falls back to OpenGL and says so once. Iterations # What Done when State 0 GLFW window with no OpenGL context, a CAMetalLayer , clear to a colour, drawing on demand, a capture A window shows the background, sleeps while idle, and -capture writes the colour Done 1 metal.FlatRenderer : pipeline, atlas, instanced quads, shaders The register application's capture matches the OpenGL one within 1/255 per channel, light and dark Done 2 The shared loop; Go UI backend choice; live resize in a transaction; moving between screens The register runs on Metal, resizes without stretching or flicker, and its CPU, GPU and memory are measured against OpenGL Done; resizing and a second screen still need a look on screen 3 Docs, tests, README disclosure go vet and go test pass in both repositories; this page says what was measured Done It was estimated at three to four days. Each step kept the OpenGL path working. Testing Without a window: unit tests for packing quads into instances, for the dirty rectangle of the atlas, and for choosing the backend. With a window: captures through both backends compared pixel by pixel; the register idle for a minute (no frames, no processor); resizing by dragging an edge; a second screen with another scale. Measured against OpenGL: processor time while moving the pointer, GPU use, memory footprint. Risks Pacing: nextDrawable blocks when every drawable is in use. Drawing on demand never holds one while idle. Continuous mode relies on display sync, and on skipping frames with no update. Retina and scale changes: the layer's contentsScale and drawableSize must follow the window as it moves between screens, or text turns blurry. This is tested on a second screen. Two backends to keep alike: the captures comparison catches drift, and both share the painter and the quad layout. OpenGL removal may never come: the work is still small, and it brings the resize and power gains with it. Decisions Native Metal for the flat path and WebGPU only for a later 3D port. Taken. Shaders compiled from source at start-up rather than shipped as a compiled library. Taken: it needs no Xcode, and costs a few milliseconds at start. Metal as the default on macOS once captures match. Taken, with -backend opengl to go back. The OpenGL flat path takes the same instanced quads. Still to do (step 5 of the audit). ← All the documentation
