guides/overlay.text: 🏷️ The overlay: labels, header and notices Sometimes a picture needs words. Which boat is the ferry? What time is it in the harbour? Did the lighthouse just switch on? The overlay answers those questions with small, light labels drawn over the 3D view, a header pinned to the top-left corner and short notices that fade away. It is visual only : nothing on it can be clicked. It is part of the scene ( Scene.Overlay ), so any program that changes the scene can change it, and headless captures ( visor -capture ) include it. Labels A scene.Label floats above something in the world: Field Meaning Node The node it follows: it moves with the node's world transform and hides with it Point Where it stands when there is no Node (a world position) Height How far above the anchor, in world units: the top of a box, the roof of a house Text A short text, cut with "…" when it is very long Icon The name of a Lucide icon ( anchor , sailboat , clock …), drawn before the text or alone in a circle Badge A very short text in a small pill under the label: 7/10 , open Tint Colour of the icon and the badge, as on a web page ( draw2d.ParseHex("#2563eb") ); the text stays dark Hidden Keep it, but do not draw it lighthouse := &scene.Label{Node: lighthouseNode, Height: 30, Text: "Lighthouse", Icon: "lighthouse"} world.Overlay.AddLabel(lighthouse) lighthouse.Badge = "lit" // change it whenever you like world.Overlay.RemoveLabel(lighthouse) Labels keep the same size on screen however far the camera is, and they are drawn only when their anchor is in front of the camera and inside the window. When two labels would cover each other, the one nearer the camera wins and the other waits until there is room: a crowded view stays readable instead of turning into a pile of pills. Labels also stay clear of the header and the notices. The header and the notices Overlay.Header is a list of lines ( scene.HeaderLine : icon, text, tint) shown in a card at the top-left corner; the first line is a little bigger and bolder, for a clock or a title. Notices are short messages under the header: world.Overlay.AddNotice("anchor", "Boat 4 moored at the north quay", graphics.Vector{}) They show newest first, at most MaximumNotices at a time (5 by default), for NoticeDuration seconds (6 by default), fading out over their last second. Their time is the overlay's own Clock , which the viewer advances at every step, so a paused or slowed program does not lose its notices early. Changing it while the scene is shown viewer.Run calls your update function on the same goroutine that draws, between frames, so the update function can add, change and remove labels, lines and notices freely, with no locking. From a glTF file A file can carry labels too, in its node extras (see glTF extras ): label , icon , badge , label_color and pinned . It is a handy way to try the overlay with cmd/visor alone. How it is drawn The overlay is the last pass of the OpenGL scene renderer, after the scene, the sky and the water: Layout (package opengl/overlay , plain Go, no graphics context needed): every label's anchor is projected to the screen, the labels are sorted nearest first, and the header, notices and labels are cut into rectangles of one atlas . The atlas is a single grey image holding coverage masks: the glyphs of the text (Go Medium and Go Bold, from golang.org/x/image/font/gofont ), the icons (the Lucide icon font) and the rounded corners of the pills (a disc, a ring and a soft shadow of each size). Pictures are drawn into it the first time they are needed, at the exact pixel size they are shown at, so text stays crisp; ASCII, Latin-1 and a few signs ( → … € • ) are drawn as soon as a size is first used. Drawing : the atlas is uploaded when it changed, and every rectangle becomes two triangles in one draw call, in screen pixels, with alpha blending and no depth test. Pills of any width are built from the disc as nine pieces: four corners that keep their size and stretched edges. Fonts. Each painter, measurer and renderer that draws text is given an overlay.Fonts when it is made: a font file for each weight, and the folders of the system's fonts. Its zero value, overlay.Fonts{} , is the default: the Go fonts and the system's usual folders. A brand's fonts go in the same value, so two windows can draw in two fonts, and nothing is read when the package is imported. Give the measurer the fonts the renderer draws with, so what is measured is what is drawn. Other scripts. The Go fonts (or a program's own) have Latin, Greek and Cyrillic. A character they lack (Chinese, Arabic, Devanagari, a symbol) is drawn with one of the system's fonts, as a system's own text is: Fonts.Folders , by default DefaultFontFolders() , are Android's /system/fonts , or the desktop's usual folders. The font is found by the name of its file, which names its script ( NotoNaskhArabic , NotoSansCJK , from Go's unicode tables); a character of no named font is looked for in every file under 8 MB, the last resort. Files are read the first time a character needs them, and a font found is kept, shared by every painter and measurer. Letters are drawn one after another, left to right: Arabic letters are not joined yet, and right-to-left text is not turned round. Emoji are drawn in their own colours, from the system's colour emoji font: each is a PNG in the font's CBDT table, found through CBLC and cmap , which colour.go reads ( x/image does not). An emoji becomes a picture in the picture atlas, scaled once to each size it is drawn at, and goes in the same draw call as the text, faded as the text is. An emoji by default (a face, a pictograph, transport) is drawn as a picture before any outline of it; another character is when it is followed by U+FE0F (❤️) or when no font has an outline of it. The variation selectors and the zero width joiner are not drawn; sequences joined by it (a family, a skin tone) show as their parts, as the font's ligatures are not read. Android 13 and later draw their own emoji from vector outlines (COLRv1, not read here) and keep the pictures in NotoColorEmojiLegacy , which is used; the fonts are tried in turn, the one for flags alone last. Tried on the Android 14 emulator: "North light 🌊 😀 🚀 ❤️ 灯台" in one field. On a high-density screen one window pixel is two framebuffer pixels; the viewer sets SceneRenderer.OverlayScale so the overlay keeps its size. The colours aim for calm and contrast: white pills at 92 % opacity with a thin border and a soft shadow, dark text ( #18212e ), and colour only where it means something (the icon and the badge). The icons The icons come from Lucide (ISC licence), copied from the lucide-static npm package into opengl/overlay/lucide : the font lucide.ttf , its licence and a generated table from names to characters. opengl/overlay/lucide/generate.go explains how to update them. An unknown icon name draws nothing and is reported once in the log. Free drawing: Overlay.Drawing Labels, the header and notices are laid out by the renderer. For anything else drawn over the view (panels, buttons, a status bar) a program fills a draw list of package draw2d every frame and sets world.Overlay.Drawing to it once. It is painted last, over the labels. var drawing draw2d.List world.Overlay.Drawing = &drawing // in the update function, every step: drawing.Reset() card := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 24, Width: 220, Height: 64} drawing.Shadow(card, 10, 10, 3, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f2e")) drawing.Rectangle(card, 10, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff"), draw2d.MustHex("#dde3ea"), 1) drawing.Icon("lightbulb", 40, 48, 16, draw2d.MustHex("#4a5768")) drawing.Text("The lamp is lit", 64, 61, 13, draw2d.Regular, draw2d.MustHex("#14202f")) Command What it draws Rectangle(area, radius, fill, border, width) A rectangle with rounded corners, a fill and a border inside its area Shadow(area, radius, blur, drop, colour) A soft shadow for a rectangle, fading out over blur pixels and falling drop pixels Text(text, x, baseline, size, weight, colour) One line of text in Go Regular, Medium or Bold Icon(name, x, y, size, colour) A Lucide icon in a square Image(picture, area, radius, tint) A picture covering a rounded rectangle, cropped evenly where their shapes differ; white tints nothing PushClip(area) / PopClip() Cuts what follows to a rectangle (nested clips intersect) SetLayer(layer) Higher layers cover lower ones, whatever order they were added in Commands wholly outside the current clip are left out as they are added, so the rows of a long scrolled list out of sight cost nothing to paint; a text goes when its line misses the clip above or below, or starts past its right edge. Fingerprint(seed) sums up a list in one number: a window that draws on demand compares it with the last frame's to skip a frame that would look the same. Coordinates are layout pixels from the top-left corner, the same units as the cursor in input.State ; on a high-density screen the renderer doubles them, so sizes match on every screen and text is drawn at its real pixel size. Shapes use the same atlas as the labels (the disc, ring and shadow pictures, cut into nine pieces), so a whole interface is still one draw call. Clipping is done on the processor: each rectangle is cut, and its atlas coordinates with it. To lay text out before drawing it, overlay.NewMeasurer(overlay.Fonts{}) measures a line exactly as it will be painted ( MeasureText(text, size, weight, scale) ); it needs no graphics context. Every command, with paths and strokes, is in drawing in 2D . Interface libraries such as Go UI build on these two pieces. Pictures A picture is a draw2d.Image : draw2d.DecodeImage(reader) reads a PNG, JPEG or GIF (a file the program embeds), draw2d.NewImage(picture) takes an image.Image , and draw2d.NewBlankImage makes one whose pixels the program writes itself. Keep it between frames: its pixels are uploaded once. To show other pixels in it (a video's next frame), write them into Pixels and call Changed ; only its own area is uploaded again. Pixel art sets Sharp : scaled up, its pixels stay square blocks instead of blending into their neighbours. The shaders read such a picture at the middle of its nearest pixel; the quads say so by adding a large offset ( SharpPictureOffset , in the module's internal/shading ) to their picture position, so every other picture is read as before and the vertices keep their layout. Pictures sit side by side in a second atlas, of colours ( overlay.Pictures , RGBA, made with the first picture). A picture's quads read their colours there and their coverage in the grey atlas, as any rounded rectangle does, so corners and clips work as for every other shape and the whole interface stays one draw call. Photos larger than 2048 pixels are scaled down to it as they are copied in; the atlas grows to 4096 pixels, and when even that is full it is emptied and holds only the pictures of the frame being drawn. A program that is only an interface, with no scene, uses opengl.FlatRenderer : it clears the window to a background colour and paints a draw list, with the same atlas and one draw call. Frosted glass: backdrops A translucent panel over a busy picture reads better when what is behind it is blurred, as frosted glass. Backdrop asks for that, just before the panel's own rectangle: panel := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 24, Y: 24, Width: 280, Height: 160} drawing.Backdrop(panel, 12, 24) // blur what is behind by 24 pixels drawing.Rectangle(panel, 12, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff10"), draw2d.Transparent, 0) // the pane over it The panel's area now shows the frame behind it, blurred, with the pane's faint white on top. How it is drawn. The painter does not blur anything itself. It marks the backdrop's quads, and before the first backdrop of each layer it asks the backend for a snapshot ( Painter.Snapshots ). The backend stops drawing there, copies the frame so far, shrinks it to half a few times and blurs the smallest copy in two passes, across and down. Then it goes on drawing, and every backdrop of that layer reads the blurred copy where it sits on screen. What it costs , and how that is kept small: Nothing, without backdrops. A list with none is still one draw call, with one more value per vertex. One blur per layer, not per panel. Ten panels of one layer share a snapshot. The price is that a panel does not blur another panel of its own layer; a dialog, on a layer above, blurs the panels under it. The blur runs on a small picture. For a 24-pixel blur the copy is halved four times, to a sixteenth of the screen's side, so the blur itself works on under half a percent of the pixels; halving is a cheap, smooth average of four pixels into one. What is left is moving the frame once: on OpenGL it is halved straight from the frame (a multisampled frame is copied first), on OpenGL ES 2 copied first, as ES 2 cannot copy and shrink at once. The textures are kept. They are made the first time and again only when the window changes size. Metal reads the drawable directly, which needs the layer's framebufferOnly off on every frame: a small cost of its own, frosted or not. Measured with OpenGL drawn by the processor (llvmpipe, no graphics card: the slowest case), a frame of ten frosted panels over stripes, against the same frame without backdrops: Window Without backdrops With backdrops 1280 × 760 3.1 ms 5.1 ms 2560 × 1520 7.0 ms 13.5 ms A graphics card does the same work in a fraction of that. An interface that draws only when something changes, as go-ui's window does, pays it only on the frames it draws; over a 3D scene, which draws every frame, it is paid every frame. A blur of 0 asks for no backdrop at all, so a system that asks for less transparency costs nothing. Not done yet: Metal blurs a flat interface's backdrops but not those over a 3D scene, which it leaves out (the panels show unblurred); and the snapshot is the whole frame, where copying only the area under the panels would save more on large windows. Light: 2D lights A 2D game looks flat until something is lit: a lamp's warm circle in a dark room, a sign that glows. Painting a halo over the picture cannot do it, because light also has to darken what it does not reach. So lights work the way Unity's 2D lights do: they are added together into a picture of light , which starts at an ambient colour, and then the frame is multiplied by it. white := draw2d.Color{1, 1, 1, 1} drawing.Image(room, draw2d.Rectangle{Width: 400, Height: 240}, 0, white) // what is lit drawing.PointLight(200, 120, 20, 80, draw2d.MustHex("#ffeeaa")) // full within 20 px, gone at 80 drawing.SpriteLight(signGlow, draw2d.Rectangle{X: 40, Y: 30, Width: 64, Height: 32}, white) drawing.Lighting(draw2d.Color{0.6, 0.6, 0.8, 0.7}) // the ambient: a dim blue drawing.Text("Score 10", 8, 20, 16, draw2d.Medium, white) // after it: unlit Lighting lights everything drawn before it, with the lights added since the last Lighting . What comes after it, such as the interface, keeps its own colours. Inside a clip ( PushClip ) it lights only the clip: a game's view lit inside an editor leaves the panels around it as they are. A colour's alpha is its intensity : an ambient of {1, 1, 1, 1} leaves everything as it is, and an alpha of 0.5 halves it. Light can brighten too. Light is kept at half: 0.5 in the picture of light leaves a colour as it is, and 1 makes it twice as bright. The multiply counts the light twice (it blends the frame by the light and the light by the frame). So a lamp in daylight still shows, up to twice the brightness, with no extra cost. How it is drawn. As with backdrops, the painter only marks where each Lighting falls ( Painter.Lightings ), and lays the lights out apart from the other quads ( Painter.Lights ). At each lighting the backend: clears a picture of light, at half the screen's resolution, to the ambient; adds the lights into it, one square each. A point light's shader fades it smoothly from its inner radius to its outer one, and a sprite light shines through its picture; draws the picture of light over the lighting's area (its clip, or the whole frame) with the multiplying blend. What it costs : Nothing, without lights. A list with no Lighting draws as before. Half the resolution for the picture of light, a quarter of the pixels: light is soft, and nobody sees the difference. Three steps per lighting , however many lights it has: a clear, one draw call for all its lights, and a full-screen multiply. The texture is kept , and made again only when the window changes size. Measured as the backdrops were (llvmpipe, 1280 × 760), a frame of twenty panels takes 1.1 ms, and 3.0 ms with eight lights. A graphics card does the same work in a fraction of that. OpenGL ES (Android and the web) draws them the same way, with what OpenGL ES 2 has: a texture to draw into and two blends. The 3DS draws them too, in its own way ( its guide ). Metal draws a flat interface's lights the same way, and lights 3D scenes with point lights as OpenGL does. That code was written on Linux, where Metal cannot be built: it waits for a check on a Mac ( go test ./metal compiles its shaders there). Lights in an overlay over a 3D scene are left unlit on Metal for now, like its backdrops there. ← All the documentation

guides/pads-keys-and-the-whole-screen.title: 🎮 Reading pads and keys, and filling the screen

sections.text: The shortest program: F11 for the whole screen
Naming the buttons: the pad's layout

guides/pads-keys-and-the-whole-screen.text: 🎮 Reading pads and keys, and filling the screen This guide is for a Go programmer writing a game or a tool with Go Renderer. At the end you will read keys (F1 to F12 too), a game pad's buttons and sticks, name its buttons the way its maker does, and put the window on the whole screen. The shortest program: F11 for the whole screen Every backend fills one input.State : the desktop window, the browser, Android and the 3DS. A program gives the application a state and reads it in its update step: state := input.NewState() state.Feed().SetKey(input.KeyF11, true) // the backend: F11 went down if state.Pressed(input.KeyF11) { state.SetFullscreen(!state.Fullscreen()) } fmt.Println(state.Down(input.KeyF11), state.Fullscreen()) // true true state.Feed().EndFrame() // the backend, after the step: a press lasts one step fmt.Println(state.Down(input.KeyF11), state.Pressed(input.KeyF11)) // true false In a real program the first SetKey and the EndFrame belong to the backend: they are on the state's Feed() , the side backends write, so go doc input.State shows only what a program reads. You write the if . This is ExampleState_Pressed in input/example_test.go , and go test ./input checks what it prints. In a window it looks like this: app := &window.Application{Input: input.NewState()} app.Update = func(app *window.Application, seconds float64) error { if app.Input.Pressed(input.KeyF11) { app.Input.SetFullscreen(!app.Input.Fullscreen()) } return nil } Keys Method True when Down(key) the key is held now Pressed(key) it went down during this step: once per press Typed(key) it went down or the system repeated it: Backspace held in a text field input.Key holds letters, digits, arrows, Space, Tab, Enter, Escape, Shift, Control, Alt, the Command or Windows key ( KeySuper ), and KeyF1 to KeyF12 . Characters typed (an "ñ", an "€") come from TypedText() , after the keyboard layout. When an interface has the keyboard (a text field), it calls ClaimKeyboard , and Unclaimed() gives the rest of the program a state without those keys. A game pad Buttons are read by position , like keys: PadA is always the bottom face button. state := input.NewState() state.Feed().SetStick(0.5, 1) // the backend: half right, all the way up state.Feed().SetPadButton(input.PadA, true) const metresPerSecond = 4 const seconds = 0.5 stickX, stickY := state.Stick() forward := stickY * metresPerSecond * seconds sideways := stickX * metresPerSecond * seconds fmt.Println(forward, sideways, state.PadPressed(input.PadA)) // 2 1 true PadDown(button) and PadPressed(button) work like Down and Pressed . The sticks are read with Stick() and RightStick() , each giving x and y from -1 to 1, right and up positive , and 0 at rest. A small dead zone round the middle reads as 0, since a stick let go never sits exactly there. Stick Read with On a pad On a 3DS Main Stick() the left stick the circle pad Second RightStick() the right stick a New 3DS's C-stick Multiply a stick by a speed and the step's seconds to move something smoothly, as above. Naming the buttons: the pad's layout Each maker prints other names on the same buttons. The bottom one is A on an Xbox pad, ✕ on a PlayStation pad and B on a Nintendo pad. A game that says "Press A" should say what the player sees: bottomButton := map[input.PadLayout]string{ input.XboxLayout: "A", input.PlayStationLayout: "✕", input.NintendoLayout: "B", } state := input.NewState() // a browser's name for a pad; a window's backend reads the GUID instead (PadLayoutFromGUID) state.SetPadLayout(input.PadLayoutFromName("Wireless Controller (STANDARD GAMEPAD Vendor: 054c Product: 09cc)")) fmt.Println("Press", bottomButton[state.PadLayout()], "to jump") // Press ✕ to jump The backend sets the layout when a pad connects; a program only reads state.PadLayout() . It is worked out from the pad's USB vendor , which every system gives, while pad names vary by driver: 054c is Sony, 057e Nintendo, anything else reads as Xbox. Only the names change: the Nintendo layout's "B" is still PadA , the bottom button. The whole screen SetFullscreen(true) asks for the whole screen, and Fullscreen() tells what was asked. The backend applies it after the frame, in its own way: A desktop window ( windowloop ) moves to the screen that holds most of it, at that screen's size. Asked no more, it goes back to its place and size. Without a screen (a headless display), the request is dropped and Fullscreen() turns false. A web page ( browser ) can take the whole screen only while it answers a key or a click: the browser forbids it otherwise. So the request waits for the next press. When the person leaves with Escape, Fullscreen() turns false, so a toggle stays right. Leaving needs no such moment, anywhere. Which backend reads what Keys, F1–F12 Pad buttons Sticks Pad layout Whole screen Desktop window (GLFW) yes first pad first pad from the GUID yes Web page yes, no F keys yet not yet not yet from the pad's name on the next press Nintendo 3DS ( nintendo3ds ) its buttons, as keys — circle pad, C-stick — always On the desktop, GLFW gives every known pad Xbox's order, so one program reads them all the same way. Not yet A browser does not read a pad's buttons and sticks yet, nor F1 to F12; only the first pad is read on a computer.

guides/scenes-in-areas.title: 🪟 Scenes in areas of the window

sections.text: The shortest program: two views side by side
A scene floating over another: a radar

guides/scenes-in-areas.text: 🪟 Scenes in areas of the window This guide is for a Go programmer who draws a scene with opengl.SceneRenderer and wants more than one view in a frame. At the end you will draw a scene into any rectangle of the window, side by side with another, or floating over it. The shortest program: two views side by side SceneRenderer.Draw fills the whole window. DrawIn fills only an area : a rectangle of the framebuffer, in its pixels. Two calls make two views, here of the sample island: package main import ( "log" "runtime" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/camera" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/graphics" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/opengl" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/opengl/overlay" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene/sample" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/window" ) func init() { runtime.LockOSThread() } // windows live on the main thread func main() { world := sample.Island() above, shore := mapCamera(world), shoreCamera(world) var renderer *opengl.SceneRenderer app := &window.Application{ Options: window.Options{Title: "Two views", Width: 960, Height: 400}, Input: input.NewState(), } app.Draw = func(app *window.Application) error { if renderer == nil { var err error if renderer, err = opengl.NewSceneRenderer(overlay.Fonts{}); err != nil { return err } } width, height := app.Input.FramebufferWidth, app.Input.FramebufferHeight half := width / 2 renderer.DrawIn(world, above, opengl.Area{Width: half, Height: height}, 0) renderer.DrawIn(world, shore, opengl.Area{X: half, Width: width - half, Height: height}, 0) renderer.DrawOverlay(world, width, height) // once, after every area return nil } if err := (&opengl.Window{}).Run(app); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // mapCamera looks straight down on the whole scene, without perspective. func mapCamera(world *scene.Scene) camera.Lens { centre, size := middleAndSize(world) return camera.Lens{ Position: graphics.Vector{centre[0], size, centre[2], 1}, Target: centre, Up: graphics.Vector{0, 0, -1, 0}, // north at the top OrthographicHeight: size, Far: size * 3, } } // shoreCamera looks at the middle of the scene from above its southern shore. func shoreCamera(world *scene.Scene) camera.Lens { centre, size := middleAndSize(world) return camera.Lens{ Position: graphics.Vector{centre[0], size / 4, centre[2] + size*0.7, 1}, Target: centre, Up: graphics.Vector{0, 1, 0, 0}, Far: size * 4, } } // middleAndSize is the middle of a scene's ground and the larger of its two sides. func middleAndSize(world *scene.Scene) (graphics.Vector, float32) { minimum, maximum := world.Bounds() centre := graphics.Vector{(minimum[0] + maximum[0]) / 2, 0, (minimum[2] + maximum[2]) / 2, 1} return centre, max(maximum[0]-minimum[0], maximum[2]-minimum[2]) } The body of main is ExampleSceneRenderer_DrawIn in opengl/example_test.go , with the three helpers next to it; go test ./opengl checks that it compiles. What an area is opengl.Area{X, Y, Width, Height} is in framebuffer pixels, from the bottom-left corner , as OpenGL counts. That is not the cursor's units: on a high-density screen the framebuffer has twice the window's pixels, and the cursor's y grows downwards. Take sizes from app.Input.FramebufferWidth and FramebufferHeight , as above. Each area gets its own aspect ratio, so a camera never looks stretched. The overlay, once DrawIn leaves out the scene's overlay (its labels, notices and Overlay.Drawing ). The overlay belongs to the whole window, so DrawOverlay(world, width, height) draws it once, after every area. It places labels with the camera of the last area drawn: in the picture, the label follows the shore view on the right. Draw(world, camera, width, height, seconds) is simply DrawIn over the whole window followed by DrawOverlay . A scene floating over another: a radar DrawIn clears its area and draws the sky behind the scene. DrawOver clears only the depth and draws no sky : the scene floats over what is already there. A radar in a corner is the classic case: width, height := app.Input.FramebufferWidth, app.Input.FramebufferHeight side, margin := height/3, height/30 corner := opengl.Area{X: width - side - margin, Y: height - side - margin, Width: side, Height: side} renderer.DrawIn(world, view, opengl.Area{Width: width, Height: height}, 0) renderer.DrawOver(world, radar, corner, 0) // no sky: the view stays round the island renderer.DrawOverlay(world, width, height) This is the inside of app.Draw in ExampleSceneRenderer_DrawOver , with view := shoreCamera(world) and radar := mapCamera(world) . Y: height - side - margin puts the corner at the top , since areas count from the bottom. Here the sea fills the radar, so it looks square. With a scene that does not reach the edges, the view behind shows through around it. A frame round the radar is a draw2d rectangle in Overlay.Drawing , in layout pixels: divide the area by the screen's scale to place it. Previewing a console's two screens The 3DS has two screens, one above the other. A computer can preview both in one window: DrawIn the top screen's camera into the upper area and the bottom one into the lower area, at the console's sizes (400 × 240 and 320 × 240) times a zoom. See on the Nintendo 3DS . Which to use Call Clears Sky Overlay Draw the whole window yes yes DrawIn its area yes no: call DrawOverlay DrawOver depth only, in its area no no: call DrawOverlay DrawOverlay nothing no the scene's, over the whole window Not yet Areas are in opengl only. The Metal, browser ( gles ) and 3DS renderers draw a scene over the whole screen.

guides/viewer.title: 🔭 The viewer
guides/viewer.text: 🔭 The viewer cmd/visor opens a glTF 2.0 scene ( .glb or .gltf ) and lets you explore it: fly around it like a bird, walk on the ground at eye height, or look at it as a flat map; move the sun to see it at dawn or at night; take a picture or measure how fast it draws. go run ./cmd/visor scene.glb go run ./cmd/visor -walk scene.glb go run ./cmd/visor -map scene.glb # a 2D map seen from straight above go run ./cmd/visor -isometric scene.glb # the same map, at the classic isometric angle go run ./cmd/visor -capture frame.png scene.glb # one frame to PNG, hidden window go run ./cmd/visor -sample island # a built-in made-up island, no file needed go run ./cmd/visor -benchmark 120 scene.glb # CPU and GPU times per pass, draw calls, triangles The viewer draws only when something changes : a key or button held, the mouse moving the camera, a camera easing to a stop, the sun turning, a notice fading, the window resized. In between it sleeps and uses no processor or GPU, and the water and clouds stand still until the next frame. -continuous draws every frame instead; a program that passes an update function (a simulation) and -benchmark always do. Editing the scene viewer.Edit shows a scene like viewer.Run , for a program that changes it in answer to the user (a level editor, a floor plan designer). Its function runs at every step, before the viewer's own controls, and receives a viewer.View : the camera that drew the frame the user is looking at and the window's size. View.PointOnPlane(x, y, height) and View.PointOnGround(x, y) turn a point of the window (the pointer, input.State.CursorX and CursorY ) into a point of the scene: on a flat floor, or on the walkable ground with its relief. The viewer keeps drawing on demand; a program that claims the mouse ( input.State.ClaimMouse , as Go UI does over its panels) keeps it from the camera for that step. camera.RayThrough is the ray behind both, for any camera. viewer.Edit(world, options, "Editor", func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64, view viewer.View) { if point, onGround := view.PointOnGround(state.CursorX, state.CursorY); onGround && state.ButtonReleased(input.MouseLeft) { placeSomething(world, point) } }) Orbit camera (default) Control Action Left drag Rotate around the target Right drag (or shift + left drag) Pan Scroll Zoom ← → Rotate ↑ ↓ Tilt + - Zoom in or out Walking (Tab switches) Control Action W A S D Move forward, left, back, right ↑ ↓ Move forward or back ← → Turn Drag with any mouse button Look around Shift Run [ ] Walk slower or faster (×1.5 per press) Map (M switches) M goes round three views: the orbit camera, a map seen from straight above, and an isometric view, then back to the orbit. Both maps use an orthographic camera: nothing gets smaller with distance, so lengths and areas can be compared anywhere on screen, as on a printed map. Fog is lifted while a map is shown. Control Action Drag with any mouse button Move the map (the ground follows the cursor) ← → ↑ ↓ Move the map Scroll, + - Zoom Q E Turn a quarter (the top view starts with north up) Tab Leave the map and walk Sun, sky and scene (all modes) Key Action J L Turn the sun I K Raise or lower the sun (below the horizon it is night) N Jump between day and night Z X Less or more vertical exaggeration (orbit only) F Fog (toggle) O Shadows (toggle) Options Option Effect -walk Start walking on the ground -map Start with the map seen from above ( -zoom and -look-at work too) -isometric Start with the isometric map -night Start at night -sun-elevation D / -sun-azimuth D Place the sun (degrees; negative elevation is below the horizon; azimuth clockwise from north) -zoom F Initial orbit distance as a fraction of the default (0.1 = ten times closer) -look-at x,z Start centred on this point, in scene units; with -walk , start walking there -heading D With -walk , start facing this way: degrees clockwise from north (−z) -pitch D With -walk , start looking up this many degrees (negative = down) -eye-height H With -walk , eye height in scene units (0 = a share of the scene size) -walk-speed S Walking speed in scene units per second (0 = a share of the scene size); [ ] then change it within a range around it, so a small scene in large units (a plant in kilometres) walks at a person's pace -no-shadows Start without sun shadows -width / -height Window size -capture frame.png Render one frame to a PNG with a hidden window, and exit (the overlay included) -benchmark N Measure N frames, print CPU and GPU times per pass, draw calls and triangles, and exit -no-vsync Do not wait for the display; the window title shows the real frames per second -cpu-profile file Write a CPU profile of the session for go tool pprof -continuous Draw every frame, so the water, clouds and plants in the wind keep moving while nothing else happens -backend B What draws: automatic (Metal on macOS, OpenGL elsewhere), metal or opengl -sample island / -sample night Open the built-in sample island (package scene/sample ) instead of a file -time S Draw every frame as if S seconds had passed: water and clouds stand still, so captures can be compared Other programs reuse these options: viewer.Options.RegisterFlags adds them to any flag set, as Go Simulator's live simulator does. In Go, viewer.Options keeps the window's size and the backend at the top and the rest in three groups, so a program finds a setting by what it is for: options := viewer.DefaultOptions() options.Start.Walking = true // Start: where the view begins (-walk, -map, -look-at, the sun) options.Rendering.NoShadows = true // Rendering: how frames are drawn (-no-shadows, -continuous, -time) options.Measure.CapturePath = "frame.png" // Measure: a capture or a benchmark instead of exploring err := viewer.Run(world, options, "Island", nil) A benchmark writes its report to options.Measure.Output (the standard output by default), with the scene's loading time when the program sets Measure.LoadingTime . ← All the documentation

guides/web.title: 🌐 In a web browser

sections.text: gles: renderers written once for OpenGL ES
browser: the canvas as a window

guides/web.text: 🌐 In a web browser Status: a first step (October 2026). The sample island and its labels draw in a browser through WebGL2, and Go UI interfaces run there too (see Go UI's docs/web.md ). The desktop is unchanged. What is still missing is listed at the end. GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build -o cmd/web-island/island.wasm ./cmd/web-island cp "$(go env GOROOT)/lib/wasm/wasm_exec.js" cmd/web-island/ python3 -m http.server -d cmd/web-island 8080 # then open http://localhost:8080 Drag to turn around the island, drag with the right button to move, turn the wheel to come closer. What was already portable Most of Go Renderer is plain Go and builds for WebAssembly as it is: the scene ( scene ), the frame planning ( internal/sceneplan ), cameras ( camera ), glTF loading ( loaders ), input ( input ), the 2D draw lists ( draw2d ) and the overlay painter with its atlas and fonts ( opengl/overlay , which rasterises on the processor and embeds its fonts with go:embed ). Only three packages are tied to the desktop, through GLFW and cgo: opengl , windowloop and viewer . So the browser needed three things: a window (a canvas and its events), a loop that does not use GLFW, and a renderer that speaks WebGL2. How it fits together Layer What it does Your program The same scene, camera and update function as on the desktop browser (js only) The canvas, its events → input.State , requestAnimationFrame , WebGL2 gles FlatRenderer and SceneRenderer , in GLSL ES 1.00, over gles.Functions frameloop The fixed-step clock, shared with windowloop overlay , scene , camera … Unchanged gles: renderers written once for OpenGL ES Browsers draw with WebGL2 (OpenGL ES 3.0) and Android phones with OpenGL ES. So the renderers are written once, in package gles , against a small interface, gles.Functions : about forty calls to make shaders, buffers and textures and to draw. Each platform implements it: Platform Implementation Browser browser.WebGL , over the canvas's WebGL2RenderingContext through syscall/js Android android.GL , direct calls into the phone's OpenGL ES ( on Android ) Tests a fake that records the calls, so the renderers are tested on any computer, without a display gles.FlatRenderer paints a draw2d.List on a plain background, like opengl.FlatRenderer : the same atlas, one draw call. gles.SceneRenderer draws a scene in its simplest form : lit meshes with vertex colours, instances, the light of the time of day ( Environment.Daylight ), fog, translucent water and, over everything, the overlay. What a frame draws is still decided by internal/sceneplan , so culling and levels of detail work as on the desktop. They use only what OpenGL ES 2.0 has (plus 32-bit indices, which every current phone has), because the first Android step went through golang.org/x/mobile/gl , which knows no newer function, and some phones may still give only that; WebGL2 accepts all of it. So the shaders are GLSL ES 1.00, there are no vertex array objects (each draw describes its vertices, a handful of calls), the atlas is a LUMINANCE texture, and the normal matrix is worked out on the processor (GLSL ES 1.00 has no inverse ). Each rectangle of the overlay is six vertices, and OpenGL ES 2 cannot draw instances either. A call per instance was the first try, and it was far too slow on a phone: the sample island's forest made about a thousand draw calls, eight thousand calls through the bindings, and a frame took half a second on the emulator. Now each batch of instances the planner hands over (a level of detail of a group of cells) becomes one mesh on the processor , every copy placed and tinted, made again only when the batch changes; the island is 16 draw calls a frame. True instancing, which WebGL2 and OpenGL ES 3 have, would save the memory of the copies, as a later step behind the same interface. Each call is costly too: a browser crosses into JavaScript at each, and x/mobile's bindings crossed to their own thread every three calls (Go Renderer's own android package calls OpenGL ES directly). So a program remembers what each uniform holds and sends only values that changed, and the vertex attributes are switched on once. On a phone dragging the island, a frame went from about 12.5 to 8.7 ms. browser: the canvas as a window Size and density. The canvas fills its place in the page; its drawing buffer is that size times devicePixelRatio , so text is rasterised at its real pixel size. As on the desktop, the cursor is in layout pixels ( WindowWidth ) and drawing in device pixels ( FramebufferWidth ). Input. Pointer events (mouse, pen and touch alike), the wheel and the keyboard fill an input.State . A finger is also the pointer, as on Android ( input.TouchPointer ), and every finger on the screen is listed in State.Touches , for gestures. Keys follow their place on the keyboard ( KeyboardEvent.code ), as GLFW's do; typed characters come from KeyboardEvent.key . The canvas takes the focus when pressed, and lets go of held keys when it loses it. Clipboard. Copied text is kept by the page and offered to the system clipboard; pasting takes what the browser's paste event brings. Reading the system clipboard at any other time needs a permission, so it is not done. The loop. browser.Run is windowloop.Run 's twin: the same fixed-step clock (now in frameloop , shared by both), the same drawing on demand. It asks for an animation frame only when something happens (an event, a size change, RequestFrame , browser.Wake ), so a page left alone does nothing at all: measured, no frames in two seconds of idling, and two after moving the pointer once (the frame and its follow-up). Inside a page's own application. A program can be one screen of a larger web application, drawing in a canvas the page gives it ( Options.Canvas in Go UI). When the page takes that screen away, it asks the program to stop ( browser.Stop ): Run returns after one more frame, and every listener the canvas added (the document's paste among them) and its size observer come off the page, so nothing calls into a program that has exited. Opening the screen again starts the program again. Why this route Option For Against Choice Go, GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm , WebGL2 through syscall/js The same compiler and standard library; go:embed and the fonts work; WebGL2 is in every browser; the same shaders as Android A large file (below); each call into JavaScript has a small cost Chosen Go with WebGPU A modern interface, close to Metal Not in every browser yet; new shaders in WGSL; the hand-written webgpu package is the author's Later TinyGo Much smaller files Partial support for reflection and go:embed , which the fonts and the glTF loader use; a second compiler to keep working Not now Software rendering to a 2D canvas No GPU needed Far too slow for the scene No Size. The island is a 5.4 MB .wasm file, about 1.8 MB compressed with gzip, which web servers usually do on the fly. The fonts and icons are inside it, so the page loads nothing else. Testing go test ./gles ./frameloop on any computer: the renderers against the fake (shaders are GLSL ES 1.00 with nothing newer, one draw call for an interface, the atlas and meshes uploaded only when they change). GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go test ./browser ./gles runs the browser package's own tests under Node.js (key, wheel and button mapping); it needs $(go env GOROOT)/lib/wasm in the PATH . In a browser: the island, turning and zooming, and the idle check above, were looked at in Chromium on macOS. Other browsers, phones and tablets have not been tried yet. Not yet The full scene renderer in WebGL2: shadows, the sky dome with stars and clouds, waves and tides, patterns, wind and snow. It is a translation of the desktop shaders to GLSL ES, a larger piece of work. True instanced drawing, so that very large forests do not cost a copy of each mesh. Loading .glb files in the page ( fetch , then loaders on the bytes). Locking the pointer for the walking camera, the on-screen keyboard, and the system clipboard at any time. WebGPU, and smaller files with TinyGo. ← All the documentation

overview.title: Welcome to Go Renderer 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Renderer 👋 Go Renderer draws pictures with a computer's graphics card : 3D scenes of islands, towns, forests, the sea and the sky, by day and by night, and the flat buttons and panels other programs put over them. It is written in Go, to learn how 3D graphics work from the inside. You describe what is in the scene ( a hill here, a tower there, the sun this high ) and Go Renderer draws it, sixty times a second, as you fly round it, walk on it or look at it as a map. It can also open whole scenes made by other tools, in the glTF format. Is it for me? ✅ You want to look at a 3D scene: open one with the viewer, no code needed. ✅ You are learning how 3D graphics work: triangles, light, cameras. ✅ You write Go and want to show a scene, a map or a simulation. ❌ You need a finished game engine or a product to ship: this is an experiment. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time just want to see what it does Try it without writing code 2 min are new to it and want to install it Get started 15 min want to learn step by step 🏴‍☠️ The quest : an island with a lighthouse, in 6 levels 90 min want to know how one part works The guides : the viewer, labels, glTF, web, Android — are looking up a type or a function The reference — Try it without writing code With Go installed and the project copied (see Get started ), one command opens a made-up island to fly round: go run ./cmd/visor -sample island Drag to turn, scroll to come closer, Tab to walk, M for a map and N for the night. Any .glb file opens the same way: go run ./cmd/visor scene.glb . All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page Get started : install, the sample island, your first scene Learn The quest : six levels that build an island with a lighthouse Guides: how each part works Architecture The viewer : every key and option The overlay : labels, header, notices, flat drawing glTF extras In a web browser On Android Metal On the Nintendo 3DS Drawing in 2D : shapes, text, images, paths and strokes Scenes in areas of the window : two views, a radar Reading pads and keys, and filling the screen Reference Packages : every type and function When something goes wrong Troubleshooting : the errors people meet, and the fix The project Contributing : the code's layout, building, testing, proposing a change Optimization plan Roadmap Towards version 1.0 : the proposal for a stable release Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev, and type go run … in a terminal. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Scene Everything a 3D picture holds: ground, houses, trees, the sea, the sky and the sun. .glb file A 3D scene in one file, in the open glTF format: many programs (Blender among them) open and write it. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. 🚧 Not done yet In a browser: the full scene renderer in WebGL2 (shadows, the sky dome with stars and clouds, waves and tides, patterns, wind and snow), loading .glb files in the page, locking the pointer for walking, the on-screen keyboard and the system clipboard at any time, WebGPU, and smaller files with TinyGo. See in a web browser . On Android: keyboards for Chinese and Japanese (not tried yet), long presses, and the full scene renderer (shadows, sky, waves) on phones. See on Android . project/optimization-plan.text: ⚡ Optimization plan Measured with go run ./cmd/visor -benchmark 120 scene.glb (GPU timer queries per pass, averages after a warm-up) on an Apple M4, 2560×1600 framebuffer. Test scene: a 60–90 km island exported by a procedural scene generator (terrain, towns, rivers, 87,069 instanced trees, floating islands). Baseline View CPU GPU shadows GPU sky GPU scene GPU total Overview (default orbit) 20.6 ms 19.0 ms 1.1 ms 20.3 ms 40.4 ms Close ( -zoom 0.08 ) 22.1 ms 20.9 ms 1.1 ms 20.4 ms 42.4 ms Walking ( -walk ) 21.0 ms 19.8 ms 1.5 ms 19.5 ms 40.8 ms Overview, -no-shadows 2.6 ms — 1.5 ms 20.4 ms 21.9 ms Every frame draws 17.5 million triangles in 16 draw calls, and the same again in the shadow pass. Trees are 94 % of them (16.5 M): 87,069 instances of meshes with 27–260 triangles, drawn whole whether they are visible, far away or behind the camera. The terrain is 0.63 M, the sky islands 0.21 M, the rest below 0.1 M. The cost does not change at 640×400: the renderer is bound by geometry, not by pixels . With shadows the CPU time jumps from 2.6 to ~21 ms: the driver stalls on the second full-scene pass (and the profiler waits for the GPU), so CPU time follows the GPU work. Loading takes 55–140 ms and the first frame 25–90 ms (uploads): not a problem today. The seabed map costs nothing after the first frame (rendered once); the sky is ~1 ms at full resolution. Result: ~25 fps with shadows, ~45 fps without, in every view. Target 60 fps with shadows in every view at 2560×1600 on this machine: GPU total under 12 ms , leaving room for simulations. Every step below is measured with -benchmark on the four views of the baseline table, and its row is added to the results section. Phase 1: draw only the trees that matter (largest gain) — done Levels of detail for instanced meshes. A mesh can carry simpler versions and the distance (in screen size) at which each one is used: full tree near, a low-polygon version (8–30 triangles) further, a crossed pair of quads or a single billboard far away. Instances are sorted into one instance buffer per level each frame (or every few frames), so each level is still one draw call. Scene API: Mesh.Levels []DetailLevel{Mesh, ScreenSize} ; glTF: the exporter writes the simpler meshes and names them in the mesh extras. From the overview almost every tree is far: 16.5 M → about 1 M triangles. Expected: scene pass 20 → ~3 ms. Spatial chunks and frustum culling. Split every instanced node into grid cells (1–2 km) with a bounding box each, and skip the cells outside the view frustum. Combined with the levels of detail, the walking view draws only nearby trees in full. Also cull plain meshes by their bounds (terrain split into chunks, see phase 2). A cheaper shadow pass. Draw only casters that touch the shadow region (it is small in close and walking views). Use the lowest level of detail for shadows beyond a short distance. Keep the shadow map between frames when the light direction, the snapped region and the casters have not changed (static scenes, a still camera); simulations mark it stale. Expected: shadows 19 → 2–4 ms. What was done in phase 1 scene.Mesh.Details holds simpler versions with the apparent size (fraction of the screen height) below which each one is used; glTF mesh extras "detail": [{"mesh", "screenSize"}] . Every instanced node is sorted into a grid of cells (about 64 instances each). Each pass (main and shadows) keeps the cells inside its frustum, chooses a level per cell from the apparent size of its largest instance at its nearest point, and draws one call per level. Instance buffers are uploaded again only when the chosen cells change. Single meshes are culled by their box and use their levels too. The shadow pass culls against the light's frustum and uses the same level as the main pass: one level coarser made tree shadows visibly angular in close views. The skill exports two simpler trees: fewer faces (below 3 % of the screen height) and, far away, an 8-face crown with a 3-sided trunk (below 0.8 %). Without the trunk the far forest looked lighter than before, so it stays. Keeping the shadow map between frames was left out: plants bending in the wind change the shadows every frame, so it would rarely apply. Phase 2: steady frame time — done Terrain in chunks with levels of detail (quadtree over the height grid, skirts to hide cracks): allows culling and keeps distant terrain cheap when scenes grow (the skill can export larger terrains). Partial uploads for simulations : when a few instances move, upload only their range ( glBufferSubData ), and orphan buffers that change every frame, instead of re-uploading everything a Dirty flag touches. Profile the CPU side once the GPU is lighter: command collection walks the whole scene every frame and uniform setting repeats per draw; cache the command list and world transforms of nodes that did not change. Sky at lower resolution if it ever matters (clouds and stars at half resolution, upscaled); today it is ~1 ms. What was done in phase 2 Steady measurements first. With vsync the GPU idles between frames and lowers its speed, so the same configuration measured 10–16 ms. Benchmarks now disable vsync and add a second round without timer queries; its time between frames is the figure to compare (below). Terrain in chunks (item 4), done in the exporter since the renderer already culls single meshes by their box and picks their levels: the skill cuts the height grid into 64×64-cell chunks, each with versions keeping one vertex in 2, 4 and 8 (used below 34 %, 17 % and 8.5 % of the screen height), and skirts under the edges, deep enough for the largest difference between a full and a coarsest edge, so neighbours of different detail leave no cracks. A generic quadtree in the renderer was not needed. Partial uploads (item 5): Instances.MarkChanged(indices...) updates only those instances in the grid (their cell box grows if they move away) and rewrites only their slot in each batch holding them ( glBufferSubData ). Updating 1,000 of 87,000 instances costs 1.3 ms on the processor against 20.3 ms to prepare the grid again (plus a full upload). Dirty still prepares everything again when instances are added or removed. Processor side (item 6): without timers it takes 0.7–1.4 ms per frame, so caching the command list is not worth it yet. Sky (item 7): instead of a lower resolution (stars are one pixel wide), the sky is drawn after the opaque scene with the depth test, so covered pixels cost nothing: 1.1 → 0.2 ms in the overview, 1.5 → 0.6 ms walking. Transparent things (water, waterfalls) are drawn after it. Phase 3: size and loading — done Smaller files. The skill's glTF writer now quantizes ( KHR_mesh_quantization ): colors in one byte per channel, normals in one byte per component, 16-bit indices when they fit, and positions in 16-bit integers with the center and the scale in the node; instance rotations and colors are integers too. Meshes that are instanced keep float positions (the node scale would distort every instance), and the levels of a terrain chunk share its box, since they are drawn with the same node. The island goes from 76 MB to 33 MB (19 → 10 MB zipped for sharing). Two fixes came with it. The renderer transformed normals with the model matrix itself, wrong for scales that differ per axis; it now uses the inverse transpose (no measurable cost). And with quantized positions the writer must store normals in the mesh's own coordinates (world normals multiplied by the node scale, normalized): with world normals the terrain looked flatter. After both, renders differ from the float file by under one colour level on average. Speed does not change (the loader expands to floats) and loading goes from ~60–100 ms to ~60 ms. EXT_meshopt_compression was left out: it needs a decoder in Go and would save a few more megabytes on a file that zips to 10 MB. Background loading was not needed: the scene loads in about 60 ms and uploads in about 80 ms. It becomes worth it for scenes several times larger. Out of scope for now GPU-driven culling with compute shaders: macOS stops at OpenGL 4.1, which has no compute shaders. It would come with a Vulkan or Metal backend. Changing the look (fewer trees, lower shadow resolution): the goal is the same image, faster. Those are the allocations per frame the rewrite should bring to zero. A busy interface costs ~31 µs to describe (300 controls) and ~150–590 µs to lay out: layout, not description, is where the 2D frame's processor time goes. Rebuilding an instance grid (36 ms, 9.6 MB) happens when instances change, not every frame; moving a thousand instances is 0.37 ms with no allocation. There were 18 benchmarks before (not the 34 the proposal counted: several names repeat with sub-cases); the overlay's were named Audit… from an earlier review, and are now named for what they measure. After phases A and B (2026-10-22) The After A/B columns are the same benchmarks once the audit's phases A and B were done, measured the same way. No frame allocates any more : planning the island, laying out the overlay and drawing an OpenGL 2D frame (with lights and a blurred backdrop) make no garbage, and a test in each package ( testing.AllocsPerRun ) keeps it so. The times did not move beyond the runs' noise (about 2 % for the OpenGL frames, which measure Mesa's software driver). The OpenGL frames still report about 130–390 bytes per frame and no allocation: their first frame is measured with the rest and grows the vertex buffers once, spread over every frame. After phases C and D (2026-10-22) The After C/D columns are the same benchmarks once the audit's phases C and D were done, measured the same way ( -count 3 , the median). Two benchmarks had grown from changes elsewhere in the binary (ordering commands by layer, +23 %; updating instances, +1 %), and three more by under 1 % (painting a frame and a line of text, clipping): each was compared with the After A/B commit in the same session, and won back with real work rather than waved off as noise: Ordering commands writes the order in place and checks the layers without a branch on the index: 488 ns from 639. Moving a box's corners skips the matrix's fourth row (a point's w is always 1): updating a thousand instances takes 352 µs from 364, and rebuilding the grid 35.3 ms from 36.5. Finding a glyph looks a character up once in its own face, not twice: 39 ns from 56. A line of text paints in 1.28 µs from 1.49, a busy application frame in 124 µs from 149, two thousand commands in 400 µs from 590. The OpenGL frames measure Mesa's software driver and move by about 2 % from run to run either way; compared with the After A/B build in one session they are the same, as are building a draw list and the loading benchmarks (prebuilding a face, a shadow mask, growing the atlas), which move by under 1 % either way between runs. The bytes of the benchmarks that make no allocation ( UpdateThousandInstances ' 12–14 KB, a frame's 13–14 or 125–134 B) are their setup, or the first frame's growth, spread over however many runs the benchmark chose; no frame allocates, and the AllocsPerRun tests still say so. ← All the documentation

How it was done Every package was read against llm-guidelines (and its Go and docs chapters) and against the proposal's two imperatives: a simple, efficient API (is the public API the smallest that does the job? what would a newcomer stumble on?) and performance (what does a frame cost, where does it allocate?). Three tools helped the reading: a small syntax-tree scan of every .go file, whatever its build tags: functions over 40 lines, names of one or two letters, abbreviations, errors.New / fmt.Errorf , panic , printing, exported names without a comment; the baseline benchmarks and memory profiles of the frames that still allocate; go doc of each package, and the imports of go-ui and go-engine, to know who uses what. Nothing was changed while auditing. Line numbers are those of commit 2adf4ce . Hand-written code. proposals/towards-version-1.title: 1. Go Renderer towards 1.0
proposals/towards-version-1.text: 1. Go Renderer towards 1.0 Status: building · Author's approval: proposal ☑ (2026-10-22, with the decisions below) plan ☑ (2026-10-22, "Si") Why Go Renderer is an educational experiment at v0.2.0. Games and libraries (Go UI, go-engine) already build on it, so a version they can trust would help them. Today nothing promises that: Little is checked automatically. Until this branch, no workflow ran the tests. The OpenGL scene renderer is never checked by a program: its tests skip without a display, and a frame that came out wrong would pass. Stub backends. software , vulkan and webgpu are hand-written beginnings of the immediate-mode contract: every call returns "Graphics API not implemented yet!". A newcomer cannot tell that from the folder list. Metal is tried by hand. It runs on the author's Mac only, and newer SDKs (macOS 27) deprecate MTLStorageModeManaged , which its textures use. No releases since v0.2.0. Paths, strokes, fullscreen, pads and DrawOver landed on main since; nothing says what may break between versions. AI-written parts are pending review. The README says so; a 1.0 should not. Central packages are thinly tested. Coverage of windowloop is 6 %, graphics 46 % and scene 50 %. What Id Requirement Check R1 Format, vet and tests run on every push and pull request, and the browser packages are vetted for WebAssembly .github/workflows/test.yaml runs green. Done by feature/docs-and-ci R2 The OpenGL scene renderer is tested automatically: frames of the sample island drawn under Mesa without a display (Xvfb or a surfaceless context), or by a software painter, compared with reference pictures within a tolerance a CI job that draws and compares; a test fails when a pass is broken on purpose R3 Each stub backend ( software , vulkan , webgpu ) is implemented, removed, or marked unavailable with an error code and a line in the docs. They are the author's hand-written code: he decides which the author's decision recorded here; the docs' backend table says the state of each R4 Metal is tried on a real Mac before each release, and builds without deprecation warnings on the newest SDK ( MTLStorageModeManaged replaced where it is deprecated) a checklist line in each release's notes; a clean build log on macOS 27 R5 Releases are tagged with notes, and 1.0 names what stays stable (the Renderer contract? scene , draw2d , input ?) and what may still change. This ties to go-engine's proposal 14 , which needs Go Renderer released first the release page; a page on what 1.0 promises R6 The author reviews the AI-written parts listed in the README, and the AI disclosure says what was reviewed the README's disclosure, updated R7 The central packages are tested where a test proves behaviour ( windowloop 's fullscreen and pads, graphics ' transforms, scene 's bounds and instances); no tests written only to raise a percentage the new tests' names say what must be true; coverage is reported, not targeted Out of scope New features (fills of paths, areas in Metal and the browser): 1.0 is about trust, not reach. Building Android and the 3DS on every push: they need the NDK and a TinyGo fork; go-engine's proposal 14 covers them for the whole family. Changing the hand-written Renderer contract or backends without the author. Decisions The author's answers (2026-10-22): The stub backends ( software , vulkan , webgpu ) stay, to be built later. The docs say so, and every function returns an error that says it is not implemented, with a code. What 1.0 promises: every package. So every package first passes an audit against the author's guidelines (llm-guidelines), and its API is made simple and efficient. Frames in CI: Mesa's software driver under Xvfb. The review: the author reviews every AI-written part once the audit is done and what it asks is simplified or rewritten. The Mac: a MacBook Air M4, where Metal has been tried so far. And above all: performance and a simple API (developer experience) are imperative. Every change of this proposal is weighed by both: an API a newcomer reads in minutes, and frames that cost no more than today, measured. Design One error package. Go Renderer has no error codes today (33 files build errors from text). A small package, failure as in go-engine ( Define , Wrap , codes compared with errors.Is ), is shared by every package; each declares its codes in its own errors.go . The stub backends return <backend>.not-implemented . The audit, before any rewrite. A reviewer reads each package against llm-guidelines (names, size of functions, early returns, error codes, generic names, nothing allocated per frame, comments, tests that prove behaviour, docs) and against the two imperatives: is the API the smallest that does the job, and what does a frame cost. Its findings go in one document, docs/proposals/1-audit.md , package by package, each finding with a severity and what to do. Nothing is changed while auditing: the author reads the findings and the plan of each package before it is rewritten. Measured performance. Before rewriting, the benchmarks that exist (34) are run and kept as a baseline, with new ones where a frame's hot path has none (the scene renderer's frame, a 2D list of three hundred controls, a pad's reading). A change that makes a frame slower or allocate more does not merge. Frames compared in CI. A test draws the sample island and a 2D list under Xvfb with Mesa (llvmpipe) and compares them with reference pictures in the repository, within a tolerance; a pass broken on purpose fails it. The CI installs Mesa and runs it under xvfb-run . Metal. The AI-written Metal renderers use MTLStorageModeShared where Managed is deprecated (it does nothing on Apple silicon); the author's hand-written stubs are left as they are. The release checklist names the MacBook Air M4. 1.0's promise. A page, docs/6-project/3-version-1.md , says that every package is stable from 1.0: what that means (no breaking change without a major version), how a change is deprecated first, and that releases carry notes (go-engine's proposal 14). Tasks [x] T1 — the failure package; the stub backends return <backend>.not-implemented ; the docs' backend table and each stub's page say they come later · R3 · a test per stub that every function returns its code [x] T2 — baseline benchmarks, and new ones for a frame's hot paths · *_bench_test.go · imperatives · the numbers kept in docs/6-project/1-optimization-plan.md [x] T3 — the audit, every package, findings in docs/proposals/1-audit.md (written 2026-10-22; awaits the author) with a plan per package · all · R6, R7 · stop: the author reads it and approves each package's plan [ ] T4 — rewrite package by package as the audit's approved plans say, each with its tests and docs, never slower nor allocating more than the baseline · per package · R6, R7 · tests, benchmarks against the baseline Phases A and B of the audit's order approved by the author for every package (2026-10-22, "Si"): A, no breaking change and a frame's cost first; B, a smaller API that breaks nothing outside. Phases C (breaking, AI-written) and D (his hand-written code) approved too (2026-10-22, "arreglalas todas"), with the decisions recorded in the audit's phases C and D : all of C; in D, Vector / Matrix and whole words, models dissolved by meaning, the contract kept but cleaned, coded errors instead of panics and prints, LoadModel in small functions, a -backend flag, readable gles names; and on the 3DS a warning path that does not link log/slog . Never slower nor allocating more than the After A/B column. [ ] T5 — frames compared in CI under Mesa · opengl , .github/workflows · R2 · the job; a broken pass fails it [ ] T6 — Metal: MTLStorageModeShared where deprecated · metal (AI-written parts) · R4 · builds clean on the newest SDK (on the author's Mac); checklist line [ ] T7 — the 1.0 page, error codes in the troubleshooting chapter, the README's status · docs · R5 · the pages [ ] T8 — the author's review of every AI-written part; the AI disclosure updated · R6 · the README Result Building. R1 is done; T1 added the failure package and the stub backends' codes; T2 kept the benchmarks' baseline in the optimization plan; T3's audit is written; the author approved its phases A and B, which are done : no frame allocates, AI-written errors have codes, and sceneplan and the shader sources left the public API. Phases C and D, approved the same day, are done too, pending his review: the API speaks in whole words, models is window , immediate and camera.Camera , ctr is nintendo3ds , and no library code panics or prints.

reference/android.text: android import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/android" Built only with GOOS=android . Package android runs go-renderer programs as Android applications, with no golang.org/x/mobile and no Java but one class for screen readers (package java): the program is a shared library (-buildmode=c-shared) that Android's own NativeActivity loads. A little C (activity.c) receives the activity's callbacks and starts main; a thread of the program's own holds the OpenGL ES context, waits on an Android looper for touches and the activity's news, and draws only when something happens. Its OpenGL ES calls are direct (gl.go), which matters: going through x/mobile's bindings, which cross to another thread every three calls, was about two thirds of what a 3D view cost on a phone. Functions Function func AskForNotifications() AskForNotifications shows Android's question to allow the program's notifications, on Android 13 and later; the package's manifest must name android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS. func EditText(field uint64, text TextInput, secret bool) EditText tells the on-screen keyboard the text of the field being typed in, so it edits that text: it suggests words from it, composes in it and deletes from it. func Feel(feeling Feeling) Feel gives a buzz of a kind, if the person has touch feedback on. func FeelLongPress() FeelLongPress gives the short buzz Android's own applications give when a touch becomes a long press, if the person has touch feedback on. func Graphics() string Graphics names the phone's OpenGL ES and GPU once the window has drawn, or what stopped it. func LastCrash() string LastCrash is the report of the last run's crash, or "" when it ended well. func NotificationsAllowed() bool NotificationsAllowed tells whether the program may show notifications: always before Android 13, and on Android 13 and later once the person allowed them (AskForNotifications). func Notify(channel Channel, id int, title, text string) bool Notify shows a notification on a channel in the system's shade, as other applications' are, even while the program is in the background: a title and a line, and touching it opens the program. func OpenLink(link string) bool OpenLink opens a link in the application that shows it: a web page in the browser, mailto: in the mail, tel: in the phone, geo: in the maps. func Run(app *window.Application, options Options, draw func(functions GL, fresh bool) error) error Run draws the application in the activity's window until the program ends (Android ends it). func ScreenReaderFocus() int32 ScreenReaderFocus is the node the screen reader is on, which the program rings; 0 for none. func ScreenReaderOn() bool ScreenReaderOn tells whether a screen reader (or another accessibility service) is on: only then is a list of nodes worth making. func Share(title, text string) bool Share offers a text (a link, a note) to the person's other applications, through the system's sheet with a title over it. func ShowAccessibleNodes(nodes []AccessibleNode) ShowAccessibleNodes hands Android what the frame shows, for the screen reader: call it on the drawing goroutine (in a step) with the nodes in reading order. func ShowKeyboard(typing bool) ShowKeyboard asks for the on-screen keyboard while a text field is being typed in, and puts it away when none is: call it in every step (go-ui's window does, with Context.Typing). func SystemPalettes() (Palettes, bool) SystemPalettes returns the phone's palettes as last read, and false on a phone without them (before Android 12) or before the window has read them. func SystemPrefersDark() bool SystemPrefersDark tells whether the phone is in its dark theme, as last read. func TakeTextEdit(field uint64) (TextInput, bool) TakeTextEdit returns what the on-screen keyboard made of a field's text since the last call: its whole text, the selection and the word being composed. func TextScale() float32 TextScale is how much larger the person wants text than the default (Settings › Display › Font size): 1, or 1.3 for a larger text. func Wake() Wake makes the window draw a frame now: for a program whose data changes on another goroutine. Constants and variables var VideoNotOpened = failure.Define("android.video-not-opened", "the video could not be opened") VideoNotOpened is a film the phone's decoders cannot open; the details say what Android said. AccessibleNode AccessibleNode is one thing on the screen a screen reader (TalkBack) reads and acts on: a button, a switch, a line of text. The program's interface makes the list in every frame while a screen reader is on (ScreenReaderOn), and ShowAccessibleNodes hands it to Android. type AccessibleNode struct { // ID tells the node apart from one frame to the next: the same while the thing stays, never 0. ID int32 // Parent is the node it is inside (a list that scrolls), or 0 for the window. Parent int32 // X, Y, Width and Height are where it shows, in layout pixels. X, Y, Width, Height float32 // Class is the Android widget it reads as, such as "android.widget.Button": the screen reader // says its kind from it ("button", "switch"). Class string Label, Value string // what it is called, and what it holds (a field's text) Pressable, LongPressable bool // a double tap presses it; a double tap held long-presses it Checkable, Checked bool // a checkbox, a switch, a radio button, and whether it is on Selected, Disabled bool Scrollable bool // scrolls, or moves a step: a list, a slider Editable, Typing, Secret bool // a field, whether the keyboard types in it, a password Heading bool // Minimum, Maximum and Current are a slider's span and value, when Maximum is above Minimum. Minimum, Maximum, Current float32 } Channel Channel is a channel notifications go on: Android 8 and later list it, by its label, in the application's settings, where the person can turn it off. The label should be in the person's language. type Channel struct { ID, Label string } Function or method func MessagesChannel() Channel MessagesChannel is a channel for the program's messages, with an English label. Feeling Feeling is a kind of buzz a touch gives, as Android's own views give them. type Feeling int const ( // FeelingLongPress is the buzz of a touch that became a long press. Before Android 11 it is a tick. FeelingConfirm // FeelingReject says something went wrong or needs a look. Before Android 11 it is the buzz of a // long press, the strongest the older phones have. Its sound is not played. type Video struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func OpenVideo(path string) (*Video, error) OpenVideo reads a film (MP4 or WebM, as the phone's decoders read it: H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, AV1) from a file and starts decoding its pictures. func (video *Video) Advance(until time.Duration, pixels *image.NRGBA) (changed, ended bool) Advance decodes the film up to a moment and, when a picture due by then has arrived, copies it into pixels (as much of it as fits). func (video *Video) Close() Close lets go of the decoder and the file. func (video *Video) Duration() time.Duration Duration is how long the film lasts; 0 when its file does not say. func (video *Video) Rewind() Rewind goes back to the film's start. func (video *Video) Size() (width, height int) Size is the film's pictures' width and height, in pixels. reference/browser.text: browser import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/browser" Built only with GOOS=js . Package browser runs go-renderer programs in a web browser, built with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm: a canvas stands in for the window, its DOM events become an input.State, WebGL2 draws through the gles renderers, and requestAnimationFrame drives the same fixed-step loop as the desktop, drawing only when something happens. CanvasNotFound = failure.Define("browser.canvas-not-found", "the page has no canvas with that id") // WebGL2Missing is a browser that cannot give the canvas a WebGL2 context.
