reference/camera.title: camera
reference/camera.text: camera import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/camera" Package camera is where a scene is seen from (a Lens) and the controllers that move it. Controllers are independent of the graphics backend: they read an input.State and write a Lens. A GroundFunc lets them follow a terrain without knowing about it. Constants and variables const ( DefaultFieldOfViewRadians = math.Pi / 4 DefaultNear = 0.1 DefaultFar = 1000 ) Default projection values, used where a Lens's fields are zero. Controller Controller moves a camera from input. type Controller interface { Update(state *input.State, seconds float64, camera *Lens) } GroundFunc GroundFunc returns the ground height at (x, z) in world units, and false when there is no ground there. type GroundFunc func(x, z float32) (float32, bool) Lens Lens is where a scene is seen from: a position looking at a target, with up saying which way is up, and how the view is projected onto the screen. type Lens struct { Position graphics.Vector Target graphics.Vector Up graphics.Vector // FieldOfViewRadians is the vertical field of view; 0 is DefaultFieldOfViewRadians. FieldOfViewRadians float32 // Near and Far are the distances of the clipping planes; 0 is DefaultNear and DefaultFar. Near float32 Far float32 // OrthographicHeight, when above 0, makes the camera orthographic: no perspective, and this // many world units fit between the bottom and the top of the screen. Maps and isometric views // use it; 0 keeps the perspective of FieldOfViewRadians. OrthographicHeight float32 } Function or method func (camera Lens) IsOrthographic() bool IsOrthographic tells whether the camera has no perspective. func (camera Lens) Projection() (fieldOfViewRadians, near, far float32) Projection returns the camera's field of view (radians) and clipping planes, with the defaults where its fields are zero. func (camera Lens) ProjectionMatrix(aspect float64) graphics.Matrix ProjectionMatrix returns the camera's projection for OpenGL, perspective or orthographic, for a screen of this width over height. Map Map looks at the ground like a map, without perspective: from straight above, with north up, or isometric, from 35.26° up and at 45° to the axes, like the drawings of a town in an atlas. Any drag moves the map with the cursor, scroll and +/- zoom, arrows move it too, and Q and E turn it a quarter. type Map struct { Target graphics.Vector Span float64 // world units from the bottom to the top of the screen Isometric bool Turns int // quarter turns: 0 has north up in the top view Distance float64 // how far the camera stands from the target, so the whole scene is in front of it MinimumSpan float64 MaximumSpan float64 ZoomSpeed float64 // fraction of the span per scroll step TargetLimits [4]float32 // optional: minimum x, maximum x, minimum z, maximum z (all zero = none) Ground GroundFunc VerticalScale float32 // scale applied to ground heights (vertical exaggeration); 0 = 1 } Function or method func NewMap(target graphics.Vector, sceneSize float32) *Map NewMap returns a map of a scene of the given size (in world units), showing all of it. func (view *Map) Update(state *input.State, seconds float64, camera *Lens) Update applies this frame's input and places the camera. Orbit Orbit rotates around a target: left drag rotates, right drag (or shift + left drag) pans, scroll zooms. Arrow keys rotate and +/- zoom from the keyboard. type Orbit struct { Target graphics.Vector Distance float64 Yaw float64 // radians around the vertical axis Pitch float64 // radians; 0 looks from the horizon, pi/2 from straight above MinimumDistance float64 MaximumDistance float64 RotationSpeed float64 // radians per cursor unit ZoomSpeed float64 // fraction of the distance per scroll step Ground GroundFunc GroundClearance float32 // minimum camera height above the ground TargetLimits [4]float32 // optional: minimum x, maximum x, minimum z, maximum z (all zero = none) VerticalScale float32 // scale applied to ground heights (vertical exaggeration); 0 = 1 } Function or method func NewOrbit(target graphics.Vector, sceneSize float32) *Orbit NewOrbit returns an orbit controller with sensible defaults for a scene of the given size (in world units). func (orbit *Orbit) Gesture(gesture input.Gesture, windowWidth, windowHeight int) Gesture applies what two fingers did (input.TwoFingers), as a map does: the ground that was between the fingers stays between them while they spread (closer), turn (the view turns with them) and move together. func (orbit *Orbit) Update(state *input.State, seconds float64, camera *Lens) Update applies this frame's input and places the camera. Ray Ray is a half-line in the scene as it is drawn: from Origin along Direction (of length 1). Heights are drawn heights, already multiplied by the scene's vertical exaggeration. type Ray struct { Origin, Direction graphics.Vector } Function or method func RayThrough(view Lens, width, height int, x, y float64) (Ray, bool) RayThrough returns the ray from the camera through a point of the window: x and y in window pixels from the top-left corner of a window width × height pixels (where the pointer is). func (ray Ray) At(distance float32) graphics.Vector At returns the point at a distance along the ray. func (ray Ray) PointAtHeight(height float32) (graphics.Vector, bool) PointAtHeight returns where the ray meets the horizontal plane at a drawn height: a flat floor, a table top. func (ray Ray) PointOnGround(ground func(x, z float32) (float32, bool), verticalScale, lowest, highest float32) (graphics.Vector, bool) PointOnGround returns the first point where the ray meets a relief: ground gives the height of the ground at a point (in true heights, as scene.Scene.GroundHeight does, false where there is none), verticalScale is the exaggeration it is drawn with, and lowest and highest bound the ground's true heights (the scene's bounds), so the search only covers where it can be. Walk Walk is a first-person controller that stays on the ground: WASD or arrows move, the mouse looks around (while a button is held, or always when the cursor is locked), shift runs. type Walk struct { X, Z float32 Yaw float64 // radians; 0 looks towards -Z Pitch float64 // radians; positive looks up EyeHeight float32 Speed float32 // world units per second RunFactor float32 LookSpeed float64 // radians per cursor unit Ground GroundFunc Blocked func(x, z float32) bool // optional: true where the walker cannot go (water, walls) VerticalScale float32 // 0 = 1 } Function or method func NewWalk(x, z, eyeHeight, speed float32) *Walk NewWalk returns a walker at (x, z) with defaults for the given eye height and walking speed. func (walk *Walk) Steer(forward, sideways float32, seconds float64) Steer walks as a stick on a phone's screen says: forward and sideways from -1 to 1 (right and ahead positive), at the walking speed. func (walk *Walk) Turn(deltaX, deltaY float64) Turn looks around by a finger's movement, in layout pixels: right turns right, down looks down. func (walk *Walk) Update(state *input.State, seconds float64, camera *Lens) Update applies this frame's input and places the camera at eye height. ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

reference/draw2d.title: draw2d
reference/draw2d.text: draw2d import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/draw2d" Package draw2d is a list of flat shapes to draw over the 3D view, in screen space: rounded rectangles with a border, soft shadows, lines of text and icons, each optionally clipped to a rectangle and placed on a layer. A program (or an interface library) fills a List every frame; a backend paints it on top of everything else. Coordinates are layout pixels with the origin at the top-left corner of the window: the same units as the cursor in input.State. The backend multiplies them by the screen's density (2 on a high-density screen), so a 13-pixel text has the same size on every screen and stays sharp. The package does no drawing and needs no graphics context: it is plain data, easy to build and to check in tests. Constants and variables var ( // InvalidColour is a colour that is not written as "#rrggbb" or "#rrggbbaa". InvalidColour = failure.Define("draw2d.invalid-colour", "a colour must be written as #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa") // ImageNotDecoded is a picture that is not a PNG, JPEG or GIF, or is damaged. ImageNotDecoded = failure.Define("draw2d.image-not-decoded", "the picture could not be decoded") ) Codes of the errors draw2d returns. var Transparent = Color{} Transparent paints nothing. Color Color is a straight (not premultiplied) RGBA colour, each channel from 0 to 1, as seen on screen: it is not gamma-corrected like the lit scene. type Color [4]float32 Function or method func MustHex(text string) Color Hex reads a colour written as "#rrggbb" or "#rrggbbaa". func ParseHex(text string) (Color, error) ParseHex reads a colour written as on a web page, "#rrggbb", "#rrggbbaa" or the short "#rgb"; InvalidColour otherwise. func (color Color) IsVisible() bool IsVisible tells whether the colour paints anything. func (color Color) Mix(other Color, amount float32) Color Mix blends towards another colour: 0 keeps this one, 1 gives the other. func (color Color) WithAlpha(opacity float32) Color WithAlpha returns the colour with its alpha multiplied by an opacity. Command Command is one shape of the list. Only the fields of its kind are used; keeping every kind in one flat struct lets a list be reused frame after frame without allocating. type Command struct { Kind Kind Area Rectangle // the rectangle, the shadow's caster, the icon's square Layer int // higher layers cover lower ones; within a layer, later commands cover earlier ones Clip Rectangle // nothing is drawn outside it, when HasClip HasClip bool Radius float32 // rectangle and shadow: corner radius Fill Color // rectangle: inside; shadow, text, icon: their colour Border Color // rectangle: the outline BorderWidth float32 // rectangle: outline thickness, inside the area Blur float32 // shadow: how far it fades out; Area is the caster grown by it and moved down. Backdrop: how far what is behind spreads (a standard deviation, as CSS's blur()) Text string // text: the line; icon: the icon's name (one field for both keeps a Command small) Size float32 // text and icon: size in layout pixels (the font's em square) Weight Weight // text Baseline float32 // text: y of the baseline; the line starts at Area.X Picture *Image // image: what it shows; Fill tints it (white shows it as it is) } Image Image is a picture a list draws: a photo, a map tile, a video's frame. A program makes one for each picture it shows and keeps it between frames, so the backend uploads its pixels once. To show other pixels in it (the next frame of a video), the program writes them into Pixels and calls Changed. type Image struct { // Pixels are the picture's colours, not premultiplied by their opacity. Pixels *image.NRGBA // Sharp draws the picture scaled to the nearest pixel, as pixel art wants, instead of blended // between pixels. On the 3DS it holds for every picture of a frame that shows a sharp one. Sharp bool // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func DecodeImage(reader io.Reader) (*Image, error) DecodeImage reads a PNG, JPEG or GIF picture (a file the program embeds, a download) into an Image. func NewBlankImage(width, height int) *Image NewBlankImage makes an Image of a size, transparent, for pixels the program writes itself (a video's frames). func NewImage(picture image.Image) *Image NewImage makes an Image of a decoded picture (image.Decode's PNG, JPEG or GIF), turning its colours into straight RGBA. func (picture *Image) Changed() Changed tells the backend that Pixels hold another picture of the same size, to upload again. func (picture *Image) ID() uint64 ID tells images apart for the life of the program. func (picture *Image) Size() (width, height int) Size is the picture's width and height in pixels. func (picture *Image) Version() uint64 Version counts the times the picture changed (Changed). Kind Kind says what a command draws. type Kind int const ( RectangleKind Kind = iota // a rounded rectangle with a fill and a border ShadowKind // a soft shadow under a rounded rectangle TextKind // one line of text IconKind // one icon ImageKind // a picture covering a rounded rectangle BackdropKind // what is behind a rounded rectangle, blurred: frosted glass PointLightKind // a disc of light: Area the square round its outer radius, Radius its inner one, Fill its colour (alpha: intensity) SpriteLightKind // a picture shining as a light over Area, tinted by Fill (alpha: intensity) LightingKind // lights what was drawn before it with the lights before it, over an ambient colour (Fill) ) List List collects the commands of a frame. The zero value is an empty list ready to use. type List struct { Commands []Command // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (list *List) Backdrop(area Rectangle, radius, blur float32) Backdrop shows, inside a rounded rectangle, what was drawn behind it, blurred: the frosted glass under a translucent panel, whose Rectangle comes next, over it. func (list *List) Fingerprint(seed maphash.Seed) uint64 Fingerprint sums up everything the list draws in one number: two lists with the same fingerprint draw the same picture (barring a hash collision). func (list *List) Icon(name string, x, y, size float32, color Color) Icon draws an icon by name (a Lucide icon, https://lucide.dev ) filling a square of size pixels whose top-left corner is at (x, y). func (list *List) Image(picture *Image, area Rectangle, radius float32, tint Color) Image draws a picture covering a rounded rectangle: scaled to fill it, and cropped evenly at the sides or at the top and bottom when their shapes differ, as photos fill cards and avatars. func (list *List) IsEmpty() bool IsEmpty tells whether the list has nothing to draw. func (list *List) Lighting(ambient Color) Lighting lights what was drawn before it in the list, in its layer and those under it, with the lights added since the last Lighting, over an ambient colour (its alpha, the ambient's intensity: 1 is plain daylight, less dims what no light reaches). func (list *List) PointLight(x, y, inner, outer float32, color Color) PointLight adds a disc of light round a point (x, y): full inside inner, fading to nothing at outer, in layout pixels, of a colour whose alpha is its intensity. func (list *List) PopClip() PopClip returns to the clip before the last PushClip. func (list *List) PushClip(area Rectangle) PushClip limits the following commands to a rectangle, inside the current clip if there is one. func (list *List) Rectangle(area Rectangle, radius float32, fill, border Color, borderWidth float32) Rectangle draws a rounded rectangle: fill inside, and a border of a width drawn inside the area. func (list *List) Reset() Reset empties the list, keeping its memory for the next frame. func (list *List) SetLayer(layer int) SetLayer makes the following commands go on a layer: for example 0 for panels, 1 for menus that open over them and 2 for tooltips. func (list *List) Shadow(area Rectangle, radius, blur, offsetY float32, color Color) Shadow draws a soft shadow for a rounded rectangle, fading out over blur pixels on every side and falling offsetY pixels below it. func (list *List) SpriteLight(picture *Image, area Rectangle, color Color) SpriteLight adds a picture shining as a light over an area, tinted by a colour whose alpha is its intensity: a lamp's glow, a sign that shines. func (list *List) Stroke(path *Path, x, y, scale, width float32, color Color) Stroke draws a path's line, width layout pixels wide, in a colour: the path's point (0, 0) goes at (x, y) of the screen and each of its units is scale layout pixels. func (list *List) Text(text string, x, baseline, size float32, weight Weight, color Color) Text draws one line of text starting at x, with its baseline at baseline. Measurer Measurer measures text the way the backend draws it, so that what is laid out is what is painted. scale is the screen's density (framebuffer pixels per layout pixel): text is drawn at size·scale pixels, whose widths do not always scale exactly. type Measurer interface { MeasureText(text string, size float32, weight Weight, scale float32) TextMetrics // HasIcon tells whether an icon name is known to the backend. HasIcon(name string) bool } Path Path is a line made of straight pieces and curves. Build it with MoveTo, LineTo, CurveTo and Close, or with Circle and RoundedRectangle; keep it, and draw it with List.Stroke. type Path struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (path *Path) Bounds() Rectangle Bounds is the smallest rectangle, in the path's units, that holds every point of it. func (path *Path) Circle(centreX, centreY, radius float32) Circle adds a circle about a centre, as a run of its own. func (path *Path) Close() Close draws a straight piece back to where the run began. func (path *Path) CurveTo(firstX, firstY, secondX, secondY, x, y float32) CurveTo draws a cubic Bézier curve from the last point to (x, y), pulled towards two control points, as SVG's C does. func (path *Path) LineTo(x, y float32) LineTo draws a straight piece from the last point to another; with no point before, it starts there. func (path *Path) MoveTo(x, y float32) MoveTo starts a new run of the line at a point. func (path *Path) RoundedRectangle(x, y, width, height, radius float32) RoundedRectangle adds a rectangle with rounded corners, as a run of its own; a radius larger than half a side is made half of it. Point Point is a place in a path's units. type Point struct{ X, Y float32 } Rectangle Rectangle is an area of the screen: its top-left corner and its size, in layout pixels. type Rectangle struct { X, Y, Width, Height float32 } Function or method func (rect Rectangle) Bottom() float32 Bottom is the y of the rectangle's bottom edge. func (rect Rectangle) Contains(x, y float32) bool Contains tells whether a point is inside the rectangle (left and top edges included). func (rect Rectangle) Inset(amount float32) Rectangle Inset shrinks the rectangle by an amount on every side. func (rect Rectangle) Intersect(other Rectangle) Rectangle Intersect returns the area two rectangles share; it is empty when they do not overlap. func (rect Rectangle) IsEmpty() bool IsEmpty tells whether the rectangle covers no area. func (rect Rectangle) Right() float32 Right is the x of the rectangle's right edge. TextMetrics TextMetrics are the measures of a line of text, in layout pixels. type TextMetrics struct { Width float32 // how far the line reaches from its start Ascent float32 // from the baseline up to the top of the tallest letters Descent float32 // from the baseline down to the bottom of the lowest letters } Function or method func (metrics TextMetrics) Height() float32 Height is the line's height: ascent plus descent. Weight Weight is how heavy a text is drawn. type Weight int const ( Regular Weight = iota // body text Medium // labels that should stand out a little Bold // titles Mono // codes and keys, in a monospaced face, so they stand apart from words ) ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

reference/failure.title: failure
reference/failure.text: failure import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/failure" Package failure gives every error Go Renderer returns a code: a stable name, as "loaders.model-not-found", that a program can check and a person can search for. A code is declared once, as a package-level variable, and is itself an error: var ModelNotFound = failure.Define("loaders.model-not-found", "the model file does not exist") Returning the code alone allocates nothing and comparing it is comparing two pointers, as cheap as Go's own sentinel errors. When the error needs its details (which file, what went wrong underneath), Wrap makes one error with them; that happens while loading or building, never in a frame. Callers check an error by its code, wrapped or not: if failure.Is(err, loaders.ModelNotFound) { … } errors.Is works the same way, since an error made by Wrap answers to its code. reference/gles.title: gles
reference/gles.text: gles import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/gles" Package gles draws go-renderer's flat interfaces and a simple 3D scene through OpenGL ES, the graphics interface both browsers (as WebGL2) and Android phones offer. It makes no graphics calls of its own: it talks to a small interface, Functions, that each platform implements (the browser package through syscall/js, an Android window through golang.org/x/mobile/gl). So the renderers are written once, in plain Go with no cgo, and tested on any computer with a fake. It uses only what OpenGL ES 2.0 has, plus 32-bit indices (an extension every current phone has): golang.org/x/mobile/gl knows nothing newer on Android, and WebGL2 accepts it all. So the shaders are GLSL ES 1.00, there are no vertex array objects (each draw describes its vertices) and the atlas is a LUMINANCE texture. Desktop programs keep using the opengl and metal packages; nothing here replaces them. Constants and variables var ( // ShaderNotCompiled is a shader the driver would not compile. ShaderNotCompiled = failure.Define("gles.shader-not-compiled", "the driver could not compile a shader") // ProgramNotLinked is a pair of shaders the driver would not link into a program. ProgramNotLinked = failure.Define("gles.program-not-linked", "the driver could not link a program") ) Codes of the errors the renderers return when they are made. Buffer Handles name objects the graphics driver keeps. 0 is never a valid one. type Buffer uint32 Enum Enum is an OpenGL ES constant. The values are the ones the OpenGL ES 3.0 and WebGL2 specifications give, so every implementation passes them through unchanged. type Enum uint32 const ( Triangles Enum = 0x0004 ColorBufferBit Enum = 0x00004000 DepthBufferBit Enum = 0x00000100 Blend Enum = 0x0BE2 DepthTest Enum = 0x0B71 Zero Enum = 0 One Enum = 1 SourceColor Enum = 0x0300 DestinationColor Enum = 0x0306 SourceAlpha Enum = 0x0302 OneMinusSourceAlpha Enum = 0x0303 LessOrEqual Enum = 0x0203 ArrayBuffer Enum = 0x8892 ElementArrayBuffer Enum = 0x8893 StaticDraw Enum = 0x88E4 StreamDraw Enum = 0x88E0 Float Enum = 0x1406 UnsignedByte Enum = 0x1401 UnsignedInt Enum = 0x1405 VertexShader Enum = 0x8B31 FragmentShader Enum = 0x8B30 Texture2D Enum = 0x0DE1 TextureUnit0 Enum = 0x84C0 TextureMinFilter Enum = 0x2801 TextureMagFilter Enum = 0x2800 TextureWrapS Enum = 0x2802 TextureWrapT Enum = 0x2803 Linear Enum = 0x2601 ClampToEdge Enum = 0x812F Luminance Enum = 0x1909 RGB Enum = 0x1907 RGBA Enum = 0x1908 UnpackAlignment Enum = 0x0CF5 Nearest Enum = 0x2600 FramebufferTarget Enum = 0x8D40 ColorAttachment0 Enum = 0x8CE0 ) The constants the renderers use. FlatRenderer FlatRenderer draws a 2D draw list on a plain background, with no scene, sky or camera: the window of an application that is only an interface. It does what opengl.FlatRenderer does on the desktop, with the same atlas and one draw call per frame. Create and use it where the graphics context lives. type FlatRenderer struct { // Target is the framebuffer Draw draws into: 0, the screen, unless the caller made one to // draw a picture offscreen. Target Framebuffer // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func NewFlatRenderer(functions Functions, fonts overlay.Fonts) (*FlatRenderer, error) NewFlatRenderer compiles the shaders and prepares the atlas; text is drawn in fonts (overlay.Fonts{} for the default ones). func (renderer *FlatRenderer) Draw(list *draw2d.List, background draw2d.Color, width, height int, scale float32) Draw clears the target framebuffer (width × height pixels) to the background colour and paints the list. Framebuffer Framebuffer 0 is the screen's own: it can be bound, though no call made it. type Framebuffer uint32 Functions Functions is the part of OpenGL ES 2.0 the renderers need. An implementation must be used from the goroutine (and thread) that owns the graphics context. Its methods are named in words (SetUniformInteger, SetTextureImage), so a reader new to OpenGL can follow the renderers; each comment gives the OpenGL ES function it stands for (glUniform1i, glTexImage2D), for a reader who knows OpenGL or looks it up. type Functions interface { // CreateShader is glCreateShader. CreateShader(stage Enum) Shader // SetShaderSource is glShaderSource. SetShaderSource(shader Shader, source string) // CompileShader is glCompileShader. CompileShader(shader Shader) // ShaderCompiled reports whether the last compilation worked, and the compiler's log. // (OpenGL ES: glGetShaderiv(GL_COMPILE_STATUS) and glGetShaderInfoLog.) ShaderCompiled(shader Shader) (bool, string) // DeleteShader is glDeleteShader. DeleteShader(shader Shader) // CreateProgram is glCreateProgram. CreateProgram() Program // AttachShader is glAttachShader. AttachShader(program Program, shader Shader) // LinkProgram is glLinkProgram. LinkProgram(program Program) // ProgramLinked reports whether the last link worked, and the linker's log. // (OpenGL ES: glGetProgramiv(GL_LINK_STATUS) and glGetProgramInfoLog.) ProgramLinked(program Program) (bool, string) // BindAttributeLocation gives an attribute its index; it takes effect at the next link. // (OpenGL ES: glBindAttribLocation.) BindAttributeLocation(program Program, index uint32, name string) // UseProgram is glUseProgram. UseProgram(program Program) // UniformLocation is glGetUniformLocation. UniformLocation(program Program, name string) Uniform // SetUniformInteger is glUniform1i. SetUniformInteger(location Uniform, value int32) // SetUniformFloat is glUniform1f. SetUniformFloat(location Uniform, value float32) // SetUniformTwoFloats is glUniform2f. SetUniformTwoFloats(location Uniform, first, second float32) // SetUniformThreeFloats is glUniform3f. SetUniformThreeFloats(location Uniform, first, second, third float32) // SetUniformFourFloats is glUniform4f. SetUniformFourFloats(location Uniform, first, second, third, fourth float32) // SetUniformMatrix3By3 is glUniformMatrix3fv. SetUniformMatrix3By3(location Uniform, matrix [9]float32) // SetUniformMatrix4By4 is glUniformMatrix4fv. SetUniformMatrix4By4(location Uniform, matrix [16]float32) // CreateBuffer is glGenBuffers. CreateBuffer() Buffer // BindBuffer is glBindBuffer. BindBuffer(target Enum, buffer Buffer) // SetBufferData replaces a buffer's contents with these bytes. // (OpenGL ES: glBufferData.) SetBufferData(target Enum, data []byte, usage Enum) // EnableVertexAttribute is glEnableVertexAttribArray. EnableVertexAttribute(index uint32) // DisableVertexAttribute is glDisableVertexAttribArray. DisableVertexAttribute(index uint32) // DescribeVertexAttribute describes attribute index in the bound array buffer: size values of // type kind each, stride bytes apart, the first offset bytes in. // (OpenGL ES: glVertexAttribPointer.) DescribeVertexAttribute(index uint32, size int, kind Enum, normalized bool, stride, offset int) // CreateTexture is glGenTextures. CreateTexture() Texture // SelectTextureUnit is glActiveTexture. SelectTextureUnit(unit Enum) // BindTexture is glBindTexture. BindTexture(target Enum, texture Texture) // SetTextureParameter is glTexParameteri. SetTextureParameter(target, name Enum, value int32) // SetPixelStorage is glPixelStorei. SetPixelStorage(name Enum, value int32) // SetTextureImage is glTexImage2D. SetTextureImage(target Enum, level int, internalFormat Enum, width, height int, format, kind Enum, pixels []byte) // ReplaceTexturePart replaces a rectangle of the bound texture's pixels, given row after row. // (OpenGL ES: glTexSubImage2D.) ReplaceTexturePart(target Enum, level, x, y, width, height int, format, kind Enum, pixels []byte) // CopyFramebufferToTexture copies a rectangle of the bound framebuffer (x, y from its bottom left) // into the bound texture at xOffset, yOffset. // (OpenGL ES: glCopyTexSubImage2D.) CopyFramebufferToTexture(target Enum, level, xOffset, yOffset, x, y, width, height int) // DeleteTexture is glDeleteTextures. DeleteTexture(texture Texture) // Framebuffers let a pass draw into a texture: the backdrop's blur. SetTextureImage with no pixels // makes the texture they draw into. // (OpenGL ES: glGenFramebuffers.) CreateFramebuffer() Framebuffer // BindFramebuffer is glBindFramebuffer. BindFramebuffer(target Enum, framebuffer Framebuffer) // AttachTextureToFramebuffer is glFramebufferTexture2D. AttachTextureToFramebuffer(target, attachment, textureTarget Enum, texture Texture, level int) // DeleteFramebuffer is glDeleteFramebuffers. DeleteFramebuffer(framebuffer Framebuffer) // SetViewport is glViewport. SetViewport(x, y, width, height int) // SetClearColor is glClearColor. SetClearColor(red, green, blue, alpha float32) // Clear is glClear. Clear(mask Enum) // Enable is glEnable. Enable(capability Enum) // Disable is glDisable. Disable(capability Enum) // SetBlendFactors is glBlendFuncSeparate. SetBlendFactors(sourceColor, destinationColor, sourceAlpha, destinationAlpha Enum) // SetDepthWrite is glDepthMask. SetDepthWrite(write bool) // SetDepthFunction is glDepthFunc. SetDepthFunction(function Enum) // DrawArrays is glDrawArrays. DrawArrays(mode Enum, first, count int) // DrawElements is glDrawElements. DrawElements(mode Enum, count int, kind Enum, offset int) } Program Handles name objects the graphics driver keeps. 0 is never a valid one. type Program uint32 SceneRenderer SceneRenderer draws a scene.Scene in its simplest form: lit meshes and instances, the light of the time of day, fog, translucent water and, over them, the overlay (labels, header, notices and the program's draw list). What a frame draws (culling, levels of detail, order) is planned by sceneplan, like on the desktop. It is a first step, not the desktop renderer: there are no shadows, sky dome, procedural patterns, waves, wind or snow. OpenGL ES 2 cannot draw instances, so each batch of instances is made into one mesh on the processor, again only when it changes. type SceneRenderer struct { // OverlayScale is framebuffer pixels per layout pixel, so labels and interfaces keep their // size on a high-density screen (0 = 1). OverlayScale float32 // Target is the framebuffer Draw draws into: 0, the screen, unless the caller made one to // draw a picture offscreen. Target Framebuffer // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func NewSceneRenderer(functions Functions, fonts overlay.Fonts) (*SceneRenderer, error) NewSceneRenderer compiles the shaders and prepares the overlay's atlas; the overlay's text is drawn in fonts (overlay.Fonts{} for the default ones). func (renderer *SceneRenderer) Draw(world *scene.Scene, camera camera.Lens, width, height int) Draw draws a frame of the scene seen by the camera, in the target framebuffer of width × height pixels. Shader Handles name objects the graphics driver keeps. 0 is never a valid one. type Shader uint32 Texture Handles name objects the graphics driver keeps. 0 is never a valid one. type Texture uint32 Uniform Uniform is where a program reads a uniform value; -1 when the program has none of that name (the compiler drops uniforms it does not use). type Uniform int32 ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

reference/immediate.title: immediate
reference/immediate.text: immediate import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/immediate" Package immediate is the immediate-mode drawing contract: a program asks a Renderer for a shape every frame, and the backend (OpenGL today; software, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU as stubs) draws it at once. Nothing is kept between frames, which makes it the simplest way to put a triangle on the screen. Scenes that last (a glTF world, an interface) use the retained renderers instead. Mesh Mesh is a list of vertices and, optionally, the indices that join them into triangles: three indices per triangle. Without indices, every three vertices make a triangle. type Mesh struct { Vertices []graphics.Vector Indices []uint32 } Model Model is a set of meshes drawn together, as a file loaded with loaders.LoadModel. type Model struct { Meshes []Mesh } Renderer Renderer draws shapes at once, with the matrices last given to SetMatrices. shader names the shader to draw with; nil is the backend's own. fill draws the inside of a shape, not only its edges. A backend that cannot draw a shape yet returns its not-implemented error code. type Renderer interface { // RenderPolygon draws a flat polygon through the coordinates. RenderPolygon(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, coordinates []graphics.Vector, shader *string, fill bool) error // RenderTriangle draws triangles, three coordinates each. RenderTriangle(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, coordinates []graphics.Vector, shader *string, fill bool) error // RenderRectangle draws a rectangle of width × height centred on centre. RenderRectangle(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, centre graphics.Vector, width float32, height float32, shader *string, fill bool) error // RenderImage draws an encoded picture (PNG, JPEG) of width × height centred on centre. RenderImage(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, bytes []byte, centre graphics.Vector, width float32, height float32, shader *string) error // RenderObject draws triangles of a 3D object, three vertices each. RenderObject(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, vertices []graphics.Vector, shader *string) error // RenderModel draws every mesh of a model. RenderModel(space graphics.CoordinateSpace, model *Model, shader *string) error // SetMatrices sets the projection, view and model matrices the next shapes are drawn with. SetMatrices(projection, view, model graphics.Matrix) } ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

reference/input.title: input
reference/input.text: input import "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" Package input holds a backend-independent snapshot of keyboard and mouse state. Window backends (GLFW for OpenGL today, others later) feed events into a State; applications, camera controllers and simulations only read from it. Besides what is held, a State remembers what happened since the last update step: keys and buttons that went down or up, keys repeated by the system, the characters typed and how many clicks a press makes (a double click). An interface drawn over the view can claim the mouse or the keyboard for a step, so the camera does not move while a slider is dragged or a name typed. Constants and variables const ( MultiClickInterval = 400 * time.Millisecond MultiClickDistancePixels = 4.0 ) MultiClickInterval is the longest pause between the presses of a double click, and MultiClickDistancePixels how far, in window coordinates, the pointer may move between them. Clipboard Clipboard is the system clipboard, given by the backend. type Clipboard interface { ClipboardText() string SetClipboardText(text string) } CursorShape CursorShape is the look of the mouse pointer. type CursorShape int const ( CursorArrow CursorShape = iota // the default pointer CursorText // an I-beam, over text that can be edited CursorHand // a pointing hand, over something to click CursorResizeHorizontal // a left-right arrow, over an edge to drag sideways CursorResizeVertical // an up-down arrow, over an edge to drag up or down CursorMove // four arrows, over something to drag around ) Feed Feed is the side of a State that backends write: the keys, buttons, pointer, touches and pads they hear of, and the end of each frame. Programs read the State itself and only need Feed to play input to their own code in tests. It is a small value that holds the state, so calling state.Feed() for each event costs nothing. type Feed struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (feed Feed) AddCharacter(character rune) AddCharacter records a character typed, after the keyboard layout and dead keys (called by the backend): "ñ" is one character, whatever keys made it. func (feed Feed) AddHorizontalScroll(delta float64) AddHorizontalScroll records sideways scroll movement (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) AddScroll(delta float64) AddScroll records scroll movement (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) BackUnanswered() bool BackUnanswered tells whether the last step had a back that nobody took, once, for the backend to leave the program. func (feed Feed) ClearTouches() ClearTouches takes every finger off, when the system takes a gesture over (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) EndFrame() EndFrame clears per-frame movement, presses, typed characters and claims; the backend calls it after each update step. func (feed Feed) HasInput() bool HasInput tells whether anything arrived during this step: keys, characters, buttons, pointer movement or scrolling. func (feed Feed) LiftTouch(finger int64) LiftTouch takes a finger off the screen (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) MoveCursor(x, y float64) MoveCursor records a new cursor position (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) PointerLeaves() PointerLeaves takes the pointer off the window once this frame ends: a finger lifted from a touch screen leaves nothing under it, so no control stays lit as if a mouse rested on it. func (feed Feed) PressBack() PressBack records the system's back: a phone's back gesture or button (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) RepeatKey(key Key) RepeatKey records that the system repeated a held key (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) SetButton(button MouseButton, isDown bool) SetButton records a mouse button transition (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) SetKey(key Key, isDown bool) SetKey records a key transition (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) SetPadButton(button PadButton, isDown bool) SetPadButton records a game pad's button as held or let go; going down presses it this frame. func (feed Feed) SetPadLayout(layout PadLayout) SetPadLayout records the layout of the pad being read; the backend sets it when a pad connects. func (feed Feed) SetRightStick(x, y float64) SetRightStick sets a game pad's second stick (a New 3DS's C-stick, a pad's right one). func (feed Feed) SetStick(x, y float64) SetStick sets a game pad's main stick (a console's circle pad, a pad's left stick), from -1 to 1 each way, right and up positive. func (feed Feed) SetTouch(finger int64, x, y float64) SetTouch puts a finger down, or moves it (called by the backend). func (feed Feed) TakeFrameRequest() (time.Duration, bool) TakeFrameRequest returns how long until the frame asked for with RequestFrame (0 when it is due) and forgets the request; false when none was made (called by the backend). MouseButton MouseButton is a backend-independent mouse button. type MouseButton int const ( MouseLeft MouseButton = iota MouseRight MouseMiddle ) The mouse buttons a State knows. PadButton PadButton is a game pad's button. type PadButton int const ( PadA PadButton = iota PadB PadX PadY PadLeftShoulder PadRightShoulder PadBack PadStart PadGuide PadLeftThumb // pressing the left stick in PadRightThumb PadUp PadRight PadDown PadLeft ) The buttons of a game pad, in that one layout. PadLayout PadLayout is the naming of a pad's buttons, after the maker of the pad. type PadLayout int const ( // XboxLayout is the default: an Xbox pad's names, the layout most pads copy. XboxLayout PadLayout = iota // PlayStationLayout names the face buttons ✕ ○ □ △. PlayStationLayout // NintendoLayout swaps A with B and X with Y, as a Nintendo pad prints them. NintendoLayout ) Function or method func PadLayoutFromGUID(guid string) PadLayout PadLayoutFromGUID is the layout of a pad from its SDL-style GUID (as GLFW gives it), whose bytes 4 and 5 are the vendor, little-endian: "030000004c05…" is a Sony pad. func PadLayoutFromName(name string) PadLayout PadLayoutFromName is the layout of a pad from the name a browser gives it (the Gamepad API's id), which holds the vendor: Chrome writes "… Vendor: 054c Product: 09cc)", Firefox starts with "054c-09cc-…". func PadLayoutFromVendor(vendor uint16) PadLayout PadLayoutFromVendor is the layout of a pad made by a USB vendor. State State is the input state for the current frame. type State struct { CursorX, CursorY float64 // cursor position in window coordinates CursorDeltaX float64 // cursor movement since the previous frame CursorDeltaY float64 ScrollDelta float64 // vertical scroll since the previous frame ScrollDeltaX float64 // horizontal scroll since the previous frame (trackpads, tilting wheels) FramebufferWidth int // updated by the backend FramebufferHeight int WindowWidth int // window size in cursor coordinates WindowHeight int // Clipboard is set by the backend; nil when there is no system clipboard (tests, headless). Clipboard Clipboard // Now tells the time, for double clicks; nil = time.Now. Tests set it to a fake clock. Now func() time.Time // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func NewState() *State NewState returns an empty input state. func (state *State) AnyHeld() bool AnyHeld tells whether a key or a mouse button is being held down: a program that draws on demand keeps drawing while one is, since holding a key (walking forward) sends no events. func (state *State) Button(button MouseButton) bool Button reports whether a mouse button is held. func (state *State) ButtonPressed(button MouseButton) bool ButtonPressed reports whether a mouse button went down during this step. func (state *State) ButtonReleased(button MouseButton) bool ButtonReleased reports whether a mouse button went up during this step. func (state *State) ClaimKeyboard() ClaimKeyboard marks the keyboard as used by an interface during this step (a text field has the focus). func (state *State) ClaimMouse() ClaimMouse marks the mouse as used by an interface during this step (the pointer is over a panel, or dragging a slider): cameras and shortcuts should leave it alone. func (state *State) Clicks(button MouseButton) int Clicks says which click a press during this step was: 1 for a single click, 2 for the second press of a double click, 3 for a triple click; 0 when the button was not pressed. func (state *State) ClipboardText() string ClipboardText returns the text on the system clipboard, or "" without one. func (state *State) CursorLocked() bool CursorLocked reports whether the application asked for a captured cursor. func (state *State) CursorShape() CursorShape CursorShape is the pointer shape the application asked for. func (state *State) Down(key Key) bool Down reports whether a key is held. func (state *State) Feed() Feed Feed returns the side of the state that backends write. func (state *State) Fullscreen() bool Fullscreen reports whether the window is asked to be on the whole screen. func (state *State) KeyboardClaimed() bool KeyboardClaimed tells whether an interface claimed the keyboard during this step. func (state *State) LockCursor(lock bool) LockCursor asks the backend to hide and capture the cursor (first-person look) or release it. func (state *State) MouseClaimed() bool MouseClaimed tells whether an interface claimed the mouse during this step. func (state *State) PadDown(button PadButton) bool PadDown tells whether a game pad's button is held. func (state *State) PadLayout() PadLayout PadLayout is the layout of the pad being read; XboxLayout until the backend sets another. func (state *State) PadPressed(button PadButton) bool PadPressed tells whether a game pad's button went down this frame. func (state *State) Pressed(key Key) bool Pressed reports whether a key went down during this frame. func (state *State) RequestFrame(delay time.Duration) RequestFrame asks the backend for another frame within a delay, even if no input arrives: the next step of an animation, a caret's blink, a tooltip due. func (state *State) RightStick() (x, y float64) RightStick is a game pad's second stick (a New 3DS's C-stick, a pad's right one), as Stick. func (state *State) SetClipboardText(text string) SetClipboardText puts a text on the system clipboard, when there is one. func (state *State) SetCursorShape(shape CursorShape) SetCursorShape asks the backend to show the pointer with a shape; it stays until changed. func (state *State) SetFullscreen(on bool) SetFullscreen asks the backend to show the window on the whole screen, or in a window again. func (state *State) Stick() (x, y float64) Stick is a game pad's main stick where there is one (a console's circle pad, a pad's left stick), from -1 to 1 each way, right and up positive; 0 at rest or without one. func (state *State) TakeBack() bool TakeBack answers the system's back in this step, and tells whether there was one to answer: the part of the program the person is in goes back (a dialog closes, a screen returns to the one before) and returns true; any other part asking after it gets false. func (state *State) Time() time.Time Time is the time now, by Now when it is set (a test's fake clock). func (state *State) Touches() []Touch Touches returns the fingers on the screen now: for gestures of more than one finger (pinch, twist). func (state *State) Typed(key Key) bool Typed reports whether a key went down or was repeated by the system during this step: what text fields use for Backspace or the arrows, so holding them keeps acting. func (state *State) TypedText() string TypedText returns the characters typed during this step, in order. func (state *State) Unclaimed() State Unclaimed returns a copy of the state without what an interface claimed: no buttons, pointer movement or scroll when it has the mouse, no keys or characters when it has the keyboard. Touch Touch is a finger on the screen: which one, and where, in layout pixels. type Touch struct { Finger int64 X, Y float64 } TouchPointer TouchPointer turns fingers into the pointer every interface already understands: one finger down moves the cursor and presses the left button, lifting it releases the button. A second finger lets the pointer go: two fingers are a gesture (pinch, twist), not a click or a drag; the pointer comes back with the next finger down once all are lifted. Positions come in screen pixels and go to the state in layout pixels, divided by the screen's scale; every finger is also in the state's touches. type TouchPointer struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (pointer *TouchPointer) Begin(state *State, finger int64, x, y, scale float32) Begin puts a finger down: the first becomes the pointer, a second lets it go. func (pointer *TouchPointer) Cancel(state *State) Cancel lets go of every finger, when the system takes the gesture over (a swipe from the screen's edge): the button is released, so nothing stays pressed. func (pointer *TouchPointer) End(state *State, finger int64, x, y, scale float32) End lifts a finger: lifting the pointer's is a click where it was. func (pointer *TouchPointer) Move(state *State, finger int64, x, y, scale float32) Move follows a finger; the pointer follows its own. TwoFingers TwoFingers follows a gesture of two fingers from one step to the next: how much they spread (pinch), turned (twist) and moved together (pan). type TwoFingers struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (follower *TwoFingers) Step(state *State) (Gesture, bool) Step reads the state's touches and returns the gesture since the last step; false when there are not exactly two fingers, or they just came down (a gesture starts at the next step). ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py
