sections.text: From a pixel to the ground

the-quest/editing-with-the-pointer.text: Lesson 5: editing with the pointer Until now the program decided everything and the person only watched. In this lesson the island becomes something you edit : a click on the ground plants a tree there. You learn viewer.Edit , the input state , and how to find the point of the world under the pointer. Mission Pieces Time Trees planted where you click viewer.Edit , input.State , View.PointOnGround 20 min The idea A laser pointer in a dark room: the dot lands on whatever the beam meets first. The viewer shoots that beam from the camera through the pixel under the mouse and tells you where it meets the ground: that is where the tree goes. viewer.Edit instead of viewer.Run viewer.Run is for programs that change the scene on their own (a simulation). viewer.Edit is for programs that change it in answer to the person : a level editor, a floor-plan designer. Its function looks like an update function, with one more argument: type EditFunc func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64, view viewer.View) state is the keyboard and the mouse at this step. view is the camera that drew the frame the person is looking at, and the window's size: what is needed to turn a pixel into a place. Edit also keeps drawing on demand : while nothing happens the window sleeps and uses no processor. Our lamp turns all the time, so it asks for the next frame at every step with state.RequestFrame(0) . A program that animates only now and then asks only then. The input state input.State is a snapshot of this step, the same on every platform: To know Ask Is a key or button held? state.Down(input.KeyW) , state.Button(input.MouseLeft) Did it go down or up during this step? state.Pressed(key) , state.ButtonPressed(button) , state.ButtonReleased(button) Where is the pointer, and how far did it move? state.CursorX , CursorY , CursorDeltaX , CursorDeltaY (window pixels) A double click? state.Clicks(input.MouseLeft) == 2 What was typed? state.TypedText() (after the keyboard layout: «ñ» is one character) The wheel? state.ScrollDelta Fingers on a touch screen? state.Touches() ; the first finger is also the pointer A drag that turns the camera also ends with the button let go. To tell a click from the end of a drag, check that the pointer did not move on that step: // clicked tells whether the left button was let go without the pointer moving: a click, not // the end of a drag that turned the camera. func clicked(state *input.State) bool { return state.ButtonReleased(input.MouseLeft) && state.CursorDeltaX == 0 && state.CursorDeltaY == 0 } From a pixel to the ground view.PointOnGround(x, y) follows the ray from the camera through a pixel until it meets a walkable mesh, and returns that point with its true height; view.PointOnPlane(x, y, height) does the same with a flat floor. They work with every camera: the orbit, walking, and the maps (press M ), where clicking is easiest. angle := 0.0 edit := func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64, view viewer.View) { angle += step * 1.5 lamp.Transform = graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 8, 0, 1}).Multiply(graphics.RotateY(angle)) state.RequestFrame(0) // the lamp never stops, so ask for the next frame now if !clicked(state) { return } point, onGround := view.PointOnGround(state.CursorX, state.CursorY) if !onGround { return } plant(forest.Instances, point[0], point[1], point[2], 1) world.Overlay.Header[0].Text = treeCount(forest.Instances) world.Overlay.AddNotice("sprout", "A tree was planted", graphics.Vector{0.3, 0.7, 0.3, 1}) } if err := viewer.Edit(world, options, "Island", edit); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } The island on the map (M): click anywhere on it to plant a tree 📝 Interfaces and the camera. When a panel is under the pointer, the camera should not turn while you drag a slider in it. An interface claims the mouse ( state.ClaimMouse() ) and the viewer then gives its cameras state.Unclaimed() , a copy without it. Go UI does this for you. view can also move the cameras: view.FrameGround(minimumX, minimumZ, maximumX, maximumZ) shows a rectangle of ground whole, and view.ZoomBy(2) comes twice as close, as zoom buttons would. Checkpoint On the map ( M ), a click on the island plants a tree there, the header counts one more and A tree was planted appears; a drag still moves the map without planting. Achievement unlocked: Gardener What you learnt viewer.Edit is for programs that change the scene in answer to the person, and it draws on demand; state.RequestFrame asks for frames while something moves. input.State tells what is held and what happened during the step. view.PointOnGround turns the pointer into a point of the world. Bonus (optional) Let a right click take away the tree nearest to the pointer, if it is within two metres. The whole program Everything from the five lessons, in one file: // Command island is the go-renderer tutorial's program: a lighthouse on an island, a forest that // sways, the sea, labels, and trees planted where you click. package main import ( "flag" "fmt" "log" "math" "math/rand/v2" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/draw2d" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/graphics" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/input" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/scene" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/viewer" ) func main() { options := viewer.DefaultOptions() options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) // -capture, -night, -walk and the rest flag.Parse() world := scene.New() // Lesson 1: a hill and a tower on it. island := &scene.Node{Name: "island", Transform: graphics.Identity(), Mesh: hill(60, 4)} tower := &scene.Node{ Name: "lighthouse", Transform: graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 4, 0, 1}), Mesh: box(2, 8, 2, graphics.Vector{0.9, 0.9, 0.85, 1}), } world.Nodes = append(world.Nodes, island, tower) // Lesson 2: a lamp on top of the tower, and a forest. lamp := &scene.Node{ Name: "lamp", Transform: graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 8, 0, 1}), Mesh: box(3, 0.5, 0.5, graphics.Vector{1, 0.85, 0.3, 1}), } tower.Children = append(tower.Children, lamp) forest := &scene.Node{ Name: "forest", Transform: graphics.Identity(), Mesh: cone(1, 3, graphics.Vector{0.2, 0.45, 0.2, 1}), Instances: &scene.Instances{}, } world.Nodes = append(world.Nodes, forest) plantForest(world, forest.Instances, 300) // Lesson 3: the sea, fog, wind and clouds; the lamp glows and the trees sway. lamp.Mesh.Material.Kind = scene.GlowKind forest.Mesh.Material.Sway = 0.3 world.Environment.Water = &scene.Water{ Level: 1, Size: 2000, Shallow: graphics.Vector{0.1, 0.5, 0.55, 1}, Deep: graphics.Vector{0.02, 0.12, 0.25, 1}, } world.Environment.FogColor = graphics.Vector{0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 1} world.Environment.FogNear, world.Environment.FogFar = 80, 400 world.Environment.Wind = scene.Wind{Direction: graphics.Vector{1, 0, 0.3, 0}, Strength: 0.5} sky := scene.DefaultSky() sky.Clouds = scene.Clouds{Coverage: 0.4, Color: graphics.Vector{1, 1, 1, 1}, Speed: 0.01, Scale: 1} world.Environment.Sky = sky // Lesson 4: a label over the lighthouse, a header, a notice and a card of our own. world.Overlay.AddLabel(&scene.Label{Node: tower, Height: 9, Icon: "lightbulb", Text: "North Point", Badge: "lit"}) world.Overlay.Header = []scene.HeaderLine{{Icon: "trees", Text: treeCount(forest.Instances)}} world.Overlay.AddNotice("anchor", "A boat came in", graphics.Vector{}) card := &draw2d.List{} world.Overlay.Drawing = card drawWindCard(card, world.Environment.Wind.Strength) // Lesson 5: the lamp turns, and a click on the ground plants a tree. angle := 0.0 edit := func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64, view viewer.View) { angle += step * 1.5 lamp.Transform = graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 8, 0, 1}).Multiply(graphics.RotateY(angle)) state.RequestFrame(0) // the lamp never stops, so ask for the next frame now if !clicked(state) { return } point, onGround := view.PointOnGround(state.CursorX, state.CursorY) if !onGround { return } plant(forest.Instances, point[0], point[1], point[2], 1) world.Overlay.Header[0].Text = treeCount(forest.Instances) world.Overlay.AddNotice("sprout", "A tree was planted", graphics.Vector{0.3, 0.7, 0.3, 1}) } if err := viewer.Edit(world, options, "Island", edit); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // clicked tells whether the left button was let go without the pointer moving: a click, not // the end of a drag that turned the camera. func clicked(state *input.State) bool { return state.ButtonReleased(input.MouseLeft) && state.CursorDeltaX == 0 && state.CursorDeltaY == 0 } // plantForest plants trees at random places on the hill, above the shore and away from the tower. func plantForest(world *scene.Scene, forest *scene.Instances, count int) { random := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2)) // the same forest every run for range count { x, z := random.Float32()*50-25, random.Float32()*50-25 height, onGround := world.GroundHeight(x, z) if !onGround || height < 1 || math.Hypot(float64(x), float64(z)) < 6 { continue } plant(forest, x, height, z, 0.7+random.Float32()*0.6) } } // plant adds a tree of a size to the forest, standing at a point. func plant(forest *scene.Instances, x, y, z, size float32) { placement := graphics.FromTranslationRotationScale( graphics.Vector{x, y, z, 1}, // where graphics.Vector{0, 0, 0, 1}, // no rotation (a quaternion) graphics.Vector{size, size, size, 1}, // how big ) forest.Transforms = append(forest.Transforms, placement) forest.Colors = append(forest.Colors, graphics.Vector{1, 1, 1, 1}) // white keeps the mesh's colour forest.Dirty = true // added one: upload them all again } func treeCount(forest *scene.Instances) string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d trees", len(forest.Transforms)) } // drawWindCard paints a card in the bottom-left corner with the wind's strength. func drawWindCard(drawing *draw2d.List, strength float32) { drawing.Reset() card := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 16, Y: 380, Width: 180, Height: 52} drawing.Shadow(card, 12, 10, 3, draw2d.MustHex("#00000040")) drawing.Rectangle(card, 12, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff"), draw2d.Transparent, 0) drawing.Icon("wind", card.X+14, card.Y+14, 24, draw2d.MustHex("#3b6ea5")) drawing.Text("Wind", card.X+50, card.Y+22, 13, draw2d.Bold, draw2d.MustHex("#1f2933")) drawing.Text(fmt.Sprintf("strength %.1f", strength), card.X+50, card.Y+40, 12, draw2d.Regular, draw2d.MustHex("#52606d")) } // hill is a round island: a grid of side × side cells, highest in the middle and under the sea at // its edges. Its surface is ground, so the walker and GroundHeight find it. func hill(side int, height float32) *scene.Mesh { mesh := &scene.Mesh{ Name: "hill", Ground: true, Material: &scene.Material{ Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: graphics.Vector{0.45, 0.6, 0.3, 1}, Pattern: scene.PatternGrass, PatternScale: 1, }, } half := float32(side) / 2 for row := 0; row <= side; row++ { for column := 0; column <= side; column++ { x, z := float32(column)-half, float32(row)-half distance := math.Hypot(float64(x), float64(z)) / float64(half) // 0 in the middle, 1 at the edge y := height * float32(math.Cos(math.Min(distance, 1.3)*math.Pi/2)) mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, x, y, z) } } for row := range side { for column := range side { corner := uint32(row*(side+1) + column) below := corner + uint32(side+1) mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, corner, below, corner+1, corner+1, below, below+1) } } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } // box is a box standing on the origin: width along x, height up y, depth along z. Each face has // vertices of its own, so its normals stay flat and its edges sharp. func box(width, height, depth float32, color graphics.Vector) *scene.Mesh { x, z := width/2, depth/2 corners := [8][3]float32{ {-x, 0, -z}, {x, 0, -z}, {x, 0, z}, {-x, 0, z}, // bottom {-x, height, -z}, {x, height, -z}, {x, height, z}, {-x, height, z}, // top } faces := [6][4]int{{0, 1, 2, 3}, {7, 6, 5, 4}, {3, 2, 6, 7}, {1, 0, 4, 5}, {2, 1, 5, 6}, {0, 3, 7, 4}} mesh := &scene.Mesh{Name: "box", Material: &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: color}} for _, face := range faces { first := uint32(len(mesh.Positions) / 3) for _, corner := range face { mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, corners[corner][:]...) } mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, first, first+1, first+2, first, first+2, first+3) } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } // cone is a tree: a cone of a radius and a height standing on the origin. func cone(radius, height float32, color graphics.Vector) *scene.Mesh { const sides = 8 mesh := &scene.Mesh{Name: "tree", Material: &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: color}} mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, 0, height, 0) // the tip for side := range sides { angle := float64(side) / sides * 2 * math.Pi mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, radius*float32(math.Cos(angle)), 0, radius*float32(math.Sin(angle))) } for side := range uint32(sides) { mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, 0, 1+(side+1)%sides, 1+side) } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } ← Lesson 4 · Lesson 6: scenes from files →

the-quest/labels-and-the-overlay.title: Lesson 4: labels and the overlay
the-quest/labels-and-the-overlay.text: Lesson 4: labels and the overlay A 3D view often needs words: the name of a place, the time, a message that something happened. In this lesson you put a label over the lighthouse, a header in the corner, a notice that fades, and a small card drawn with draw2d , Go Renderer's flat drawing. Mission Pieces Time Names and messages on screen Overlay , labels, the header, notices, draw2d 15 min The idea A map in a museum has little cards on it: a name pinned over each thing, a title in the corner, and the guide's latest news. The overlay is that glass over the scene: it stays the same size however close you come. All of it lives in world.Overlay , drawn over the scene in screen space: it stays the same size however far the camera is, and costs one draw call. A label over the lighthouse world.Overlay.AddLabel(&scene.Label{ Node: tower, // follows the tower, and hides with it Height: 9, // metres above the tower's origin: just over the lamp Icon: "lightbulb", // any Lucide icon by name: https://lucide.dev/icons Text: "North Point", Badge: "lit", // a short word in a pill under the label }) A label without a Node stands at a Point of the world instead. Keep the pointer to change it later ( label.Text = "…" , label.Hidden = true ) or remove it ( world.Overlay.RemoveLabel ). The header and notices The header is a few lines pinned to the top-left corner: a clock, a count, a status. A notice is a short message under it that fades after six seconds ( Overlay.NoticeDuration ), newest first: world.Overlay.Header = []scene.HeaderLine{{Icon: "trees", Text: treeCount(forest.Instances)}} world.Overlay.AddNotice("anchor", "A boat came in", graphics.Vector{}) // a zero tint: the text's colour func treeCount(forest *scene.Instances) string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d trees", len(forest.Transforms)) } 💡 Without code. A glTF file can carry labels too: a node with "label" , "icon" or "badge" in its extras gets one, and "pinned": 1 makes it a line of the header instead ( glTF extras ). Drawing your own: draw2d Labels and notices are fixed shapes. For anything else, Overlay.Drawing takes a draw2d.List : rounded rectangles, soft shadows, lines of text, icons and pictures, in layout pixels from the window's top-left corner (the renderer multiplies them on a high-density screen, so text stays sharp). It is the same list Go UI fills with its panels and buttons. card := &draw2d.List{} world.Overlay.Drawing = card drawWindCard(card, world.Environment.Wind.Strength) // drawWindCard paints a card in the bottom-left corner with the wind's strength. func drawWindCard(drawing *draw2d.List, strength float32) { drawing.Reset() card := draw2d.Rectangle{X: 16, Y: 380, Width: 180, Height: 52} drawing.Shadow(card, 12, 10, 3, draw2d.MustHex("#00000040")) // before what casts it drawing.Rectangle(card, 12, draw2d.MustHex("#ffffff"), draw2d.Transparent, 0) drawing.Icon("wind", card.X+14, card.Y+14, 24, draw2d.MustHex("#3b6ea5")) drawing.Text("Wind", card.X+50, card.Y+22, 13, draw2d.Bold, draw2d.MustHex("#1f2933")) drawing.Text(fmt.Sprintf("strength %.1f", strength), card.X+50, card.Y+40, 12, draw2d.Regular, draw2d.MustHex("#52606d")) } Text takes the baseline , the line letters sit on, not the top of the text. Later commands cover earlier ones; SetLayer puts what follows on a higher layer, and PushClip cuts it to a rectangle. To redraw the card when the wind changes, call drawWindCard again from the update function: Reset keeps the list's memory, so a frame allocates nothing. Labels, the header, a notice and the wind card over the island 📝 Buttons? draw2d paints; it does not know about the mouse. For panels, buttons, fields and lists that react, use Go UI , which fills this same list. Checkpoint North Point floats over the lighthouse with a lit badge, the header counts the trees, A boat came in fades after six seconds, and the wind card sits in the bottom-left corner. Achievement unlocked: Herald What you learnt Overlay draws in screen space over the scene: labels, a header, notices and a free drawing. Labels follow a node or stand at a point; notices fade on their own. draw2d.List paints rectangles, shadows, text, icons and pictures in layout pixels. Bonus (optional) Keep the header honest: add a second line that says whether it is day or night, and update it at every step. ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 5: editing with the pointer →

the-quest/light-sky-and-water.title: Lesson 3: light, sky and water
the-quest/light-sky-and-water.text: Lesson 3: light, sky and water So far the island floats in grey. In this lesson you fill scene.Environment : the sea around it, fog in the distance, wind in the trees, clouds, and the night, with a lamp that glows in it. Mission Pieces Time The sea, the wind, clouds and the night scene.Environment , Water , Sky , GlowKind 15 min The idea The scene's weather report : one struct says where the sun is, how far the fog reaches, how high the sea comes and which way the wind blows. There is no clock in it: the sun's height is the time of day , as a sundial reads it. The environment Everything that is not a node lives in world.Environment : the sun, the sky, fog, water, wind, snow and the season's tint on leaves. scene.New() starts from scene.DefaultEnvironment() , a clear afternoon; you change only what you need. The sea Water is an endless animated plane at a height. It is coloured by how deep the water is over the ground below it, so the shore shines turquoise and the open sea turns dark blue on its own: world.Environment.Water = &scene.Water{ Level: 1, // one metre above zero: the hill's edges go under Size: 2000, // how far the plane reaches Shallow: graphics.Vector{0.1, 0.5, 0.55, 1}, Deep: graphics.Vector{0.02, 0.12, 0.25, 1}, } Fog and wind world.Environment.FogColor = graphics.Vector{0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 1} world.Environment.FogNear, world.Environment.FogFar = 80, 400 // FogFar 0 means no fog world.Environment.Wind = scene.Wind{Direction: graphics.Vector{1, 0, 0.3, 0}, Strength: 0.5} The wind moves the clouds and bends every material with a Sway . Plants are modelled with their base at the origin and a height of one; the higher a vertex, the more it bends: forest.Mesh.Material.Sway = 0.3 Clouds scene.Sky describes the sky over a whole day: stars, a moon with phases, clouds, constellations, or pictures (a skybox). Start from Earth's: sky := scene.DefaultSky() sky.Clouds = scene.Clouds{Coverage: 0.4, Color: graphics.Vector{1, 1, 1, 1}, Speed: 0.01, Scale: 1} world.Environment.Sky = sky The island in the sea in the evening light, the forest's shadows long Day and night There is no clock in the renderer: the sun's height is the time of day . Above the horizon it is day, near it twilight, below it night, when the moon lights the scene and the stars turn about the pole. Environment.SunDirection points towards the sun; the viewer's keys I K J L move it and N jumps between day and night, and the flags -night , -sun-elevation and -sun-azimuth start there. A lighthouse should shine at night. A glowing material is lit like any other by day and shows its own colour in the dark: lamp.Mesh.Material.Kind = scene.GlowKind go run . -night The island at night, the lamp glowing yellow on the dark tower Lamps that light around them A glowing lamp shows itself, but lights nothing around it. A point light does: it shines from a point all around, full within its inner radius and fading smoothly to nothing at its outer one, and lights the lit materials it reaches, besides the sun and the sky: world.Lights = []scene.PointLight{{ Position: graphics.Vector{2, 3.2, 0, 1}, // the lamp, at the top of the tower Color: graphics.Vector{1, 0.85, 0.5, 1.5}, // warm, at one and a half times (alpha is the intensity) Inner: 0.5, Outer: 6, }} How many? As many as the scene wants, but each draw takes at most the four nearest whose reach meets it ( MaxLightsPerDraw in the module's internal/sceneplan ), chosen once a frame on the processor, so the shaders stay short on every platform: this is what Unity's and Godot's forward renderers do on phones. Lamps far apart can light a whole village; four lamps piled on one small thing are as many as it shows. Move a lamp by changing its position between frames. The 3DS bakes the lamps into its colours with the sun (its guide). Material kinds Kind Shading LitKind Sun or moon, sky light, point lights, shadows, fog: most things UnlitKind Its colour as it is (plus fog): flags, markers, things that should not darken GlowKind Lit by day, shining in the dark: lamps, windows, glowing flowers WaterKind An animated water surface: a river or a lake above the sea's level WaterfallKind Translucent falling water Checkpoint The hill rises out of a sea, turquoise at the shore and dark further out; the trees sway; with -night , the lamp glows yellow over the dark island. Achievement unlocked: Weatherman What you learnt Environment holds the sun, the sky, fog, water, wind and snow. The sun's height is the time of day; the night comes with the moon and the stars. Sway bends plants in the wind; GlowKind shines at night; Lights light around them. Bonus (optional) Give the island a winter: snow above two and a half metres, fading in over half a metre, and foliage turned a little brown. ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 4: labels and the overlay →

the-quest/making-things-move.title: Lesson 2: making things move
the-quest/making-things-move.text: Lesson 2: making things move A lighthouse needs a lamp that turns, and an island needs trees. In this lesson you learn the update function , how a child node follows its parent, and how instancing draws three hundred trees for the price of one. Mission Pieces Time A lamp that turns, and a forest the update function, child nodes, Instances 15 min The idea A clockmaker sets the hands on the dial, and the dial on the clock: move the clock and the hands go with it. A child node is a hand on its parent's dial. And a forest is a rubber stamp : one tree, stamped three hundred times, each copy in its own place. The update function viewer.Run 's fourth argument is a function the viewer calls at a fixed step , sixty times a second whatever the frame rate, before it draws: type UpdateFunc func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64) step is the time since the last call, in seconds (always the same, 1/60). Changing the scene inside it is safe: it runs on the same goroutine as the drawing, so there is nothing to lock. A child node The lamp is a flat bar on top of the tower. As a child of the tower it takes the tower's transform first, so its own Translate is measured from the tower's foot: lamp := &scene.Node{ Name: "lamp", Transform: graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 8, 0, 1}), // eight metres up the tower Mesh: box(3, 0.5, 0.5, graphics.Vector{1, 0.85, 0.3, 1}), } tower.Children = append(tower.Children, lamp) Turning it is a new transform at every step: angle := 0.0 turnLamp := func(world *scene.Scene, state *input.State, step float64) { angle += step * 1.5 // radians per second lamp.Transform = graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 8, 0, 1}).Multiply(graphics.RotateY(angle)) } if err := viewer.Run(world, options, "Island", turnLamp); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } Moving a node costs nothing to upload: only its matrix changes. Move the tower and the lamp goes with it. 📝 When does the viewer draw? Without an update function it draws on demand : only while you move the camera or a key is held, and sleeps in between. With one, it draws every frame, since a program that animates may change anything at any step. A forest with instancing Three hundred nodes of three hundred meshes would be three hundred draw calls. A node with instances draws one mesh many times in a single call, each copy with its own transform and tint: forest := &scene.Node{ Name: "forest", Transform: graphics.Identity(), Mesh: cone(1, 3, graphics.Vector{0.2, 0.45, 0.2, 1}), Instances: &scene.Instances{}, } world.Nodes = append(world.Nodes, forest) plantForest(world, forest.Instances, 300) The tree is a cone: // cone is a tree: a cone of a radius and a height standing on the origin. func cone(radius, height float32, color graphics.Vector) *scene.Mesh { const sides = 8 mesh := &scene.Mesh{Name: "tree", Material: &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: color}} mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, 0, height, 0) // the tip for side := range sides { angle := float64(side) / sides * 2 * math.Pi mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, radius*float32(math.Cos(angle)), 0, radius*float32(math.Sin(angle))) } for side := range uint32(sides) { mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, 0, 1+(side+1)%sides, 1+side) } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } Each tree is a transform built from a position, a rotation (a quaternion; {0, 0, 0, 1} is none) and a scale, and a colour that multiplies the mesh's own (white leaves it as it is): // plant adds a tree of a size to the forest, standing at a point. func plant(forest *scene.Instances, x, y, z, size float32) { placement := graphics.FromTranslationRotationScale( graphics.Vector{x, y, z, 1}, // where graphics.Vector{0, 0, 0, 1}, // no rotation (a quaternion) graphics.Vector{size, size, size, 1}, // how big ) forest.Transforms = append(forest.Transforms, placement) forest.Colors = append(forest.Colors, graphics.Vector{1, 1, 1, 1}) // white keeps the mesh's colour forest.Dirty = true // added one: upload them all again } The forest is planted where the hill is above the shore, and not on the lighthouse's doorstep, so of three hundred tries a little over two hundred grow: // plantForest plants trees at random places on the hill, above the shore and away from the tower. func plantForest(world *scene.Scene, forest *scene.Instances, count int) { random := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2)) // the same forest every run for range count { x, z := random.Float32()*50-25, random.Float32()*50-25 height, onGround := world.GroundHeight(x, z) if !onGround || height < 1 || math.Hypot(float64(x), float64(z)) < 6 { continue } plant(forest, x, height, z, 0.7+random.Float32()*0.6) } } The lamp on top of the tower, among the trees Telling the renderer what changed The renderer uploads meshes and instances to the graphics card once. When you change them later, say so, or it keeps drawing the old ones: You changed Do A node's Transform or Hidden Nothing: read every frame Instances added, removed, or most of them moved instances.Dirty = true A few instances instances.MarkChanged(3, 17) : only those are uploaded A mesh's positions, colours or indices mesh.Dirty = true A walkable mesh Also world.InvalidateGround() , so GroundHeight sees it Forests of a hundred thousand trees stay fast: instances are kept in cells, cells out of sight are skipped, and a mesh with simpler versions ( Mesh.Details ) uses them far away ( architecture ). Checkpoint The lamp on top of the tower turns, about a turn every four seconds, and a forest of cones covers the hill but not the tower's doorstep. Achievement unlocked: Clockmaker What you learnt The update function runs at a fixed step on the drawing goroutine: change the scene there. Children inherit their parent's transform. Instancing draws one mesh many times; Dirty and MarkChanged tell the renderer what changed. Bonus (optional) Make the trees different: tint each a slightly different green, and turn each about its trunk by a random angle. ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 3: light, sky and water →

the-quest/meshes-and-nodes.title: Lesson 1: meshes and nodes

sections.text: A mesh is a list of triangles

the-quest/meshes-and-nodes.text: Lesson 1: meshes and nodes In this lesson you build the ground of the island, a hill, and stand a tower on it. You learn what a mesh is made of and how a node places it. Mission Pieces Time A tower on a hill scene.Mesh , scene.Node , materials, viewer.Run 15 min The idea A mesh is a tent made of triangles : a list of poles (the vertices) and which three of them hold up each piece of cloth (the indices). The node is where you pitch the tent : a position, a turn and a size. Build the tent once; pitch it anywhere, as often as you like. Coordinates Go Renderer's world has y up . The ground lies in the x–z plane, and north is towards −z (the viewer's map shows it at the top). Units are whatever you decide: in this tutorial one unit is a metre, so the tower is eight metres tall. A mesh is a list of triangles A scene.Mesh keeps its numbers in flat slices, the way the graphics card wants them: Field Holds Example Positions x, y, z of every vertex, one after another {0,0,0, 1,0,0, 0,0,1} is three vertices Indices Three vertex numbers per triangle (optional: without them, every three vertices are one) {0, 2, 1} Normals The direction each vertex faces, for the light Filled by ComputeNormals() Colors r, g, b, a per vertex (optional) Multiplied with the material's colour Material How the surface is shaded &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: …} Ground Whether people can walk on it true for the hill Triangles are counter-clockwise when seen from the side they face : the order of the three indices decides which side is the front. Get it backwards and the light falls on the wrong side (or Material.DoubleSided shades both). The hill A grid of squares, each made of two triangles, whose height falls from the middle to the edge: // hill is a round island: a grid of side × side cells, highest in the middle and under the sea at // its edges. Its surface is ground, so the walker and GroundHeight find it. func hill(side int, height float32) *scene.Mesh { mesh := &scene.Mesh{ Name: "hill", Ground: true, Material: &scene.Material{ Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: graphics.Vector{0.45, 0.6, 0.3, 1}, Pattern: scene.PatternGrass, PatternScale: 1, }, } half := float32(side) / 2 for row := 0; row <= side; row++ { for column := 0; column <= side; column++ { x, z := float32(column)-half, float32(row)-half distance := math.Hypot(float64(x), float64(z)) / float64(half) // 0 in the middle, 1 at the edge y := height * float32(math.Cos(math.Min(distance, 1.3)*math.Pi/2)) mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, x, y, z) } } for row := range side { for column := range side { corner := uint32(row*(side+1) + column) below := corner + uint32(side+1) mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, corner, below, corner+1, corner+1, below, below+1) } } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } ComputeNormals works out smooth normals from the triangles, so the hill is shaded as one rounded surface. PatternGrass mottles its colour from the world position, with no texture to load; the other patterns are cobbles, masonry, plaster, shingles and planks. The tower A box needs sharp edges, so each face gets vertices of its own (a shared corner would have one normal, halfway between two faces, and the box would look like a blurred pebble): // box is a box standing on the origin: width along x, height up y, depth along z. Each face has // vertices of its own, so its normals stay flat and its edges sharp. func box(width, height, depth float32, color graphics.Vector) *scene.Mesh { x, z := width/2, depth/2 corners := [8][3]float32{ {-x, 0, -z}, {x, 0, -z}, {x, 0, z}, {-x, 0, z}, // bottom {-x, height, -z}, {x, height, -z}, {x, height, z}, {-x, height, z}, // top } faces := [6][4]int{{0, 1, 2, 3}, {7, 6, 5, 4}, {3, 2, 6, 7}, {1, 0, 4, 5}, {2, 1, 5, 6}, {0, 3, 7, 4}} mesh := &scene.Mesh{Name: "box", Material: &scene.Material{Kind: scene.LitKind, BaseColor: color}} for _, face := range faces { first := uint32(len(mesh.Positions) / 3) for _, corner := range face { mesh.Positions = append(mesh.Positions, corners[corner][:]...) } mesh.Indices = append(mesh.Indices, first, first+1, first+2, first, first+2, first+3) } mesh.ComputeNormals() return mesh } A node places a mesh A mesh is drawn where a scene.Node puts it. The node's Transform is a 4×4 matrix: move it with graphics.Translate , turn it with graphics.RotateY (or RotateX , Rotate about any axis), size it with graphics.Scale , and combine them with Multiply . The hill is four metres high in the middle, so the tower stands at y = 4 : func main() { options := viewer.DefaultOptions() options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) // -capture, -night, -walk and the rest flag.Parse() world := scene.New() island := &scene.Node{Name: "island", Transform: graphics.Identity(), Mesh: hill(60, 4)} tower := &scene.Node{ Name: "lighthouse", Transform: graphics.Translate(graphics.Vector{0, 4, 0, 1}), Mesh: box(2, 8, 2, graphics.Vector{0.9, 0.9, 0.85, 1}), } world.Nodes = append(world.Nodes, island, tower) if err := viewer.Run(world, options, "Island", nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } 📝 Vector 's fourth number. A point has 1 there and a direction 0: a translation moves points but not directions. Colours use it as opacity. options.RegisterFlags gives your program every flag of the viewer for free: try go run . -walk , go run . -map or go run . -capture island.png . A white tower on a green hill Checkpoint A cream tower stands on a green hill, its shadow on the grass. Press Tab and walk round it, at eye height on the hill. Achievement unlocked: Mason What you learnt A mesh is positions and indices, counter-clockwise from the front, with normals for the light. A material says how it is shaded; Pattern adds surface detail with no texture. A node places a mesh with a matrix; Ground: true makes it walkable. Bonus (optional) Put a small house beside the tower: a box 3 m wide, 2.5 m tall and 4 m deep, painted in planks, four metres east of it and turned 30°. ← Tutorial · Lesson 2: making things move →

sections.text: Carrying the scene inside the program

the-quest/scenes-from-files.text: Lesson 6: scenes from files Building meshes in Go is good for learning and for things a program generates. Real islands are modelled in a 3D editor, or built from a map by a tool. In this lesson you load a glTF file, add the renderer's own information to it through extras , and carry the scene inside the program. Mission Pieces Time The island from a file loaders.LoadScene , extras, ReadScene 10 min The idea glTF is a shipping container for 3D : every tool packs it the same way, so the renderer can unload one from anyone. What the standard boxes have no room for (the tide, the walkable ground, a label) travels in the extras , a note taped to each box. glTF in one paragraph glTF 2.0 is the open format for 3D scenes: nodes, meshes and materials, in a .gltf (JSON beside its binary buffers) or a single .glb . Blender exports it ( File → Export → glTF 2.0 ), and so does Go Scene Builder, which turns a 2D map and a relief into a whole scene. Opening a file world, err := loaders.LoadScene("island.glb") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } viewer.Run(world, options, "Island", nil) That is the whole of cmd/visor , give or take its flags: go run ./cmd/visor island.glb opens any file without writing a line. The loader reads the node tree, positions, normals, vertex colours ( COLOR_0 ), indices, the base colour of materials with doubleSided and alphaMode , compressed attributes ( KHR_mesh_quantization ) and instancing ( EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing ). Textures are not read: colour comes from materials, vertex colours and the procedural patterns. Extras: what glTF cannot say glTF has no word for the tide, the walkable ground or a label. It lets any object carry free JSON, its extras , and Go Renderer reads its own there. In Blender, custom properties become extras when Include → Custom Properties is ticked in the exporter. On Extra Becomes The scene environment : sunDirection , fog , water , wind , sky , snow … world.Environment (lesson 3) A mesh, a primitive or a node "ground": true Mesh.Ground : walkable, found by GroundHeight A material "kind": "glow" , "sway": 0.3 , "pattern": "cobbles" , "patternScale": 0.5 Material.Kind , Sway , Pattern (lessons 1–3) A mesh "detail": [{"mesh": 3, "screenSize": 0.05}] Simpler versions drawn far away A node "label" , "icon" , "badge" , "label_color" , "pinned" A label, or a line of the header (lesson 4) A node's extras, all of them, are also in node.Tags , for your program's own data: a lighthouse's range, a building's owner. For example, a node exported like this: { "name": "harbour", "mesh": 0, "extras": { "label": "Harbour", "icon": "anchor", "berths": 12 } } gets a label with an anchor, and node.Tags["berths"] holds 12 (a float64 , as JSON numbers are). The full list is in glTF extras . Finding nodes A loaded scene is the same scene.Scene you built by hand, so everything in lessons 2 to 5 works on it. To animate a node, find it by name: func findNode(nodes []*scene.Node, name string) *scene.Node { for _, node := range nodes { if node.Name == name { return node } if found := findNode(node.Children, name); found != nil { return found } } return nil } lamp := findNode(world.Nodes, "lamp") Carrying the scene inside the program A program for a web page or a phone has no files beside it. Embed the .glb and read it from its bytes ( ReadScene takes any io.Reader ): //go:embed island.glb var islandFile []byte world, err := loaders.ReadScene(bytes.NewReader(islandFile)) The buffers must be inside the file, as a .glb 's are; a .gltf with separate .bin files needs LoadScene . Checkpoint go run ./cmd/visor island.glb opens a scene made elsewhere (Blender, Go Scene Builder), and its labels, sea and walkable ground come with it. Achievement unlocked: Librarian What you learnt loaders.LoadScene opens a .glb or .gltf ; ReadScene reads embedded bytes. Extras carry what glTF cannot: the environment, the ground, material kinds, labels. A loaded scene is an ordinary scene.Scene : find nodes by name and change them. Final challenge · Lighthouse keeper Back in lesson 5's program, build a second lighthouse on the island's eastern shore, shorter and red, with its own lamp turning the other way and its own label. Hint: the tower is another node with box ; the lamp a child of it; GroundHeight says where the shore's ground is; the edit function already turns one lamp and can turn two. Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge at night: North Point and the red East Light, both lamps glowing Rare achievement unlocked: Lighthouse keeper Well done Every achievement of the quest Where next You have used every part of Go Renderer a program usually needs. From here: Put an interface over the island : panels, buttons, sliders, with Go UI . Its own tutorial starts where this one ends. Run it elsewhere : in a web browser and on Android . Understand the inside : architecture , the overlay , and how a frame is planned and drawn. Look things up in the reference . ← Lesson 5 · Tutorial · Reference →

the-quest/the-quest.text: Tutorial: an island with a lighthouse The quest map: Mason, Clockmaker, Weatherman, Herald, Gardener, Librarian, then the final challenge, Lighthouse keeper In six short lessons you build one program, a step at a time: a hill rising out of the sea, a lighthouse whose lamp turns, a forest that sways in the wind, the sky by day and by night, labels over things, and trees you plant with a click. Each lesson adds a little to the program of the one before it and ends with something you can run. The island at the end of lesson 4: a lighthouse among trees, a label over it, a header, a notice and a card of the program's own Before you start , follow Get started : Go, a C compiler and Go Renderer cloned beside your module. Each lesson takes ten to twenty minutes. Every lesson has the same shape, as in a quest: the idea in everyday words, the code , a checkpoint to know it works, a bonus with its solution folded, and an achievement to unlock. A final challenge waits at the end of lesson 6. Lesson You learn You end with 1. Meshes and nodes Triangles, normals, materials, placing things with a transform A tower on a hill 2. Making things move The update function, children of a node, instancing a forest A lamp that turns, a forest 3. Light, sky and water The environment: sun, fog, sea, wind, clouds, the night, glowing materials An island in the sea, by day and by night 4. Labels and the overlay Labels over the world, the header, notices, free 2D drawing Names and messages on screen 5. Editing with the pointer viewer.Edit , the input state, finding the ground under the pointer Trees planted where you click 6. Scenes from files glTF, the renderer's extras, embedding a scene in the program The same island, made in another tool Every lesson closes with practice : a small change to try on your own, with a solution folded under it. The complete program is at the end of lesson 5. 💡 Captures. Every program built on viewer takes the viewer's flags. -capture shot.png draws one frame into a picture and exits, which is how the pictures in these lessons were made; -time 3 draws it as if three seconds had passed, so two captures can be compared. ← Get started · Lesson 1 →

troubleshooting.text: 🧰 Troubleshooting This page is for anyone whose build or window does not work. Find the message you see, and read the fix under it. Building fatal error: GL/gl.h, X11/Xlib.h or wayland-client.h: No such file or directory The window goes through GLFW, which cgo compiles from C. C needs the headers of OpenGL, X11 and Wayland, and Go needs a C compiler. On Debian or Ubuntu: sudo apt install gcc libgl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev Fedora's packages are in get started . The first build compiles GLFW, so it takes a minute; later ones are quick. cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found, or build constraints exclude all Go files cgo is off, or there is no C compiler. Install one ( gcc , or Xcode's command line tools on macOS with xcode-select --install ) and check that go env CGO_ENABLED prints 1 . Packages that need no window ( scene , draw2d , input , internal/sceneplan ) build without cgo. Only opengl , windowloop , viewer , metal and cmd/visor need it. Warnings on macOS: 'glClear' is deprecated, MTLStorageModeManaged is deprecated They are warnings, not errors: the program still builds and runs. OpenGL has been deprecated on macOS since 2018. Every OpenGL call warns when GLFW and go-gl compile. On a Mac, the viewer draws through Metal by default; see Metal . Metal : newer SDKs (macOS 27) mark MTLStorageModeManaged as deprecated. metal/flat_darwin.m and metal/scene_darwin.m use it for textures the processor writes. Replacing it is part of the proposal towards 1.0 . Opening a window VersionUnavailable or GLX: Failed to create context The renderer asks for OpenGL 4.1, core profile . The graphics driver offers less. Check what it offers: glxinfo -B | grep "core profile version" Update the driver, or use Mesa's software one ( LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 ), which gives 4.5 on any computer, slowly. In a virtual machine, turn on 3D acceleration. A blank or black window, or GLX extension not found, under Xvfb Xvfb is a display with no screen, for servers and CI. It draws OpenGL only through Mesa's GLX. Install Mesa's drivers, then try again: sudo apt install xvfb libgl1-mesa-dri xvfb-run go run ./cmd/visor -sample island -capture island.png -capture draws one frame into a picture and exits: no need to look at the window. On Wayland: the window has no title bar, or opens on X11 instead GLFW 3.4 can talk to Wayland directly: it prefers Wayland when WAYLAND_DISPLAY is set and its Wayland support was built, and X11 otherwise. Some Wayland desktops (GNOME among them) draw no title bar for such windows. To run under X11 through XWayland instead, unset the variable for one run: env -u WAYLAND_DISPLAY go run ./cmd/visor -sample island windowloop.not-on-main-thread: the window loop must run on the main thread Windows only receive their events on the program's first thread (macOS insists). Lock it in package main : func init() { runtime.LockOSThread() } Other platforms In a browser: build constraints exclude all Go files in …/opengl opengl , windowloop and viewer need GLFW, which does not exist in a browser. A web page uses browser and gles instead; see in a web browser . The CI vets every package a page can use with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm . Android: ld: cannot find -llog, or the app closes at once An Android program is a shared library built with the NDK's compiler for each architecture, with CGO_ENABLED=1 GOOS=android and -buildmode=c-shared . The whole command, and the 16 KB alignment recent phones need, are in on Android . The Nintendo 3DS: unknown target nintendo3ds The 3DS build needs a TinyGo with the nintendo3ds target (a separate fork, not upstream TinyGo) and devkitPro's libctru and citro3d. See on the Nintendo 3DS . Still stuck? Open an issue with the command you ran, the whole message, your system, and what go version and glxinfo -B print.
